HARVEY WARLOW
Grand Master

CHESTER HARVEY WARLOW
Grand Master
1947-1948

Chester Harvey Warlow, our 82nd Grand Master, was born in
Virginia, Cass County, Illinois, June 30, 1889. At the age of six months,
he was brought to Fresno, California, where he has resided continuously
with the exception of the years spent at school and wh-ile in the armed
forces of our country.
He was educated in the Fresno public schools and attended Kemper
Military Academy at Boonville, Missouri, from 1904 to 1906. He holds
the degrees of Bachelor of Arts and Doctor of Jurisprudence from
Leland Stanford, Jr. University as well as having attended Harvard
Law School.
Brother Warlow practiced law in Fresno from 1913 until 1930 at
which time he became Fresno Trust Officer of the Security First National Bank of Los Angeles. He served in that capacity until 1943 when
he retired from active business.
In addition to his legal work, Brother Warlow has certain oil interests and is President of both the Ward Oil Company and the Seneca
Oil Company. For many years, he has been a director and member of
the Executive Committee of Independent Oil Producers' Agency of
California.
Our brother has made an outstanding contribution to his state and
community in civic activities as evidenced by the following record:
President Fresno County Chamber of Commerce, 1929
Chairman Highway Committee San Joaquin Valley Council
California State Chamber of Commerce, 1929
Organizer and chairman San Joaquiil Valley State Wide Water
Committee, 1929-1938.
Director and co-organizer of Sierra National Parks Highway
Association, 1925-1940
Leader in Community development of Kings Canyon Highway,
Generals Highway and Fresno-Yosemite Highway
Member of California Highway Commission.
During World War I, he enlisted in the regular army on August
17, 1917 and soon thereafter was commissioned Second Lieutenant in
the Air Service and on June 15, 1918 was commissioned First Lieutenant.
His Masonic service is as varied and active as his civic and business
life. He was initiated into Fresno Lodge No. 247 F. & A. M. on December 30, 1921: Passed on February 3, 1922 and Raised to the Sublime

Degree of Master Mason on March 10, 1922. He served as Master of
Fresno Lodge in 1928. In 1929, he was appointed Inspector of the 61 st
Masonic District serving for two years. In 1934, he was appointed ·
Assistant Grand Lecturer and served until 1941 at which time he was
elevated to Grand Lecturer. This service continued until his election to
the office of Deputy Grand Master in October, 1946. On October 17,
1947, Brother Warlow was elected and installed Grand Master of
Masons in California.
In addition to his service to the Grand Lodge of California, he has
been an ardent worker in the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite of
Freemasonry in the Valley of Fresno. He received the 32° of that
rite on April 6, 1931 and on October 10, 1939 was elevated to Knight
Commander of the Court of Honor and on December 18, 1943 was
coroneted to 33° Mason. He served Fresno Lodge of Perfection as
Venerable Master in 1941.
His other affiliations are Fresno Rotary Club, American Legion and
University Sequoia Sunnyside Club.
On March 31, 1917, Brother Warlow was united in marriage to
Marion St. John, a native of Petaluma, California.
Throughout his entire life. Brother Warlow, or "Chet" as his host
of friends know him, has been a kindly. thoughtful and serious individual. Yet, on occasion, his dry humor and friendly smile have brought
happiness to many and have been the means of bringing peace and
harmony where dissension and disunity might have prevailed. His
wholesome philosophy of life and forthright purpose have done much
to bring to his brethren a sense of responsibility and a desire to follow
his inspiring leadership.
Student, philosopher. poet. lawyer, banker, geologist. public servant.
lover of nature-what a myriad of worlds to draw from! Is it any
wonder that we have taken him to our hearts?
"Chet's" entire outlook on life might be summed up in his favorite
expression: "Faith, hope and charity. but the greatest of these are
three good friends."

DEVOTIONAL SERVICES
"The Three Levels of Masonry"
Very Rev.]. M. Malloch, Grand Chaplain
You will be interested to know that the song "Give Unto the Lord,"
which has just been sung by Brother Sydney Charles, is an original
composition by our Grand Organist. He wrote to me some weeks ago
to ask if I thought an original composition by him would be in order and
fit into my program. I urged him to be as original as possible. We have
heard a piece of music never used before, and we can congratulate ourselves on having a Grand Organist who is a notable composer as well
as a very able interpreter of the works of others.
You will note that I am wearing a cassock of the Church. I am
wearing it with the Grand Master's permission and approval. Maybe
we should regard it as part of the Warlow Rite. It may start a tradition
of attire for Grand Chaplains.
I am going to speak to you this morning on The Three Levels of
Masonry.

9

The first level is Operative Masonry. In the broadest sense of the
term we are all Operative Masons. We work, we build, we earn our
living. We have very little use for the healthy man who fails to bear
his own economic load in the community. We work for three fundamental reasons:
1. To satisfy the urge to activity. We want to be doing something.
Work is a psychological necessity.
2. To earn a living for ourselves and our loved ones. Work is an
economic necessity.
3. To do our part in building the great temple of the economic
order. Work is a social necessity.
Masonry has always taught the nobility of labor. A Lodge from its
opening to its close is said to be at labor.
In the wide sense in which I am using the term, Operative Masonry
is the economic aspect of Speculative Masonry. It is symbolized in the
Craft by the Twenty-four Inch Gauge, which teaches us to divide our
time between service, work, and play. In the twenty-four hours of the
day, according to Masonry, we are to find "a part for the service of
God and a distressed worthy brother; a part for our usual vocations;
and a part for refreshment and repose.' (Monitor, page 5.)
It is the duty of a Mason to discipline himself to do good work in
his usual vocation, to show the industry the Bee Hive symbolizes, and
to take full responsibility for the service he renders in his business or
profession. "It might have pleased the Great Creator of heaven and
earth, to have made man independent of all other beings; but as dependence is one of the strongest bonds of society, mankind were made
dependent on each other for protection and security, as they thereby
enjoy better opportunities of fulfilling the duties of reciprocal love and
friendship." (Monitor, page 41.)
The complexity of modern life requires a throughgoing division of
labor and a consequential sense of full responsibility for good and
reliable work.
Build it well, whate'er ye do;
Build it strong and straight and true;
Build it clean and high and broad; ·
Build it for the Eye of God.
It is the duty of a Mason to take vital interest in the economic problems of his time. Our economic order is characterized by Big Business,
Big Labor, and Big Government. Our scientific, technological age makes
bigness in all three inevitable. One can't manufacture an automobile in
an old-time blacksmith shop or carry on modern medical research in a
corner drug store. Our scientific, machine civilization makes big industrial enterprises an absolute necessity. Big private enterprises in turn

10

11

result in a labor movement strong enough to secure for labor wages
large enough to guarantee an adequate buyer's market for big business
and a government wise enough to keep the two together in a balanced
economy. The problem is to solve the main problems arising out of the
inevitable complexity of this bigness. These problems are unemployment, excessively high prices, and the fluctuating economic cycle, and
they cannot be solved on the basis of doctrinaire political platforms.
It is the moral obligation of a Mason to seek for real solutions of-these
problems and not to succumb to political panaceas and propaganda.

Masons are not afraid of philosophy, of speculation. They believe
in thinking things through. This is not true of human beings in general.
Most people think that philosophy is a disease of words, a way of saying
in language which nobody can understand what everybody knows
anyway. William James, the great philosopher, met Josiah Royce,
almost equally great as a philosopher, on the campus of Harvard
University one day. "Royce, what is a philosopher?" asked James.
Royce, being a philosopher, passed the question back. "A philosopher;·
said James, "is a blind man looking in a dark room for a black cat that
isn't there" . . . "And what is a theologian?" he added. Again he
answered his own question, "A theologian is a fellow who thinks he has
found the cat." Masons take a more optimistic view of philosophy.
They accept the words of promise: "You will know the truth, and the
truth will make you free" (John 8:32). They agree with the poet:
Truth, crushed to earth, shall rise again;
The eternal years of God are hers;
But Error, wounded, withers in pain,
And dies among his worshippers.
-William Cullen Bryant

It is the duty of a Mason in our time to help recover the values of
leisure time. We need more time for refreshment and repose in our
social order. The pressure of modem life is breaking us down physically
and mentally. Our ancient brethren believed in working six days and
in resting on the seventh, for "in six days God created the heaven and
the earth, and rested on the seventh day." (Monitor, page 22.) We
need the Sabbath rest. God made man to work. He also made him to
rest. Evefy Sunday should be a day of rest and worship. It takes time
to be holy, as the familiar hymn suggests. The violation of Sunday is
the worst spiritual crime of modem times. Religion depends for its
vitality and health upon its holy days, and the greatest of these is
Sunday.
0 Sabbath rest by Galilee!
0 calm of hills above,
Where Jesus knelt to share with Thee
The Silence of eternity
Interpreted by love!
There can be no interpretation of life by love without Sabbath rest.
God does not cause the grass and the trees to toil all the year around.
He does not obliterate the seasons. He does not want men to toil ever
and rest never.

II.
The second fevel of Masonry is the Speculative. Speculative Masonry is the architecture of the soul, of life, of personality.
Build thee more stately mansions, 0 my soul,
As the swift seasons rolll
Leave thy low-vaulted past!
Let each new temple, nobler than the last,
Shut thee from heaven with a dome more vast,
Till thou at length art free,
Leaving thine outgrown shell by life's unresting sea!

-Oliver Wendell Holmes

The Masonic Craft is the most impressive of all fraternities, because
it has more philosophy as well as more history than any other. In terse
English, there is more to it.
Masonry is an Implemental Philosophy. It teaches by symbols,
ritual, initiation. It recognizes the fundamental psychological fact that
man is a body as well as a spirit, and that he can learn through the
use of his five senses. The tools of operative Masonry are the symbolic
implements by which the ideals of the Masonic life are imparted and
taught. Some of the tools recognized monitorially are the Lambskin
Apron, the Common Gavel, the Square, the Compass, the Level, the
Plumb, the Trestle Board, the Globes, and the Trowel.
Masonry is also Instrumental PhUosophy. This is exceedingly important. Masonic philosophy or speculation is the instrument or means
by which the Mason is led to great systems of_ truth. Masonry did not
originate its own principles and teachings and it does not exhaust them.
Masonry, as its reference to the Seven Liberal Arts and Sciences indicates, accepts the whole world of human knowledge and wisdom. It
believes in the accumulating knowledge of the experimental sciences,
in the wisrom of philosophy, and in all the creative arts. The President
of Harvard University divides the curriculum of education into these
three disciplines.
Masonry believes in religion. Some Masons affirm that the Lodge
gives them all the religion they need. That is their own conclusion from
or interpretation of the Masonry they have learned. It is not the offi-

13

cial creed of the Craft. Masonry may be all the religion a man has
(and he might have one worse). That it is all the religion he needs is
questionable.

of Samuel Johnson in his LIFE OF MILTON are still true: "To be
of no church is dangerous." (Ross Digest, Sections 815, 868, 869,
.870, 872).

Masonic Law states clearly and unequivocally that Masonry is
not a substitute for religion and that it was never designed to take
the place of religion. On the contrary, "as the handmaid of religion,
it may and often does, act as the vestibule that introduces its votaries
into the temple of divine truth." In other words, it is religiously as well
as educationally instrumental.

Masonic philosophy is practical. It is elementary, elemental, and
designed for immediate use. It summarizes in simple form the essentials
of ethics and morality. In one way or another, it teaches the ultimate
values of beauty, truth. and goodness. Keats wrote:
Beauty is truth, truth beauty,-that is all
Ye know on earth, and all ye need to know.
Masonry teaches the cardinal virtues of temperance, fortitude, prudence,
and justice: and the theological virtues of faith, hope, and love. "So
faith, hope, love abide, these three: but the greatest of these is love."
(I. Cor. 13:13).

Masonry requires belief in the existence of God as the Great
Architect of the universe but beyond this does not offer any definition
of the Supreme Being. Masonry requires that the "Book of the Law,"
the Spiritual Trestle Board, the Great Light, shall constitute an indispensible part of the furniture of every Lodge but does not determine
which volume shall be regarded as the sacred embodiment of the
"revealed will of God." It takes care, however, that the volume on the
altar shall be one about which the Mason concerned can say,
Here's a book whose wondrous pages
Guard the wisdom of the ages,
Here poised in azure deep, divine,
The stars of truth .forever shine.
Masonry insists on belief in a resurrection to a future life but presents
no blueprints of the Hereafter. It leaves all these undefined problems of
theology to the judgment of the individual or to the other institutions in
which he puts his trust. (Landmarks 19, 20, 21 ) .
The relationship of Masonry to organized religion is quite clear. It
is not officially in any sense in competition with organized religion.
Unlike the Church which seeks to save souls through the truth and
grace God has given her to dispense, Masonry supplies no scheme of
redemption from sin and makes no claim to be "the way. the truth,
and the life."
The first of the Fifteen Points of the Old York Constitutions of 926
required that every Mason should "frequent Holy Church." This is no
longer part of the Written Law of Masonry. The Law of California
Masonry states that Masonry holds that attendance at church is not
a Masonic duty. It is not too much to say. however, that the spirit of
Masonry leads to a recognition of organized religion in some formchurch, synagogue, mosque. or temple. To the truly Masonic mind,
religion is essential, and religion, like all other human interests, inevitably becomes organized. The Church, as John Henry Newman
said, is the "concrete representative of things invisible." In spite of
the confusion and mediocrity of our sectarian religious world, the words

Masonic philosophy names the areas of human responsibility: to
Self, to Neighbor, and to God. (Monitor, pages 17 and 40). Shakespeare said,
This above all: to thine own self be true,
And it must follow, as the night the day,
Thou canst not then be false to any man.
-Hamlet
Belief in the worth of the individual is the basis of democracy. A
distinguished teacher of the law has said that the essence of democracy
is the Judaeo-Christian concept of man. That concept is that man has
the dignity which comes from being created in the image and likeness
of God and gets his rights as a person, not from kings or even from
himself, but from God. The good state grows out of the good individaul. A good world will arise out of good persons. William N. Ponton
put the whole matter into a perfect formula when he said, "The Brotherhood of Man begins with the Manhood of the Brother." In Masonry
"the Pot of Incense is an emblem of a pure heart." In America as in
Masonry, we have no titles save those which designate our jobs but we
do have a nobility of soul, an aristocracy of character. Tennyson wrote:
Howe' er it be, it seems to me,
'Tis only noble to be good.
Kind hearts are more than coronets,
And simple faith than Norman blood.
Our duty to our neighbor means more today than ever before in the
long history of the human race. Our neighbor in this global age is the
whole human race. Masonic philosophy has long recognized the unity
of mankind, however. "By the exercise of Brotherly Love we are taught
to regard the whole human species as one family. the high and the low,
the rich and the poor. who, as created by one Almighty Parent, and

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

inhabitants of the same planet, are to aid, support and protect each
other". (Monitor, pages 12 and 13).
The important thing to believe now with reference to our universal
neighborhood is that permanent peace is a possibility. People will say
that we have always had wars and always will. The Mason must
arm the exact opposite of this. He must help create an atmosphere of
public faith in peace in which the statesmen of the world can work.
Remember that faith is contageous. The very stars in their courses are
fighting on the side of the believers in peace. Scientific research is
making war too dangerous to trifle with. In using the atomic bomb,
mankind is playing with the very fingers of God Almighty. Peace is
coming to the world by providential necessity.
- These things shall be, a loftier race
Than e'er the world has known shall rise
With flame of freedom in their souls,
And light of knowledge in their eyes.
Man's duty to God, as Masonry clearly teaches, is the most important duty of all. The reason for this is very clear in our Western
tradition of philosophy. We are dependent beings. We did not bring
ourselves into being. We have no reason whatever to believe that
we can destroy ourselves. Everything we have and use-the _w hole
order of nature, of reality-has been given us. It comes from some
infinite source not of our own making. We call this infinite, necessary
source of all other being God. "We," as a stoic poet said long ago,
"are His offspring." "In Him," as St. Paul exclaimed, "we live and move
and have our being."
Man's dependance places him under moral obligation to the Creator
who gave him life. Strangely enough many people are blind to this
obligation. They ignore the fact that the Ten Commandments include
man's duties to God as well as his duties to his fellow men. Consequently they are only half moral at best.
The Creator is a God of beauty and truth. There is a conspicuous
order in things. "The beauty of God," said St. Thomas, the Angelic
Doctor, "is the cause of the being of all that is.'' God's creation is also
characterized by truth. In fact it is so truthful that it always gives the
same answers to all the accurate researchers of the world of science.
There can be no conflict between religion when it is religion and science
when it is science. Precision in science is reverence for the laws of
God. His ways of doing things, and consequently indirect worship of
the Author of all the fields of scientific investigation. lncidently the
old Romans who invented the word religion used it to mean both reverence for the laws of God, His ways of doing things, and consequently
indirect worship of the Author of all the fields of scientific investiga-

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

15

tion. lncidently the old Romans who invented the word religion used
it to mean both reverence for the gods and conscientiousness. We use
the term in the same way today. Reverence and conscientiousness are
fundamentally and eternally correlative.
God alone is the Giver of life, mortal and immortal. This mortal
life has to be taken on God's terms. Immortal life has to be taken on
the same terms. God is the Creator and the Sustainer. He is also the
Saviour. Man wonders if there is a life beyond the grave, if there is
a land fairer than day. The religious man does more than wonder
about it. He asks the Giver of all life to grant him life everlasting.

III.
The third and highest level of Masonry is the Contemplative. The
words "Speculative" and "Contemplative" are used as equivalents in
Masonic literature and rites. The fact must not be overlooked, however, that Contemplative Masonry is a hightened form of Speculative
Masonry. Reverence and admiration for the glory of God in the Creation can lead to a felt personal relation to the Supreme Being and sometimes to a mystical sense of the Divine Presence. (Monitor, page 22).
Contemplative Masonry solves the Problem of Evil. a problem
which staggers speculation and philosophy. All men of experience in
this mortal life have learned the lesson of the Mosaic Pavement that
life is checked with good and evil. that it is bittersweet. The contemplative Mason puts his whole trust in God. Whittier wrote :
I know not where His islands lift
Their fronded palms in air;
I only know I cannot drift
Beyond His love and care.
Contemplative Masonry solves the problem of ultimate happiness.
Man gains happiness through the spiritual possession of values, particularly of the values of Life, Truth, and Love. The possession of
God means complete happiness, for God, as Dante said, is the Supreme
Value, the Value of Values. He is perfect Life and perfect Truth and
perfect Love.
Contemplative Masonry keeps religion from being mere moralizing,
merely goody-goody. Eric Gill said that a thief who loves God is
more religious than an honest man who does not love God. ·Religion
at its best is the love of God which passes all understanding. Masonry
rises to its perfection when it adores the felt Presence of the ineffable
Being. Who is the Great Architect of the Universe and the Grand
Master of all living things.

MESSAGE OF THE GRAND MASTER

This summary of my journeyings has astounded me, no less than it
may surprise you, but the joys of these journeys and the pleasures of
these meetings with my Brethren. not only here in California but elsewhere, as hereinafter noted; the heartiness of the receptions tendered me
and the permanent friendships established, have more than compensated for the time and effort spent, and have fired my enthusiasms and
funded my knowledge of the Craft.
At some of my receptions here in the State, I have noted my travels to
the Grand Masters' Conference in Washington, D. C., and my return
to California by a circuitous route through Cuba, Yucatan, Guatemala,
and Mexico.
I shall not repeat those observations here, but I do report the reception extended to your Grand Master and your Grand Secretary by the
Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Guatemala. and record the gracious
hospitality offered by, and the fine friendships established with, the following distinguished Brethren of that Jurisdiction: The Most Worshipful Grand Master Jose Maria Moscoso Espino; the Very Worshipful Ventura Echeverria, Grand Orator: the Illustrious Luis Gaytan, 33°,
Grand Commander of the Supreme Council. A. & A. S. R. of Guatemala:
and the Illustrious Alfred Lamport, 33°, Grand Secretary of the Supreme
Council. Masonry in that Jurisdiction is upon a very high plane, and the
individual graciousness and courtesies of these Brethren were augmented
by the holding of a formal Special Communication of the Grand Lodge
of Guatemala in honor of your Grand Master and your Grand Secretary.
May I report that on our return to California, I had made up, not at
Grand Lodge expense, a Grand Master's lapel button similar to our
Charles Albert Adams button, which the Grand Master of this Jurisdiction is privileged to wear. I caused that button to be delivered to the
Grand Master of Guatemala, to be worn by that Officer as a constant
reminder of the hospitality extended to us and as a continuing token of
the cordial relationships which exist between our Grand Jurisdictions and
the Brethren of our respective Lodges.
Except during the war period, each Grand Master of this Jurisdiction, in turn, has had the privilege of visiting our Lodges situated in the
Hawaiian Islands. The enjoyment of this portion of my travels was

Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
Each year the Grand Master of Masons in California stands before
a general assemblage of the Craft. and presents to it those matters
which to him appear to be of importance or of interest to Masonry
in general. On this occasion it is my privilege so to do, but I cannot and
will not endeavor to bring before you all the matters which fall within
these bounds.
Masonry in California has prospered. Its Lodges. and its Grand
Lodge Officers and Committeemen have each and all functioned
smoothly and efficiently. The total membership of the Craft has increased materially. The principal tenets of Free Masonry. Brotherly
Love, Relief and Truth, have been duly observed, and Masonry in California continues to ocupy a place of high esteem among all the peoples of
our State as well as in the hearts of our Brethren.

VISITATIONS AND TRAVELS

"To travel continuously one hundred and thirty days covering the
total distance of over two thousand miles and being able to visit only one
third of the Lodges in the Jurisdiction gives some impression, not only
of the extent of our State, but the magnitude of the labor devolving upon
the Grand Master.* * *Strong as is the temptation to do so, to detail our
experiences would unduly prolong this document."
So spoke your Grand Master at the Sixtieth Annual Communication
of your Grand Lodge.
.
How times have changed! Then three hundred and thirty-two
Lodges in our State; now five hundred and ninety Chartered Lodges,
with six more under dispensation.
Like the Grand Master of those days. I do not intend to prolong this
document unduly. I shall not here record all my visits and travelings,
but I would be withholding desirable information and be remiss in expressing my appreciation if I did not say something upon this subject.
In attending to the Masonic duties and privileges of this high office
during the past year, your Grand Master has traveled more than 13.000 ·
miles by airplane, more than 4,000 miles by train, and more than 20,000
miles by automobile. I have addressed audiences totaling more than
25.000 persons and, while it has not been possible to visit all the Lodges
in California or even all the lnspectorial Districts individually, yet by
grouping the Lodges and the Districts I have had direct contact with the
Officers and members of more than 95 % of the Lodges of this State; not
counting those here assembled at this Communication of the Grand
Lodge of California.

While upon the subject of Visitations and Travels I must say to the
Craft that it cannot expect its Grand Masters to devote as much of their
personal time to Masonic meetings and travels as a few of your recent
Grand Masters have been able to do. Do not misunderstand me, my
Brethren, I am not complaining personally, for I have been fortunate
enough to have had the time and the physical stamina to enjoy happily
the privileges of meeting with my Brethren on very numerous Masonic
occasions. Nevertheless. very few men, regardless of position or substance, can have their personal affairs in such shape that they can completely neglect them for a full twelve months.
Many willing and capable workers in the vineyard, Masons of potentially great leadership are, on account of this prospect, deterred from
even accepting positions where they may be regarded as "Grand Master
material.'' and even those who do and who are eventually asked "to step
in line," do so with continuing worries about the time demands which
they are certain will accrue during their "year."

DISPENSATIONS FOR NEW LooGES

The establishment of a new Lodge is a matter of grave concern, and
certainly a dispensation for that purpose is not to be had merely for the
asking. Our law provides that the Grand Master "may in cases of manifest propriety and necessity grant * * * a dispensation to open and hold
a Lodge * * * ." Accordingly, and before any applications for the formation of new Lodges had been received, I established a new and uniform
procedure of investigation to be made after an application had been perfected legally under Part II, Section I. of our Ordinances. Just as an
applicant for the Degrees for Masonry should be thoroughly investigated before balloting, so should there be formal and extensive investigation before consenting to the formation of a new Lodge. All the facts
prc>bative of the permanence and continuing welfare of a proposed new
Lodge, as well as its probable effect on neighboring Lodges, should be
on file before action is taken on the petition.
I assigned the duty of assembling this information to the already
established Committee on Charters, with the direction that they report
their findings of facts, without recommendation, relative to the following items which seemed necessary to enable the Grand Master to act intelligently upon such an application, To Wit:
1. The economic and social status oI the community from which the
Lodge expected to draw its membership.
2. The history and "work" record of already established Lodges in
or near the situs of the proposed new Lodge.
3. The personal talents, accomplishments, and position, as men and
as Masons, of each of the Officers and Brothers of the proposed new
Lodge.
4. Any other matters of special importance germane to the particular
application.
The Committee on Charters was happy to undertake this duty and,
thereupon, set up a questionnaire form which served as a guide for assembling the necessary information. As requests for dispensations were
received, they were assigned to the Committee for investigation and report, and I congratulate the members of that Committee upon their full
conception of the Grand Master's intentions, the efficiency and completeness of their investigations, and their hearty cooperation in this new
procedure.
May I emphasize again that .their reports were factual only and without recommendation and that, in each instance, these reports have been
filed in the Grand Lodge Office as a permanent record of the particular
Lodge.

I regret very much that I could not grant conscientiously some of the
applications for dispensations for new Lodges and, also, that I must report that some groups were discouraged from making applications at
this time, all for the reason that they could not, in my judgment, make a
showing of "manifest propriety and necessity." Upon this basis, applications for dispensations were disapproved for new Lodges at Rio Linda,
in Sacramento County, and at Bijou, in El Dorado County, and a late
petition from Los Olivas in Santa Barbara County is being referred to
my successor. It would have been much pleasanter for your Grand
Master to have said "Yes," joyously, in each instance. To these very
earnest Masons let me say, "Do not be discouraged permanently. If your
present Grand Master has been in error, on the negative side, as to
what constitutes 'manifest propriety and necessity', this error can be
corrected readily by his successors in office. However, a mistake on
the affirmative side could not be rectified so readily, and a weakness
appearing some five or ten years after the Lodge had been formed would
make the new Lodge a liability rather than an asset to Masonry in
California!'
These earnest Brethren may take heart in the fact that this is a
rapidly growing state, having doubled its population in the last eight
years, and in the fact that the great westward treck is still continuing.
As a new community becomes established, permanently and soundly, beyond the reach of a possible future depression, there a new Lodge may
be instituted safely and, by the same token, new Lodges in well established, expanding cities will certainly become necessary.
Masonry is on the march in California. Our principal problem is to
see that the advancement is orderly and that, using ancient Masonic
language, all our Lodges be "permanently established at particular
places."
I bequeath this plan of procedure relative to the creation of new
Lodges to my successors in office, trusting that they may find merit in it,

and earnestly believing that Masonry in California will be benefited
thereby.

On the 14th day of April. 1948, I regretfully caused the Grand Lodge
of California to be convened by the Very Worshipful Arthur M.
Warren, Grand Lecturer, for the purpose of conducting the funeral
of one of my best and most intimate friends, the Worshipful Sidney K.
Lehman, Assistant Grand Lecturer. The funeral service was delivered
by Worshipful Earle C. Graham, Master of Los Angeles Lodge No. 42,
acting as my special representative. My absence from this solemn occasion was necessitated because my attendance was required in Sacramento to fill out a quorum of a California Commission which otherwise
could not have transacted important State business.
That I did not have the privilege of saying this last farewell to one
who was so close to me, one who had served Masonry in such a magnificent manner for so many years and who had inore than earned the right
to have the Grand Master speak our parting words, has intensified the
pain of the passing of this grand Mason.
At this communication, at the proper time, and in more fitting words
the memory of his many virtues will be noted, but I desire to record that
Sidney K. Lehman was a grand man .-and a grand Mason, a true and
ardent worker in the vineyard, a man whose place in the hearts of his
Brethren can never be filled.
MASONIC CLUBHOUSES

The two clubhouses, which are maintained and operated by the
Grand Lodge of California for the benefit of students of Masonic

25

families who are attending the University of California at Berkeley and
the University of California at Los Angeles, are a credit to the Craft.
I visited each of these clubhouses. I found them well managed and
their facilities well used by as fine a group of young Americans as one
could hope to find anywhere. The Clubs are definitely serving the purpose for which they were established, and the Fraternity should be as
proud of this "work" as it is of its two Masonic Homes.
The clubhouses themselves are beautiful structures, but it seemed to
me that the equipment and the interior finishings of the clubhouses at
Berkeley had deteriorated and were below the usual Masonic standards.
I. therefore, urge the Craft to give special heed and support to the report
and recommendations of the Board of Trustees of the Masonic club
house of the University of California at Berkeley in order that these
deficiencies may be corrected soon. This is not a criticism of the Board
of Trustees. It is simply a noting of the effect of war restrictions, then
rightly imposed, but which are now removed. Authorization by Grand
Lodge should be given for these improvements.
FIRE

Within a single week fire destroyed the buildings of North East
Lodge No. 266 at Fort Bidwell and of Georgetown Lodge No. 25 at
Georgetown. The halls, furnishings, and priceless records, including the
original roving Charter of Georgetown Lodge No. 25, were lost.
These two old Lodges and the Fraternity in general have suffered
irreparable loss. I commend to Grand Lodge an earnest consideration of
the financial problems of these two Lodges occasioned by this destruction. A study of the requirements of rebuilding and refurnishing their
Halls should be made, and I urge a generous hand to aid the keeping of
Masonry alive in the two communities.
These calamities again emphasize the necessity of urging Lodges
to have their Charters photostated, as provided by Resolution of the
Grand Lodge ( 1947 Proceedings, page 258). to keep their records and
valuabl~ furnishings in fire proof vaults and to carry adequate insurance
upon their properties.
COMMITTEES OF INVESTIGATIONS ON APPLICATIONS FOR DEGREES

It has come to the attention of your Grand Master that during the
past few years several men who had previous records as felons have
been admitted to membership in this Fraternity.
These are not pleasant words, nor will they, during the years to come,
look well in print, but where we publicly parade our virtues we should
likewise explore our own shortcomings, especially where it is for the
benefit of the Craft. It seems incredible that Committees of Investigations
should have been so lackadaisical and so negligent in the performance of
their duties that these "records" should not have been uncovered and re•
ported to the Lodge before ballot, but such, my Brethren is the fact. It
is astounding that two of these cases occurred in the same city, and not

27

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

a large city, though not in the same Lodge. This certainly illuminates
that Masonic community's view of the responsibilities of the Investigating Committee.
Some would have charges of un-Masonic conduct filed against those
negligent investigators, but this ultimately would result in Brethren refusing to serve on Committees of Investigation. Rather do I choose to
emphasize, by these to-be-printed words, that each Committeeman
should explore every avenue of inquiry into an applicant's past life and
that, where the applicant has lived in several communities since "growing up," inquiry should be made of Masons in each locality, so that no
records of incarceration or moral shortcomings should remain undisclosed. In order that the .facts hereinabove presented may be brought to
the attention of the Craft in general. I request that each Master .see to
it that this portion of the Grand Master's message be read in his open
Lodge. It is my hope that the Brethren of the Craft may be shocked
thereby into a realization of the full duties and responsibilities incident
to the acceptance of an appointment as a member of a Committee of Investigations.
"Upon each member of the Lodge devolves the duty of carefully
guarding its portals." Masonry would soon deteriorate if Lodges and
members of Investigating Committees showed themselves so careless of
their honor and reputation, so unmindful of their obligations as to entitle
men not worthy and well qualified to be called "friend and brother by
all Masons withersoever dispersed around the globe."

China, Massachusetts Jurisdiction, presented to the Grand Lodge of
California a copy of the Bible published entirely in the Chinese language, requesting that it be held each year by the Lodge which has rendered the best service to Masonic charity.
I am reasonably familiar with the activities of our Lodges and the
charitable work which they are doing. I am proud of that work. but it is
impossible, with any reasonable degree of justice to pick out, from the
five hundred and ninety-six Lodges, one Lodge and say that it has rendered the best service to Masonic charity during this past year. No one
Lodge deserves this signal honor, yet, paradoxical as it may seem, all of
our Lodges deserve it. I. therefore, direct that, for this year and until. a
futute Grand Master sees fit to make an award of the Pettus Bible, it be
held in the custody of the Grand Secreta.r y and loaned to any Lodge of
this Jurisdiction for use at the initiation, passing, or raising of any good
man and true of Chinese ancestry who is being admitted to our mysteries.

PAINTINGS OF PAST GRAND MASTERS

At the present time our Gallery of Paintings of Past Grand Masters
contains macabre near likenesses of three distinguished Brethren. Three
other Past Grand Masters have apparently feared tei sit for their portraits. This deficiency in our gallery of men of distinction should be rectified. In the first place, the allowances made in recent years for portrait
paintings have been insufficient to secure the work of re.ally fine artists
and, secondly. the appropriation has always been made for painting the
picture of the Past Grand Master. To travel long distances, at frequent
intervals, to a studio for sittings is a great imposition upon a Past Grand
Master who is trying to get back to his personal affairs after devoting a
year to Masonry. l, .therefore, recommend that an allotment be made in
appropriate amount to improve and complete the present gallery and
that presently, and in the future, the appropriation each year be made
to paint the picture of the then incumbent Grand Master when it will not
be too inconvenient for him to accommodate himself to the requirements
of the artist.

EUROPEAN MASONIC RELIEF

During the past year your Grand Master has been importuned by
several Brethren to allow solicitations of money and clothing by Masons,
in the name of Masonry and through Masonic Lodges: the donations to
be sent overseas and distributed by this or that constituent Lodge of
some particular Grand Jurisdiction.
Laudible as is the purpose and as great as is the need, I have been
reluctant to grant these requests for several reasons:
1. If solicitations were to be allowed and donations were to be sent
to Lodges in one country, we would of necessity have to do the same for
Lodges in all other countries where Masonry and war suffering still
exist.
2. Our membership traces its ancestry to every country in Europe.
We could not discriminate, nor could we segregate and apportion the
donations, without considerable confusion and possibly some feeling between the different nationality groups of our Brethren.
3. The regulations of exports from the United States and the regulations of· importations to the several countries are complicated, multi fold,
and even confusing. and require the attention of persons not readily
available to local Lodges.
4. The Grand Lodge of California is not presently equipped to handle the physical aspects of the collection, concentration, cleaning, segregation, and dispatch of the volume of clothing that would be assembled
for this distribution.
.
There were many other reasons, too numerous to set forth here.
which appeared in the picture, but still there was, and is, a crying need.
If collection, dispatch, and distribution is to be effected, it will have
to be done by Grand Lodge, with correspondence and planning on
Grand Lodge level. It will require a special committee with special appro-

28

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

priations to cover the cost of these operations. It will probably require the
services of a paid employee, or employees, to do this job.
.
I submit this problem to the Grand Lodge without recommendation
but, Brethren. the need is great.
I do want to call attention to the fact that this Grand Lodge has made
donations of substantial amounts of money for European Masonic Relief through well organized channels, but the above matter is not primarily a financial problem. It is one of getting goods to our distressed
Brethren before the next winter.
DEOSIONS

.

1. Veritas Lodge No. 640, by Resolution adopted January 8, 1948,
and approved by the Grand Master January 13, 1948. raised the annual
dues of their members from $12.00 to $15.00 per year.
· On inquiry I held:
a. That the Resolution became effective January 13, 1948.
b. The dues are paid quarterly. in advance. and that the Resolution
could not be retroactive.
c. That dues for the first quarter of 1948 remained at $3.00 and became, for all subsequent quarters, $3.75.
d. That all the Brethren of the Lodge paying dues were required to
pay $14.25 as dues for the year 1948, whether or not they had
previously paid $12.00 and received a dues receipt showing payment in full for the year 1948.
e. That the dues receipts for the year 1948 issued on the $12.00
basis should be taken up, and new receipts issued upon the payment of the additional amount, or that the old receipts could be
taken up and endorsed showing the additional payment.
2. Pentalpha Lodge No. 202 inquired about presenting a Fifty Year
Veteran Button to one who was raised more than fifty years ago but,
who during a portion of the time, has been suspended for nonpayment
of dues. The Brother had now paid all dues accrued and accruing during
the period of suspension and was in good standing. I held that it was not
the "payment of dues" but the "being a Master Mason in good standing"
for fifty years that governed and that the period of "gooding standing"
had to total fifty years but need not he continuous.
3. A letter was presented to Delta Lodge No. 471 noting that several
Brethren were forming "A Dollar a Month Club" for the benefit of the
Stockton Chapter Order of DeMolay. The Master was requested to
read the letter in open Lodge and "to recommend this activity to your
membership."
The Master refused to read the communication on the ground that
the request was improper under the provisions of Section 126 of our
Ordinances.
I held that the Master was correct in his ruling and was not on this
account to be criticized or charged with being unsympathetic to the

29

Order of DeMolay, which is doing such excellent work among the youth
of our Jurisdiction.
4. Bethlehem Lodge No. 453 proposed to open on the Third Degree
of Masonry, confer a Degree on one candidate and then close. It proposed thereafter on the same day to open on the Second Degree of
Masonry, and confer that Degree on five candidates.
I held that they could confer only four Second Degrees under these
conditions.
Section 221, of our Ordinances, says "* * * *nor shall it confer
more than five Degrees in any one day."
This limitation is not confined to one particular Degree but applies
to all three of the Degrees collectively.
5. Hornitos Lodge No. 98 elected an Entered Apprentice Mason to
receive the Second and Third Degrees of Masonry in that Lodge, ·residence having been established and waiver of Jurisdiction obtained. The
candidate did not come forward to take his Degrees and subsequently
asked for the return of his fees and his contribution to the Masonic
Homes, stating that he was "going away."
.
I held that the candidate was not entitled to the return of either his
fees or his contribution: that it was bad policy for the Lodge to grant the
request, as they stood ready to complete the contract of conferring the
Degrees, but that, if the candidate moved from the State, established a
residence elsewhere. and asked for a waiver of Jurisdiction to .another
Lodge, then Hornitos Lodge might properly refund both the fees and the
contribution, if it granted the waiver.
6. In Unity Lodge No. 368, Brother X received the First Degree of
Masonry on March 7, 1947. Thereafter he moved to Illinois, established
a domicile there and requested Courtesy Degrees to be conferred by a
Lodge in that state.
Pursuant to the Edict of Grand Master John R. Moore. dated January 11, 1947, ( 1947 Proceedings, page 246) California refused to make
the request. Brother X then applied for, and received, a waiver of
jurisdiction to enable him to petition a Chicago Lodge for the Second
and Third Degrees of Masonry, stating that he was "to permanently
reside in Chicago," He did not make the application, but returned to
California on August 23. 1948. The Lodge asked if they could confer
the remaining Degrees upon Brother X without his having to re-establish
a Masonic residence in California by remaining in the state for one year.
I held that they could confer the Degrees as soon as the candidate
demonstrated his proficiency in the candidate's lectures.
Unity Lodge No. 368 did not lose jurisdiction by granting the
waiver.
Only by the Illinois Lodge electing Brother X to receive the Second
Degree of Masonry would California's jurisdiction terminate. Even if
Brother X had applied for and been rejected by the Chicago Lodge,

7. Responding to an inquiry from the Santa Clara Masonic Officers'
Association the Grand Master decided in effect as follows:
a. That Officers' Associations are required by sub-section 3rd of Section 53 of the Ordinance and are encouraged by the Grand Lodge
as conducive to the proper administration of Lodges and the
instruction of Lodge Officers in Masonic law and custom.
b. That the individual Lodges. within such an Officers' Association,
may under Section 157 of our Ordinance, contribute to the reasonable expenses of such Association while functioning as such. in
the amounts agreed upon by the respective Lodges. and that such .
contributions are "necessary expenses of the Lodge."
c. That the providing. by the Association, of a reasonable meal for
those Lodge Officers in attendance. including the Inspectors,
where the real purpose of such provision is to facilitate and expedite the business of the Association, is a proper expenditure of
the Association's funds.
d. That the providing of a banquet for the Officers. or providing a
meal primarily for social purposes, is not proper.
e. That the payment of the expenses of travel, food, and housing.
or any of these items directly to or for the individual Officers of
the Lodges in atten~ance at such Officer meetings is not a proper
charge against the Lodge which the Officer represents. and
cannot be paid either by the Lodge or by the Association, except
to the extent above indicated.
f, That joint or united meetings of two cir more lawfully organized
District Officers' Associations with the approval of the Inspector
of each participating District are proper and do not offend our
law.
8. The by-laws of Mt. Davidson Lodge No. 481 provided that "the
stated meetings of this Lodge shall be holden on the first Monday in
each month: except that in any month when t~e regular meeting date
shall fall on January 1st, or July 4th, legal holidays, etc."
This year Independence Day fell on Sunday, July 4. and the legal
observance of this date, as is usual in such cases, was on July 5. The
Lodge inquired if it should hold it's stated meeting for July on the flfth
of the month or on the next succeeding Monday. I held that July 5 was
the proper meeting date.
9. On inquiry from Temple Lodge No. 14, I held that the realized
proceeds from the sale of stock bequeathed to the Lodge was not revenue
within the provisions of Section 159 of our Ordinances so that 20%
thereof could be used for the purposes of refreshment. I held that the
term "revenue," as used in this section, meant income from investments

and properties, dues received from member, and fees received from applicants, but that profit or loss upon the sale of capital assets of the
Lodge was not to be included in the calculation of the amount available
for refreshment and fraternal intercourse.
10. York Lodge No. 423 reported that a candidate was elected to receive the Degrees of Masonry and that, thereafter, and before his initiation, it was discovered that he had been previously rejected by another
Lodge and had not so reported in answer to Questions 8 and 9 of his
application.
At the next stated meeting of the Lodge, the Master reported the
facts, declared the previous ballot null and void and the candidate rejected. I held that the Master had no authority to declare the ballot void
on this account and that the proper method of procedure was to make
objection to the candidate's initiation pursuant to Section 237 of our
Ordinances and then, at the end of the sixty day period, to declare the
candidate rejected.
11. A Degree Team in Northern California conferred the Third
Degree of Masonry in a manner not in conformity with the Ritual and
work as adopted by Grand Lodge and taught by the Grand Lecturer.
This particular group had, on quite a number of previous occasions, become entirely "too enthusiastic", and had failed to heed gentle admonitions given by several Brethren. It seemed necessary that the Grand
Master should intervene, and I thereupon deprived them of the privilege
of doing further work.
Sub-section 6 of the Section 34 of Ordinances specifically gives the
Grand Master power "to compel its (any Lodge) conformity to Masonic
usage."
This necessarily includes the Brethren working in the Lodge. I also
believe that it is within the inherent power of the Grand Master to deny
any Brother or group of Brethren the privilege of participating in Degree work where he, or they, in so doing, persist in doing it contrary to
the words and form prescribed by ·Grand Lodge.
On receipt of this expression of my will and displeasure, the Director and several members of this particular Team appeared before me in
person and, while somewhat minimizing the action of the Brethren conferring the Degree, nevertheless apologized and gave real assurances
that any further work that they might be permitted to do would conform strictly to our regulations and the Grand Lecturer's instruction.
Now I could deprive them of the privilege of working 'but I could
not grant them unlimited authority to work. Our law is plain, "Teams
work only upon invitation of the Master of the Lodge, obtained without
. pressure, and work subject to his responsibility as to their proficiency."
What I did was to allow the Brothers to go back to work, subject to these
limitations of our law.

32

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

There might arise cases where the Master of the Lodge should be
"punished" for permitting "over-enthusiasm," for his is the responsibility
to see that the work is done correctly, but here corrective measures were
applied directly to the offenders.
Degree teams of co-workers are to be encouraged where the candidate is a member of the organization which the team represents, but Masonry is not a playground. It seeks to teach wise and serious truths, and
a candidate is not brought to the realization of this purpose if his De·
gree is conferred in an undignified manner. This particular incident requires no further attention, but is here reported to emphasize the fact
that our Degrees must be conferred strictly in accordance with the work
as adopted by the Grand Lodge and the instruction of the Grand Lecturer, and not otherwise, or serious consequences may befall the offenders.
12. The Master of a Lodge in Northern California, whose term was
expiring in January 1948, with the consent of his Lodge, spent more than
the cumulated 20% of the Lodge's revenue for purposes of refreshment
and fraternal intercourse. The overdraft, as reported, was a substantial
amount. I immediately suspended the Master of ~he Lodge, put the Senior
Warden in charge, directed an audit of the Lodge books, and ordered
that the Installation of Officers for the ensuing year be held up. pending
a full investigation. Two days later the Inspector of the District reported
that the Master and three or four of the Brethren of the Lodge, without
bargaining, had voluntarily made a gift to the Lodge of a sum equivalent
to the total overdraft. I inquired if the contributions made would in anywise be a burden on the donors and, on being informed that they were
each well able to make the donation, I restored the Master to authority
and permitted the installing of Officers elected for the ensuing Masonic
year.
Certainly the Master's punishment for this transgression has been
sufficient, and the matter is reported here only as a warning and advice to
other Masters as to their responsibility for the supervision of Lodge finances, as well as all other Lodge affairs.
I am pleased that the Master of this Lodge voluntarily offered a solu- •
tion which permitted me to be gracious to him, and I am happy that he
is now enjoying the title of Past Master, because his administration in all
other respects rightfully deserved the plaudits of his Brethren.

1. The right of Masonic Lodges to become "Mother Lodges" by issuing warrants of.~onstituti?,n ce~sed in 1717, both among the "Ancients"

Lodge, it is to be noted that they never attempted to act as a Lodge, for

day language we :would describe as a Masonic Club functioning only ~s

It is interesting to note that the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts

African Lodge No. 1. on and after July 3, 1776, was merely a group
of Masons ( 1) hoping to get a warrant of authority to ac.t as a Lodge.
They knew that they were not a Lodge, for they never attempted to
functipn as such, and shortly thereafter, in 1776, they accepted a limited
"Permit" from Provincial Grand Master John Rowe "to walk on St.

If they were a duly constituted Lodge, claiming authority as such
from Army Lodge No. 441, why did they ask of, or accept from Provincial Grand Master Rowe, a document of authority which, under such
circumstances, limited their rights, powers, and privileges to a lesser

On account of the declaration of March 17, 1776, made by the
Grand Lodge of Massachusetts, and for other reasons, the authority of
Provincial Grand Master Rowe on July 3, 1776, has always been seriously questioned. At best African Lodge No. 1 in 1776 became only a limited Lodge under Rowe's authority(?), and continued as such until they
got a Charter and were constituted in May 6, 1787. (The Charter was
dated Sept. 29, .1784.)
4. African Lodge No. 1 was not a regular Lodge. The Grand
Lodge of Massachusetts (Ancient) was formed on March 8, 1777,
and claimed exclusive jurisdiction of Massachusetts. The St. John's
Grand Lodge of Massachusetts (Modern) was formed on July 29,
1790. These two Grand Lodges united to form the present Grand
Lodge of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts in 1792. Neither one of
these original Massachusetts Grand Lodges ever recognized or accepted
African Lodge No. 1 as legitimate, though African Lodge No. 1 is now
claimed to have been a limited (a St. John's or Hedge Lodge) from shortly after July 3, 1776, to May 6, 1787, and a regularly constituted Lodge
under English authority (Modern) from this latter date until 1791,
when it renounced that authority and attempted to form a Grand Lodge
of its own, out of a so-called "general assembly of the Craft." From the
very inception of its organization up to and including the time of its at-

tempt to found its own Grand Lodge, the status of African Lodge No. 1
(African Lodge No. 459} was questionable, and each individual step in
its endeavor to obtain "legitimacy" is subject to question upon one point
or another. It is quite significent that neither of the then existing Grand
Lodges of Massachusetts ever recognized, or accepted, or had Masonic
intercourse with African Lodge No. 1. This certainly could not be
charged to race prejudice, for race prejudice did not exist in New England. and certainly not in Massathusetts, until some time after the Civil
War, if ever. If African Lodge was unaccepted and unrecognized by
authoritative Masonry in the l 700's, when all the facts of its organization and its activities were fresh and well-known to the Masons of that
time, what excuse is there for its recognition after all these years.
Masons are recognized only upon the basis of indisputable, affirmative
evidence. If the Negroes could not make that affirmative proof at the
close of the Eighteenth Century, why recognize them now when so many
of the material, alleged facts are still subject to honest and reasonable
question.
·
5. African Lodge No. 459 irregular, becomes clandestine.
Stating the matter in the most favorable light to African Lodge, that
Lodge up to 1790 was at best an irregular Lodge, but its action subsequent to that date make it unquestionably clandestine. We may disregard all the irregularities in the formation of African Lodge and overlook all the questionable authorities contributing to its establishment.
We may even assume that it became "legitimate" on its Constitution as
African Lodge No. 459 on May 6, 1787, but what happened in its affairs
after that time made it and all its successors clandestine.
As pointed out above, the Massachusetts "Ancients" in 1777, and
the Massachusetts "Modems" in 1790, each formed their own Grand
Lodge. "Ancient" Masonry and "Modern" Masonry were the only
recognized Masonry existing in the world at that time. These two
Grand Lodges were claiming exclusive jurisdiction over Massachusetts
during this period, and they settled their differences and united into the
present Grand Lodge of Massachusetts in 1792. Provincial Grand
Master Rowe (Modem} had died in February 1787.
Past Grand Master Melvin F. Johnson of Massachusetts says,
"African Grand Lodge ( 1791) was formed by a general assemblage of
the Craft." This general assembly ( 1 ) of the Craft (Modern) could not
have been authorized by ·Rowe, and there was already a Grand Lodge of
Massachusetts (Modern) existing in that commonwealth.
With the "Ancient" and the "Modern" Brethren formally organized,
who in authority could call and who could attend legally this so-called
"general assemblage of the Craft" in 1791 to form the African Grand
Lodge? With hundreds of Master Masons in Massachusetts, what
Masons met in which corner of what room and presumed to call themselves a "general assemblage of the Craft," and then create for themselves a Grand Lodge.

At that moment this group of Negro Masons, whatever their status
may have been before that time, became clandestine, and all their successors have been clandestine ever since. If the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts is right in saying that, because the skins of these Masons were
black, they had this right to renounce the English Masonry and the
Grand Lodge of Massachusetts (Modern) and form a still third Grand
Lodge in the same territory: then, by that same token, our Chinese
Brethren, our French Brethren, our Italian Brethren, our German Brethren, our Hawaiian Brethren, and our Filipino Brethren, here in California, can walk out of this room and each group form its own, separate Grand Lodge of California. On this principle, each of these
separate groups, even though they be but a handful of Masons, can
assemble, call themselves "a general assemblage of the Craft," vote to
establish its own Grand Lodge, and add to the general confusion of
Masonry. All of this is an absurdity, but no more absurd or Masonically
illegal than what the African Brethren ( 1) of Massachusetts did in 1791,
as contended now by Massachusetts. No other conclusion can be drawn
but this that, regardless of what happened before, from 1791 to this
date, every socalled Mason of Prince Hall affiliation is clandestine and
every regular Mason, made so in a regular Lodge anywhere in this whole
world, who at anytime affiliated with one of the Prince Hall constituent
Lodges, or any of the other groups stemming therefrom, became thereupon clandestine.
Out of the mouth of the most enthusiastic present day Caucasian
supporter of Negro Masonry comes the words which destroy all the socalled proof of Prince Hall Masonry's regularity and leave that Masonry exposed as being truly clandestine.
Massachusetts says. page 7, of her pamphlet: "Thus for 170 years
African Lodge and its successors have been functioning in Massachusetts in good faith and with justifiable belief that their origin and procedure were as regular and legitimate as we have thought ours to be."
The word "justifiable" above used can only mean that Massachusetts
believes her own regularity to be no more or less than that of the Negroes. When she puts herself on this level. what action does she expect
the other Grand Jurisdictions of the world to take, especially when she,
for 170 years has been, and all the other Jurisdictions of the world have
been and still are, so firmly convinced that Prince Hall Masonry is
clandestine?
THE IssuE Is NoT NEGRO MASONRY BuT DUPLICATE
TERRITORIAL JURISDICTION

Our present differences with the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of
Massachusetts are but incidentally concerned with its belief as to
the regularity of Prince Hall Masonry. It is something much more fundamental in Masonic affairs that concerns us. It is most unfortunate
that the real issue has been obscured by highly technical and meticulous

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

37

discussion of the origin of Negro Masonry in the United States and its
present status, and that the situation has become confused with considerations of civil liberties and extra-Masonic political policies and expediencies. The question of civil liberties for American citizens with dark
skins is not before us and has no place in this discussion. This decision
should be made solely upon the merits of the Masonic case. Race, color,
or creed should not influence that decision.
The real issue is that the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts, after one
hundred and sixty years of claiming and exercising exclusive territorial
Jurisdiction, and after exclusive territorial jurisdiction has become firmly
established as the Masonic law and c·ustom of all jurisdictions of the
United States and the goal to which all other organized Masonry in all
other countries of the world is striving, now suddenly renounces that
principle and boldly shares its jurisdiction in violation of that historic
position.
It is to be noted that Section 116 of Ordinances of the Grand Lodge
of California provides:
"A Lodge shall not recognize any Body, purporting to be a Masonic
Lodge, which shall be holden within the jurisdiction of the Grand
Lodge of any State or Territory of the United States without authority from such Grand Lodge * * * .''
It is unfortunate that Massachusetts does not have a similar ordinance or, if she has. she does not heed it, for Prince Hall affiliates are
attempting to be, and operate as, Masons in California.
Massachusetts ·asserts her right to share her jurisdiction (Pamphlet
of March 12, 1947, page 15) in the following words:
"Assuming that our Grand Lodge has rightfully had and now has
exclusive Masonic Jurisdiction over Massachusetts, then we certainly have the right to allow another Grand Lodge to share that
Jurisdiction to such an extent as we see flt.''
California contends that, at least so far as the Jurisdictions within the
territorial boundaries of the United States are concerned, the day of
superimposed or duplicate Masonic Jurisdictions is long since at an end,
and no excuse for it exists especially where the same language is spoken.
Massachusetts in her formal Resolution complained of the approaching chaos in extra-Masonic "existing social conditions," yet by her very
action she brings this confusion into Masonic affairs. She says that in
so far as she is concerned, Prince tfall Masonry in Massachusetts is just
as legitimate as she is. Carried to its logical conclusion, every race is entitled to its own Masonic Grand Lodge. Under these conditions, when
matters of inter-jurisdictional Masonic concern arise, it will then be
necessary to discover the color of the skin or the native tongue of the
individuals concerned before other Jurisdictions may know which of the
many Grand Lodges in a particular state is to be contacted, and there
can be no final Masonic authority in that Jurisdiction.

If Massachusetts desires to recognize the African Brethren (?), heal
them or any of them, and take them into her fold, that is entirely her
business and is entirely proper, Masonically, for Masonry unites men .
of every country, sect, and opinion.
We agree with Past Grand Master Johnson of Massachusetts on at
least one point, "Culture, not color," is the determining qualification.
That is the kind of Masonry which California practices. Past Grand
Master John R. Moore, Past Grand Master Lloyd E. Wilson, who is
our present Grand Secretary; and your Grand Master now before you,
each has "sat" in Lodge with many regular Masons of African ancestry.
One of these, incidentally. was Master of a Lodge holding a Charte1
from the United Grand Lodge of England. We have here in California
many Masons. not of the Caucasian race. Without making any comparisons, let me say that full-blooded Filipinos and full-blooded Hawaiians are members of our Lodges and, at this moment within this Grand
Lodge, there sits a Brother of pure Chinese blood who has served
two terms as Master of our Confidence Lodge No. 203, situated in
Monterey County. in the State of California. Several of our Lodges
presently have elective Officers who are Chinese, and many such Brethren have served our Lodges as Masters. All these Brethren are individuals of culture, knowledge, and understanding, and they are good
men and true and of real Masonic character.
Further, our Grand Lodge records show that a full-blooded Negro
sat as an invited guest in one of the Annual Communications of this
Grand Lodge, ( 1873 Proceedings, page 25), and we have the most
cordial relationships with the Grand Lodge of New Jersey which has a
constituent Lodge whose membership is composed entirely of Negroes.
I say these things here to demonstrate clearly that we mean what we
say when we say that Negro Masonry is not the real issue. It is an
issue to the extent that Massachusetts has recognized as legitimate in
Massachusetts a parent group which has so-called Masonic Lodges in
California. It also is an issue to the extent that Massachusetts, by her
action, is aiding in this attempted invasion of California's Masonic Jurisdiction.
That the Grand Jurisdiction of Massachusetts, by its action of March
12, 1947, did and is aiding this effort to invade the Jurisdiction of the
Grand Lodge. J;. & A. M. of California, is clearly evidenced by the following quotation from a so-called Masonic publication printed in California and issued under date of September 1948. It is needless for me
to add that this journal is not an official Masonic publication and has no
Masonic standing whatever with the Grand Lodge of California. I also
add that it is NOT a Negro publication.

may clear the minds, not only of the Brethren of our two great Jurisdictions, but also may simplify the issue for the leaders of the other
Grand Jurisdictions of this United States. We pray that some clear
thinkers and some kind friends in some of these Jurisdictions may whisper good counsel, gently admonish Massachusetts of her error, and suci:eed in convincing her that she is following a false Messiah, not out of.
but into, a Masonic wilderness.

Lodge. For their thoughtful labors, I thank them, not only on my
behalf but on the behalf of the 182,000 Masons in California, whom
they serve. Well done!
INSPECTORS

Since 1934, as Assistant Grand Lecturer and in other Masonic offices,
I have had the privilege of working with the Inspectors of the several
Masonic Districts. I thought I possessed some knowledge and appreciation of the value of the work which they are doing for Masonry and
perhaps I do, but during this year they. as my representatives. have been
unusually loyal and courteous, frank and helpful. diligent and industrious. They have given unstintingly of their time to the demands of the
Masons of their Districts and to the requests of their Grand Master on
even more than convenient occasions. No man, until he has held the office
of Grand Master of Masons, can fully appreciate their work. For their
help to me, I sincerely thank them.

RECOMMENDATIONS

GRAND LECTURER AND ASSISTANTS

Our Grand Lecturer. Arthur M. Warren, and his assistants, Obed
W. Carr, Walter H. E. VonKonsky. Mervyn E. Hanshaw, and Frank
Harwell, Jr., have each and all worked well in the vineyards. The activities of these Brethren do not bring them in direct contact with the Officers and Brethren of the several Lodges except at quite infrequent intervals. yet their Committee work and their supervision of the Ritualistic
work of the Fraternity is reflected in the skill of the Inspectors, and the
work being done in our Lodge room.
It is with great regret that I accepted the resignation of Past Grand
Master Gilbert C. DeForest from the office of Assistant Grand Lecturer
and as a member of the Ritual Committee. Brother DeForest is a per£ectionist, and his long service to Masonry in this particular branch of
our work, as well as in our other fields, has been of great value. His retirement is a distinct loss.
GRAND SECRETARY

Past Grand Master Lloyd E. Wilson, as Grand Secretary, is conducting, in a manner that is highly satisfactory, an office of great importance to Masonry. He is also maintaining the Jurisdiction of California
in a position of great respect among the Masonic Grand Jurisdictions of
the world. Not only in the minutiae of technical, administrative detail
but also in the broad over all picture of Masonic operations and interjurisdictional affairs, Brother Wilson has a knowledge and understanding of Masonry that is of inestimable value to the Craft. To the Grand

I believe that the quality of our trials and of our Masonic justice can

which removes from them the burdens and responsibilities of sitting in
judgment upon one of their own members.
In many jurisdictions the trials are conducted by special panels of

trial, and the case for the prosecution is presented by a representative

Everywhere in my travels I found friendship and brotherly love, cour~

upon me, for the wealth of the finer things of life that have become mine
by reason of your considerations, and for the privilege of serving.

CONCLUSION
And so we come to the end of these lines Almost forty years ago a distinguished gentleman, who is with us to~
day, stood, as I now stand before this Most Worshipful Grand Lodge
of California, and said, "The usefulness of men and institutions is to be
determined by what they give rather than by what they receive * * *
the past can only be justified by more potential labors in the present and
by passing on to posterity an organization improved and broadened in
its scope and usefulness."
The brilliant wisdom of those words still gleams with undiminished
luster and the battle cry, "Our charity must minister to the minds and
souls of men, as well as to their bodies," is both a summation of our glori~
ous progress and a guide~post pointing to a further broadened scope of
usefulness in the magnificent future that lies before us.
For more than a quarter of a century his philosophy of usefulness ·has
been mine. At the commencement of this term, the high office with which

RESOLUTIONS
The Grand Secretary then read the following resolutions, all of
which were referred by the Grand Master to the Committee on Policy
and General Purposes :
TO INCREASE REFRESHMENT FUND

Whereas, Section 159 of the Ordinances of Grand Lodge of California provides that a Lodge may not expend to exceed twenty per
cent of its total revenue for purposes of refreshment and the promo~
tion of fraternal intercourse, and
Whereas, this provision was made at a time when the cost of
living was considerably less than it is at present, and
Whereas, for this reason the limitation set by said section for
purpose of refreshment and fraternal intercourse is now insufficient
to maintain the minimum enjoyment of those features necessary for
keeping the brethren of the Lodge in proper contact, and
Whereas, the decrease and number of new candidates is lowering
the base on which said allowable percentage can be calculated, now
therefore,
Be It Resolved, That the Grand Lodge be requested to consider
the amendment of Section 159 of its Ordinances to allow a greater
percentage of the total revenue for a member Lodge to use for refreshments and promotion of fraternal intercourse, by changing the maximum percentage therein provided from 20% to 30%.
Respectfully submitted,
BRYCE C. RATHBUN,

Senior Warden Security Lodge 581.

PLAQUE FOR WESTERN STAR LODGE NO 2

Whereas Western Star Lodge No. 2, one of the three pioneer
Lodges which formed this Grand Lodge in 1850, is holding its centennial this year, celebrating the issuance of its charter from the
Grand Lodge of Missouri on May 10, 1848;
And whereas this charter is the oldest one in point of date of
issuance of all charters of Masonic Lodges in California;
And whereas, since its Roll-call night held on May 10, 1948,
when 104 of its 126 members signed the register, this Lodge has been
host to thirty-eight other California Lodges which have come to the
old mining town of Shasta in northern California and have conferre1
degrees as guest Lodges in the hall of Western Star Lodge No. 2:
And whereas the Grand Master of the State of Missouri came all
the way from that state during the summer of 1948 to pay a visit to
this Lodge and to present it a congratulatory plaque from the Free
and Accepted Masons of Missouri:
And whereas almost three thousand Masons have signed the
tiler's register as visitors during this year and thousands of nonMasons have visited the hall to view the Masonic relics on deposit
there:
It would seem flt that the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted
Masons of California at this 1948 annual communication should pay
some tribute towards this pioneer Lodge .which has continued to carry
on in a little mining town long after the gold~rush days have passed
it by;
Be It Therefore Resolved, That the Grand Lodge of California
present to Western Star Lodge No. 2 of Shasta, California, a small
bronze plaque suitable for hanging on its walls containing some congratulatory message from the Grand Lodge to the subordinate Lodge
upon its centennial year, the Grand Master being authorized to give
the message and to arrange for the proper presentation of the plaque
to the Lodge.
Respectfully submitted,

F. Ross,
Past Master Reading Lodge 254.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons
of the State of California:
Compensation paid to Grand Lodge Officers, Committeemen and
Representatives, has always been computed on the basis of "twice
the single first class one way railway fare, plus Pullman sleeper, where
necessary." Compensation for the 1948 convocation has been computed on this basis.
Our attention has been called to the wording of Section 66 of the
Ordinances, which says that the compensation shall be "the exact
cost of transportation for one person from the location of each Lodge

in the jurisdiction to the place of meeting of Grand Lodge and return,
viz: the unlimited flrst-class railroad fare, together with connecting
steamer or stage fare, and cost of berth in sleeper when required."
It has been suggested to us that this provision means that compensation should not exceed the cost of a first class round trip ticket, plus
sleeper when necessary.
If this is what is intended, and if such a plan is adopted, a substantial reduction can no doubt be made in the total amount required
to meet the traveling expenses allowed representatives and others.
