The following resolutions were referred by the Grand Master to
the Committee on Ritual:
OFFICERS COACH

I propose that Ordinance Section 53, Sub Section 3-A' be amended.
The present wording of Sub Section 3-A is as follows:
To appoint in each Lodge within his District an Officers' Coach,
who shall be a qualified Past Master of the Lodge, and who shall
serve at the pleasure of the Inspector. The Officers' Coach shall
assist in teaching the ritual to the Officers of his Lodge, and assist
in preparing them to qualify for advancement.
I propose that Ordinance Section 53, Sub Section 3-A be amended
to read:
To appoint in each Lodge within his District an Officers'
Coach, who shall be a qualified Past Master of the Lodge, and who
shall be acceptable to the Officers thereof. The Officers' Coach
shall serve at the pleasure of the Inspector and shall assist in
teaching the ritual to the Officers of his Lodge, and assist in preparing them to qualify for advancement.
It is my opinion that the Officers of a Lodge shall not be compelled
to accept an Officers' Coach who does not meet with their approval.
As the ordinance now stands they have no choice in the matter, and
can be compelled to accept an Officers' Coach who is not satisfactory
to them.

Respectfully submitted,
JOSEPH F. HOGAN,

Master Beverly Hills Lodge No. 528.
STEREOPTICON EQUIPMENT

Whereas, The Most Worshipful Grand Master of Free and
Accepted Masons of the State of California has issued an order to all
Masonic Lodges under his jurisdiction prohibiting the use of stereopticon equipment in connection with the Lodge degree work; and
Whereas After due and proper consideration the members of
Oceanside Lodge No. 381 Free and Accepted Masons of the State of
California have concluded that the use of said equipment is of value
not only to those who are now members of the Fraternity but also of
great and distinctive value to those who are receiving their first steps
in Masonry; now therefore
Be It Resolved, That the Worshipful Grand Master be and is
hereby respectfully requested to reconsider his order prohibiting the
use of stereopticon equipment and that said order be recinded.
I hereby certify that the foregoing resolution was adopted by
Oceanside Lodge No. 381 at its stated meeting held September 13th,
1948.
Respectfully submitted,
WILLIAM R. CREGAR, P. M..
Secretary.

Nation" in Nation's Business for August 1948, Felix Morley comments
that:
"It is an interesting experience to glance again at one of those
standard arithmetic books which young America studied at school
* * *. Some of the material set forth in those venerabl~ texts is
still reliable. But other sections seem to have no relation whatsoever to life today.
"Measures of weight, of capacity and of distance are as valid
now as they were forty years ago. The pound avoirdupois is still
16 ounces; the gallon continues to contain four quarts; the yard
totals the same 36 inches that it used to have."
and points out that these facts may be verified.
"But in another field of measurement * * * the old arithmetics
seem hopelessly out of date * * * ,
"There one may read that in the United States: 'The unit of
value is the dollar. Its standard weight in gold 25.8 grains'."
This is only one of the factors contributing to depreciation of the dollar.
We shall not delve into the intricate causes or whether it has been due
to impractical theorists and opportunist politicians that the dollar is not
now what it used to be. I am merely interested in emphasizing the fact
and leave it to you, if interested, to explore the subject. Currently, the
United States dollar is referred to as the "sixty cent dollar." Of course,
that is an inaccuracy because its value may be more or probably less
depending on what you are attempting to buy. One may be inclined to
complacency in the case of investments which may be held to maturity
if essential. but to the expert as dollar income from funds is to be
used for operation during the period of depreciation of the dollar the
principal is, in effect, depreciated.

value, but include some of satisfactory ratings. In such instances, where
the income is negligible, accounting convenience determines policy.
We have also found during the year that in the portfolio of some
funds there were excess "F" or "G" bonds, a situation arising from
donations and bequests. Satisfactory arrangements were made to redeem
and reinvest in the same security of different date.
Attention is again invited to the exceedingly large percentage of
Government bonds in portfolios. This may not be corrected, even if
desirable, without amendment of the regulations governing investments,
but as circumstances may develop the advisability of extending the
qualified investments, appropriate legislation should be considered.
As it is manifest that there is great responsibility on the officer
serving as Grand Treasurer as relates to custody and investment, I am
prompted to recommend that consideration be given to creation of the
office of Assistant Grand Treasurer, who shall be a member of the
Grand Lodge, having had successful investment experience, to be
appointed by the Grand Master pursuant to consultation with the Grand
Treasurer, with specified duties and responsibilities subject to the direction of the Grand Treasurer.
Also without criticism or dissatisfaction with individual performance,
particularly the Grand Secretary or Assistant Grand Secretary and
that office, I believe by reason of the nature and greater volume of disbursements made by the Grand Secretary, that the transactions should
be subject to a current monthly audit by the professional auditors. It is
manifestly unjust to impose upon an auditing committee of individuals
where there are so many and varied transactions as there now are in
the office of the Grand Secretary. I have informed the Grand Secretary
of my contemplated recommendation.
Respectfully submitted,

F. v. KEESLING
Grand Treasurer.

REPORT OF GRAND SECRETARY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
I have the honor to present to you herewith my Seventh Annual
Report as your Grand Secretary.
The year just closed has been as busy and active a year as can be
imagined. The cooperation of the Lodge Secretaries has been outstanding as has been the work of the Grand Lodge office staff.
LEGISLATIVE PROCEDURES

The granting of dispensations for six new lodges has brought to
light a membership situation which I recommend be referred to the proper
Committees for consideration. The Law provides various ways in which
membership may be acquired, and one of these is "By having been named
in a dispensation for a new lodge as one of the petitioners therefor"
(Section 162 - 3rd). A literal construction of this Section means that
when the Grand Master signs the dispensation for a new Lodge, the
members named in the petition cease membership in the former Lodge,
because we do not permit membership in more than one lodge in this
jurisdiction at a time.
There is always a period between the granting of the dispensation
and the institution of the lodge, and it is possible that this may be a
considerable length of time, due to the engagements of the Grand
Master. In this interval, the petitioning members are actually not members of any lodge, and have been deprived of all of their privileges, even
that of visitation, because their dues receipts are on file in the Grand
Lodge office with the petition.
It is possible to cure this situation by a "mechanical" device, rather
than resorting to legislation: namely, by having the Grand Master date
and sign the dispensation on the night of institution. If this practice is
to be followed, it should be made an established matter of policy. This
has not been the practice in years past
FEES FOR DEGREES

At the risk of repeating my statement in last year's report, attention
is again called to the fact that the $25.00 Masonic Homes Contribution
is provided for in the Law of Grand Lodge and has nothing whatever
to do with the amount of the Fees for Degrees as set forth in the Uniform Code of By-Laws. The Masonic Homes Contribution must be

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

collected in addition to any other requirements, and the same is true of
the George Washington Masonic Memorial Contribution of $1.00.

MEMBERSHIP

58

GENERAL OFFICES OF GRAND LODGE

Plans for the modernization of Grand Lodge Offices have been held
in abeyance pendfog a determination as to the building of a Memorial
Temple. Provision should be made. however, so that if it becomes
apparent during the year that a new Temple will not be built, steps may
be taken to proceed with the modernization of existing offices, for which
plans have already been prepared.
MEMBERSHIP

In presenting the membership figures for the year, I show comparative figures for 1947 and 1948 for ready reference, and have also given
the figures for 1918, 1928 and 1938, for the purpose of showing our
growth by decades.
It is interesting to note that while the number of lodges has increased
only 56% in the last thirty years, the membership is almost three times
as great.
In the past twenty years the number of lodges has increased only
6% whereas the membership gain has been in excess of 30%.
There is a striking parallel between what is happening today in
membership and what happened following the close of World War I.
That war ended in 1918 and applications for degrees continued to increase in 1919 and 1920 and the first decrease came in 1921--three years
after the close of the war. The total membership. however, continued to
grow until 1931.
World War II ended in 1945 and applications for the degrees continued to increase in 1946 and 1947, with the first decrease coming in
1948-again three years after the close of the war. If the parallel is
completely followed out, we may, however, expect a growth in the total
number of members for a considerable number of years.
I think it is worth directing attention to what happened in a fiveyear period-1931 to 1935, both inclusive-with respect to suspensions
for non-payment of dues. In that period, our lodges suspended for nonpayment of dues, 17,938 members. There is no necessity here to review
the existing conditions at that time, but if some of the "prophets of depression" are right in their prophecies, it is not too early to take the
necessary steps to prevent the recurrence of any such needless loss. The
time to prevent arrearages which lead to suspensions is while they are
still minor delinquencies.

VISITATIONS

In February I attended the Conference of Grand Secretaries of
which I have the honor to be Vice-President and the meeting of the
George Washington Masonic National Memorial Association of which
I am a Director.
In company with the Grand Master (and at my own expense) on
the return from Washington, I visi"ted the Grand Lodges of Cuba,
Guatemala and the York Grand Lodge of Mexico. The knowledge thus
gained of Masonry in these countries has been of great value and
inspiration to me.
Last year the Grand Secretary and the Past Grand Master of the
Grand Lodge of Idaho attended this Grand Lodge and in accordance
with our "home and home agreement" I attended that Grand Lodge with
the Grand Master during September.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

71

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge
Free and Accepted Masons of California:
Section 50 of our Ordinances provides that the Grand Lecturer shall
render at each Annual Communication a full and detailed account of
his services during the year, and to set forth therein, a report of the
condition of the Lodges throughout the Jurisdiction.
Accordingly, I present herewith an accounting of the ritualistic acitvities of this Grand Lodge.
Our Constituent Lodges are still busy in the important work of bringing Masonry into the hearts and minds of men. While the number of
applicants has fallen off, there is still a firm desire on the part of many
to join with us in the quest for light and instruction.
During the Masonic year just closed, the Grand Lecturer in company
with other Grand Lodge Officers has attended the Constitution Ceremonies of the three Lodges chartered in 194 7 and also three of the six
Instituting Ceremonies of the new Lodges now working under dispensation. In addition, it has been my privilege to meet with our brethren at
many of the Masonic gatherings throughout the jurisdiction. Without
exception, the intense interest in things Masonic continues with undiminished fervor. It is an inspiration to go among the workers in Masonry, for it brings a renewed vigor and drive to those of us who are
charged with responsibility.
INSPECTORS-Under our present system, the most important
ritualistic officers in the jurisdiction are our Inspectors. It is their hard
work and capable guidance that makes for our high standards of operation. These men give long hours of service at great sacrifice to their
families and their businesses.
During the past year the heavy turnover in their ranks continues.
Three Inspectors have been appointed to take the place of those who
have been called by death to their great reward; twelve have replaced
those who have resigned for various reasons. The Inspectors who have
passed away will, I am sure, be properly eulogized by our Committee
on Necrology. Those who have found it necessary to retire will, I am
certain, be remembered for their valuable contribution to the Craft.
It is rather diffcult to make reference to a particular individual for
special mention when there are so many who deserve recognition.
I would be remiss, however, if I did not call attention to the outstanding service of Worshipful Brother Chester C. Morris who after
25 years of faithful service found it necessary to give up some of his
arduous duties. He served the 38th District in particular and was Dean
of the East Bay Inspectors for more years than he probably will admit.
His service was honorable and I found him to be a loyal friend. His

72

..

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

contribution to California Masonry will not be forgotten by the hundreds
of officers who served under him during his 25 years as Inspector.
The same can be said of Worshipful Brother Frank G. Falloon,
formerly of the 75th District, who occupied ~ similar P?sitio? as Dean
of the Los Angeles group. His loyal and faithful service will be well
remembered by his brethren in the southland.
Following custom, a report form was sent to the various Inspectors
calling for desirable information. To my great delight, 119 of our 123
Inspectors promptly returned their questionnaires. This is the finest
response that has ever been made and I express my thanks at this time
for their courtesy.
The information furnished has provided much valuable material
which will enable the Assistant Grand Lecturers to concentrate on weak
spots and otherwise correct certain conditions. The hig~-ligh~ of the
reports, however, was the fact that in the discharge of thei~ dut~es over
60 000 miles of official travel were covered. Another question disclosed
th~t only 17 of our 123 lnspectoral Districts in the Juris~iction are not
organized into Officers' Associations. Most o~ these are i~ remote sections where travel conditions render it impractical to organize. I am sure
this information will bring joy to the hearts of Past Grand Master John
Stewart Ross who breathed life into this splendid idea.
It might be of interest also to note that several of the Inspectors are
now successfully organizing Coaches' Association under the same setup as officer groups.
ASSISTANT GRAND LECTURERS-The past year has seen
several changes in our line-up of Assistant Grand Lecturers.
Past Grand Master Gilbert C. De Forest, who with the exception
of his four years on the progressive line in Grand Lodge, served as
Assistant Grand Lecturer since 1936. Owing to personal matters. he
found it necessary to retire from active work in our Ritual. Those of us.
who have worked with Gil found him to be a source of strength and he
will be sorely missed. Worshipful Brother Mervyn E. Hanshaw, Inspector of the 49th District, was appointed to take his place on March
16, 1948 and he has entered upon his duties in a creditable manner.
Our hardest blow was the sudden death of Sidney K. Lehman, who
was Assistant Grand Lecturer of Division D in Southern California
from the very beginning of the present system in 1933. No man was
more beloved than our dear friend Sid and his place will be hard to fill.
He had a gracious manner and in the long years of our friendship, I never
heard him utter a harsh work about any one. Our one consolation is that
he will live in our hearts for all time. On April 19, 1948 Worshipful
Brother Frank Harwell, Jr.. Inspector of District 84, was appointed as
his successor with the unanimous approval of his colleagues of southern
California.

SCHOOLS OF INSTRUCTION-The mid-year Schools of Instruction for Inspectors were held in the various Divisions as follows:
Division Bon May 15-16, 1948 conducted by Assistant Grand Lecturer Walter von Konsky, also present: Assistant Grand Lecturer Mervyn E. Hanshaw and the Grand Lecturer.
Division C on June 5-6, 1948 conducted by Assistant Grand Lecturer
Obed W. Carr; also present: Assistant Grand Lecturer Walter von
Konsky and the Grand Lecturer.
Division D on May 7-8-9, 1948 conducted by Assistant Grand Lecturer Frank Harwell, Jr.. also present: Assistant Grand Lecturer Walter
von Konsky and the Grand Lecturer.
Due to the reorganization of Division A, it was impossible to hold a
meeting of the entire division. However, a number of Inspectors of this
division met with Division B at their meeting on May 15th and 16th.
The School of Instruction required to be held at this Grand Lodge
session was held on the Saturday and Sunday preceding this session and
was well attended.
RITUAL COMMITTEE-During the course of the year, the
Ritual Committee has considered several matters which have been placed
in their hands. At an appropriate time during the present session, a
separate report will be made.
RECOMMENDATIONSInspectors Expense: Due to additional duties in connection with
newly formed Lodges, increased activity in the lnspectaral group
and the expanded mid-year School Program, it is recommended that
the appropriation for Inspectors' Traveling Expense be increased
from $3,000.00 to $3,500.00.
2. Ritual Committee Expenses: The Ritual Committee as presently
formed does not have as much experience as in previous years and
it is desirable that the Assistant Grand Lecturers should be afforded
the opportunity of meeting together more frequently. It is, therefore,
recommended that the appropriation for this purpose be increased
from $2,500.00 to $3,000.00.
3. Amendment to Section 53 of Ordinances: Section 8 requires each
Inspector to report the working condition of each Lodge in his
District to the Grand Lecturer on or before the first day of May of
each year.
In discussing this section with the various Inspectors, they have
asked that additional time be provided to properly evaluate the conditions in their respective Districts, particularly in the case of current Lodge Officers. I see no objection in complying with their request and the following recommendation is made:
That Paragraph 8 of Section 53 be amended by striking out
the word "May" and substituting therefore the word "July".

"THE MASONIC CITIZEN IN TO-DAY'S WORLD"
JunGE ALBERT C. WOLLENBERG, Grand Orator

t

Most Worshipful Grand Master, Past Grand Masters, Grand Lodge
Officers, Distinguished Guests and Members of Grand Lodge:
As Americans and as Master Masons, we gather here in one of the
most crucial hours of all time.
Specifically, we are met to transact the affairs of our Grand Lodge,
to discuss its problems and consider its program. But in a broader sense
we are here to wrestle with far greater and more serious issues.
Now, more than ever before, a harried world needs to see the light
by which Master Masons work, to live according to the square, and to
·
keep passions within due bounds.
In many lands statesmen are struggling to preserve a hard won
peace. Against terrifying odds they are seeking to tighten the links in
the weakened chain of human brotherhood, to guarantee human rights
for all mankind, and to make this world a safe place for everyone.
Perhaps we, of the Craft, should set the example. I believe we
should. ·
Ours is an ancient creed. Our philosophy and our teachings have
withstood the test of time and tempest. The teachings that are needed
for a world at peace are the precepts of Freemasonry; the ideals that
make for peace are the principles for which we have worked through
generations.
Today mankind is at the crossroads. Jealousies and intrigues threaten
to undo the sacrifices of countless heroes who gave their lives that man
might dwell in peace, in justice and in decency.
Our great democratic ideology is at stake. Foreign isms threaten us.
Only by democracy's preservation can we hope to attain the ideals for
which we stand.
Man has harnessed the forces of nature as never before. Unseen
power has been seized by the cunning of science and human ingenuity
to fashion force not for good but for evil-for destruction and devastation.
Either we must learn to live together or we must resign ourselves
to die together. The A tom bomb leaves no other choice.

76

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

Freemasonry, we all agree, has paved the way for men to live
together in peace, in brotherhood, in truth and in dignity. That is why
I believe we ·Master Masons, in our Lodges or in our respective fields
of endeavor, face a challenge greater than in any time that has come
before.
The founding fathers of this nation, impelled by a true faith in
democracy and many of them steeped in the fundamentals of Masonic
learning gave this nation and through it the civilized world, a great
human document--one of the greatest ever put on paper. The Constitution of the United States guarantees every person living in free
America equality, justice and fair play.
Between the lines of that Constitution and the Bill of Rights therein
contained and interwoven in its concept and spirit, are the basic principles underlying our great fraternity.
If the time should come when that code becomes a law of nationsof all nations and of all peoples everywhere-men of every creed and
every race and every nation will be following the teachings of Freemasonry.
And that code is nothing more than a common desire to put into
practice the basic tenets of decent living that inspired our recent sacrifices on the battlefields. In that struggle we won the war. Now we are
engaged in a new fight to win the peace.
To win the peace we must banish selfishness and bigotry and
jealousy from the earth. We must make brotherhood a living theme.
We must infuse its spirit into the hearts of man. To do this we must
achieve unity here at home.
We know that through the years the enemies of Freemasonry have
been the foes of human liberty and justice. And we know from history
that the forces which have trod upon the apron and the trowel are the
forces that denied the dignity and the freedom of the common man.
Let us pause to look into events of recent years-within our own
fresh recollections-at the work of tyrants across the seas.
In Germany and in Italy, where Dictators sought to impose the
integrity and power of the State above the individual. Masonry was
one of the first to go. Masonic Grand Lodges and all subordinate Lodges
in Germany were dissolved. All of the most important Masonic dignitaries were sent to concentration camps. The Gestapo seized the membership lists of Lodges and looted their libraries, Temples and homes.
The same procedure was repeated by the Fuehrer when he took
over Czechoslavakia, Poland, Holland, Belgium and Norway. When
France fell, the Vichey government promptly caused the two Masonic
bodies of France to he dissolved, their property seized and sold at
public auction.

Today the nations of the world, through the United Nations, are
trying to put that same creed into practice everywhere. We in America
are lending our fullest moral and political support.
Everywhere men of fairness, of intelligence and of dignity are
striving to support our government and through it the United Nations.
From Washington has come, not so long ago, a momentous document, the report of the Committee on Human Rights. In a word it spells
democracy, it spells America.
From some quarters of the nation we hear rebellion against its
findings but you and I know that its tenets have been incorporated into
the platforms of our major parties. And rival candidates for the Presidency are spousing them.
What are those principles so sharply pointed up by the report of
the Committee?
Actually what, in essence, do they contain but the same Masonic
teachings of fair play, of equality, justice and brotherhood that you
and I hear again and again within the Lodge room.
And because they are so identical with our own Masonic teachings,
I believe that you and I have a responsibility to see that the Committee's principles become a vital part of our every-day living.
The Committee has recognized, as you and I know, that within our
land work un-American forces, preaching bigotry, spreading lies against
one group of good Americans or another.
Their purpose is to gain power by divide and conquer strategyby turning Christian against Jew, native against foreign born, negro
against white, worker against employer.
But you and I-and the rank and file of good Americans know, that
our democratic way of life depends upon unity and that to preserve
democracy we must preserve our national unity. And when unified
there is nothing on this earth America cannot accomplish.
We must be ever alert to the teachings of the rabble rousers and the
hatemongers in our midst. Whether they rant against the Jews or the
Catholics or the Protestants-whatever lies they spread-we must
recognize them for what they are-c;ommon traitors to America and to
the brotherhood for which we stand.
As the Late Wendell Wilkie, a champion in the struggle for human
liberty and equality, once said:
"Our way of living together in America is a strong but delicate
fabric. It is made up of many threads. It has been woven over many
centuries by the patience and sacrifice of countless liberty-loving
men and women. It serves as a cloak for the protection of the poor
and rich, of black and white, of Jew and Gentile, of foreign and
native born.

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

79

"For God's sake let us not tear it asunder. For no man knows
or.ce it is destroyed, where or when man will find its protectiv~
warmth again."
And. then there are the words of that widely-known radio champion
of the rights of men-Kate Smith-who, though a woman, speaks as
might any good Master Mason. She says:
"I don't pretend to know all the things that will have to be done
for a lasting peace-but I do know something about people.
"It seems to me that faith in the decency of human beings-is
what we must have more of, if there is to be a future for all of us
in this world. We read in the papers every day about conferences
on the best way to keep the peace.
"Well, I'm not an expert on foreign affairs-and I don't pretend
to know all the complex things that will have to be done for a
lasting peace. But I am a human being-and I do know something
about people. I know that our statesmen-our armies of occupations,
our strategists-may all fail, if the peoples of all the world don't
learn to understand and tolerate each other.
"Race hatred-social prejudices-religious bigotry-they are thf
dise~ses th~t. e~t a.way the fibres of peace. Unless they are ex.
termmated it is mevitable that we will have another war.
"And where are they going to be exterminated? At a conference
ta?le? ~ot by a long shot. In your own city, your own church, your
children s school. perhaps in your own home. You and I must do
it~very father and mother in the world, every teacher, everyone
who can rightfully call himself a human being.
"Yes, it seems to me that the one thing the peoples of the world
have got to learn if we are ever to have a lasting peace, is-tolerance.
Of what use will it be if the lights go on again all over the worldif they don't go on in our hearts?"
The lights. What light is Kate Smith actually talking about?-It
is the light by which Master Masons work. The world needs more of it.
You and I. in my judgment, can see that the world gets it. At least, all
of us can set an example.
Not long ago I read a pledge for Americans-a few crisp and wellpointed lines written by a distinguished American jurist and statesman
-:-Judge Joseph A. Proskauer, retired member of the New York Bench.
I m going to read that pledge because its spirit and its purpose is one
that will strike responsiveness in the heart of every Master Mason:
"I will daily deal with every man in business, in social and in
political relations, only on the basis of his true individual worth.
"I will never try to indict a whole people by reason of the
delinquency of any member.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

"I will spread no rumor and no scandal against any sect.
"In my daily conduct I will consecrate myself, hour by hour, to
the achievement of the highest ideal of the dignity of mankind,
human equality, fellowship and brotherhood."
There is much more that I could say but it's all locked within our
faithful breasts-it all sums up in the secrets of a Master Mason.learned in our travels along the rough and rugged road. And so, I am
going to close with the story of the little boy who wanted his father
to read him the comic paper-a story that touches closely what I've
tried to say.
. A father was busily engaged in his reading one evening and he
didn't want to be disturbed. Close by on the floor sat his little son. The
boy kept pleading, "Please, Daddy, please, read me the funnies."
The father begged for time. kept asking for just a few more minutes.
He wanted to finish what he was reading.
But the little boy was persistent. The father's patience was being
exhausted. On a table close to his chair he spied a newspaper, its pages
open to a large, complicated map of the world. The man grabbed it
and pulled a pair of scissors ·from the drawer. He called the boy to his
side and said:
"Look, son, I'm going to cut up this map of the world. You put it
together again-the right way, of course-every bit of it-and when
you've done that, bring it to me. I'll read you the funnies then."
The boy was off and his father settled down to what he was ~ure
would be a long and comfortable period of reading "With9ut interruption.
, But he was mistaken. Soon the boy was back. He had put the map
of the world together again-perfectly-piece by piece. · . ·.
"Son," said the startled father, "you've done it-a hundred times
faster than I had expected. You've earned your right to. have me read
you the funny papers. But-first, tell me,-how' d you ever do it so
quickly?"
The boy looked up wistfully and smiled. "This way, Dad," he
began. "You didn't notice, but before you started cutting, I saw the
other side of that page and on the other side of the map of the world was
the simple-very simple:- figure of a man. So I just put the man together and when I'd done that, the world was together again, too."
My brethren, let all of us, you and I. dedicate ourselves anew to
preaching the creed of Masonry-a creed that will put men together
again-and I am certain, as you must be, that once we've done that,
the world will be together again too.

Report of Committee
on
Twenty-ninth Annual Observance of Public Schools Week

Adopted.

To the M. W. Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California.

~

The report of this Committee last year began by quoting the opinion
of the Master of one of our Lodges with respect to the extraordinary
success of the observance of Public Schools Week in his community.
That opinion was quoted because it was typical of what a great many
other Masters said in their reports. Again this year, and for the same
reason, we introduce our review of the reports from the Lodges by
quoting the Master of a Lodge which for many years has consistently
reported very successful observances in the community in which it is
located. Among other things, he said:
"I was told by school authorities that this was the best and
largest observance ever held:-both from the standpoint of attendance and public interest. There was also more active participation by the older students."
Such was the success of last year's observance in that community.
as elsewhere, that comment such as this seems to us especially noteworthy. And as has been intimated, it is only typical of scores contained in reports from other Lodges. We quote only one, and that,
in part. for another reason. In the course of an extremely interesting
report, the Master of that Lodge said :
"This year's observance was one of ·the finest-due to the
quality of the programs presented and to the enthusiastic interest
the public has in the current school program of building projects,
and in the financial support which will be required."
It is undoubtedly the extraordinary public interest in the problems
confronting the schools which accounts, in great part, at least, for this,
and last year's success; and because these problems are being persistently brought to the attention of the people in every community.
While it would appear that there has been some amelioration, the
problem of teacher shortage has not yet been solved: and with the
increase in the school population in California, it has become increas-

84

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

ingly difficult to provide a sufficiently large number of class rooms.
Double, and in some instances, triple, school sessions are far more
common than they should be. In one city, the situation was forcefully
brought to the attention of the people in a splendid editorial urging all
citizens, as well as parents of school children, to avail themselves of the
opportunity presented by the observance of Public Schools Week, to
get first hand information of the problems confronting the schools. It
seems to us that the following excerpts from that editorial are well
worth quoting:
"During the interval between 1940 and 1946, California's population increased 38 per cent in comparison with a National gain of
6 per cent.* * * Our schools are crowded to the point where every
public-spirited citizen is ashamed. Education is being handed out
on an assembly line basis with the hours available for each student
sharply reduced, and with double and triple sessions in some of
the schools. There are now 11 7 double, and 7 triple sessions; and
more ·expected next Fall."
"A double session means that a child's time in school is materially reduced so that his seat can be occupied by another pupil.
By double sessions children lose approximately two and one-half
school months per year on the upper level, and one and one-half
months on the lower level."

. "If you are interested in making this a great and popular city,
if you want the citizens who will take your places to have the best
education possible. then set aside a couple of hours of your time
this week to visit the schools, talk with the teachers and get to the
heart of their problems, and discuss your findings with your friends:
and then maybe we can all pull together to remedy a situation that
should never have been permitted to exist."
This was but .one of an unusually large number of editorials constituting an extremely important part of the publicity given our latest
observance. Along the same lines as the one just quoted was another
reminding the people of that community that local district taxes and
bond issues would not finance the class room need; that the State would
have to assist out of the $20,000,000 fund appropriated by the Legislature for "impoverished" districts; that the class room shortage is
matched by teacher shortage; that more than 11,000 emergency teachers,
twenty-five per cent of all teachers in the State, have had to be recruited
to keep the schools open; that the birthrate is booming; that a million
or more babies have been born in California since 1940; and that last
year's total is well over 250,000--and concluding with these queries"Are make-shift class rooms adequate? Are the needs increasing? Are

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

85

,.
finances sufficient? Can the local property owner pay the whole bill?
Incidentally, in the issue of the newspaper carrying that editorial
there was a clever and effective publicity stunt. Interspersed throughout
the pages were "spot announcements" similar to those used in broadcasting, referring to Public Schools Week, and urging the public to visit
the schools.
Many of the editorials were devoted to the observance itself as a
factor in community life, pointing out its value, and crediting our Fraternity with its inauguration. One of these might well serve as a Bulletin
of Suggestions for those charged with the responsibility of making the
arrangements for an observance. After referring to the various proclamations which had been issued, the editorial continued: ·
"Public Schools Week is not proclaimed as a week of festivities and exercises. though many schools interpret is as such, and
in arranging their programs. they put on special events as a form of
entertaining the parents and visitors."
"Each school should hold open house and each parent should
be encouraged to visit the schools during this time, not to be entertained by a special program, but to see and learn the regular
routine of every day school life."
"Every parent should be given the opportunity to visit and
observe just what goes on in the school room, get a firsthand view
as to how and to what end, and in what direction, the mind of their
child is being guided, get a better understanding of what is expected of the children, and of most importance, become acquainted
with those in charge of the teaching of their children."
"Every parent should make it a point to visit the schools. enter
the class rooms, get acquainted with the teachers. watch closely
what is being done, and resolve that our children shall never lack
the mutual understanding between home and schools which is
essential to good education. * * * Public Schools Week should be
a week of parent education, a week spent in bringing the parents
and the teachers closer together; and not a week of festivities that
leaves a wrong impression in the minds of the parents."
"Many parents, today. feel that there is too much play in our
schools; this no doubt is caused by the fact that in .most cases when
they. the parents. are invited to the schools, a special program is
put on, they see the more talented children perform, and get the
impression that things of this kind are of the n;iost importance in
the routine of class room study. * * * Public Schools Week should
be a week of serious effort to better acquaint the parents more
thoroughly with what goes on in the class room and bring the

86

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

parents and the teachers closer together and create a better understanding between the two."
There were this year an unusually large number of plays and
pageants. It was no doubt due to the fact that this is the first of California's three "Centennial Years"; and because of the hope expressed by
the Superintendent of Public Instruction, in a bulletin set to the school
people, that teachers and principals would make available to their pupils
material that would enable them to express an appreciation of various
aspects of California history. The motif of practically all of them was
the celebration of some event in the history of California from the discovery of gold January 24, 1848 to the admission of California into the
Union in 1850.
The favorite theme seems to have been the discovery of gold. From
a city in which the observance is always an unqualified success there
came a report of what was said to have been the first reproduction of
Stephen Longstreet's play "One Hundred Years Ago," with the original
script and music of its presentation at the Coloma Centennial on January
24, 1948.
This was referred to by the Chairman of the Committee as "probably
the highlight of the observance, or at least the most spectacular single
event," and with the comment that "it was excellently presented and
enthusiastically received and further demonstrated the abilities of the
students and faculty of our High School."
Now while this and the other pageants and plays, of course, furnished entertainment, they served another purpose. They were, (to
quote Superintendent Simpson), "Stimulating programs that emphasized
the educational value of the Centennial Celebration"; and they must
have aroused, not only in the participants, but as well, also in the audiences, a desire to learn more about California's dramatic history and
magnificent traditions; as they portrayed the romance, drama and
achievements of the century just behind us. They do not, therefore,
fall into the category referred to as "entertainment" in the editorial to
which attention has been called.
Even where.there was no play or pageant, there were many observances, as there have been in the past, with a "theme" or "motif"; and
among these themes this year were "Centennial Year," "Influence of
Covered Wagon Days," "Gold Rush Cavalcade," "Gold Discovery,"
and "California the Golden." Many of the programs built around such
themes included music, tableaux and dancing of pioneer days, with the
participants in the garb of that time. In some of the observances a program of this sort was presented on the last night of the week by the

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

87

pupils of schools which had held open house during the week with visits
by the parents and the public.
The Freedom Train was also a motif of several observances, either
in that form alone, or in combination with other words and phrases such
as "The Public School-Keep It Our Foremost Freedom Train," and
"Freedom Train's First Team-The Teacher, Your Child and You."
Incidentally, among the school exhibits in one city there were facsimiles, made by the students, of many of the documents displayed in
the Freedom Train.
Materially contributing to this year's unprecedented success was
the hearty support received from those organizations which so enthusiastically cooperate with us each year: American Legion, (Department of California), American Legion Auxiliary, American Association
of University Women (California State Division). California C. I. 0.
Council, California Congress of Parents and Teachers, California Farm
Bureau Federation, California Federation of Women's Clubs, California
League of Women Voters, California State Chamber of Commerce,
California Teachers Association, California Junior Chamber of Commerce, California State Federation of Labor, California Teachers Association, California School Trustees Association, and Association of California County School Superintendents.
From the newspaper clippings, it appears that with the proclamation
of the Grand Master and that issued by Governor Warren, wide publicity was also given the announcements and statements issued by the
cooperating organizations: and of course, the local papers everywhere
carried in full the proclamation issued by the Mayor of the City.
In connection with the reference to proclamations, mention should
here be made of the fact that this year, for the first time in the history
of Public Schools Week in Hawaii, there was a proclamation issued by
the Governor of the Territory. Mention was made of this by the newspapers there: and incidentally, included with the press clippings covering (to quote the report) "one of the most successful years and one
that we can all be well proud of," was an editorial endorsing the observance, and with complimentary reference to our Island brethren. We
quote the following excerpts:
"In emphasizing Public Schools Week, each year the Masons
of Hawaii give support to one of our most cherished institutionsthe Public Schools."
"On the strength of the Public Schools of the nation largely
rests the character of future citizenship."
"Public Schools promote the American tradition in democratic
education and useful citizenship."

The Heads of the Co-ordinate bodies of Masonry were especially

this could be done. And the Grand Commander, John Stewart Ross,

The reference to the Observance made by the Grand Commander
in his report to the Grand Commandery (and perhaps because he is
one of our Past Grand Masters, and has always been a strong sup~
porter of the movement from the time of its inception, when he was the
Inspector of" what was then the 69th, and is now the 108th, Masonic
District), was especially comprehensive. He reviewed the history of
the Observance, defined its purpose, and expressed the hope that the
representatives present would endeavor to make it convenient to join
with the Lodges in the observance of the week in their community:and not merely because they would deem it their duty, but with the
expectation of finding the experience an enjoyable, as well as a profitable
one.

It seems to us that the following excerpt from the Grand Commander's report might well be called to the attention of every Mason:
"The value of this Observan_ce cannot be judged from experi~
ences in any one community, in any one year, and under any one
leadership. Conditions may be such in a community that its
necessity may not be apparent; but if permitted to lapse, its value
may become apparent only when it is too late: because destructive
forces work the more effectively when other forces are asleep. In
this, as in all other things, leadershiP. is all~important."
Because of what has been said with respect to the cooperation received from the Masonic bodies to which reference has been made, it

as Sovereign_ Qrand Inspector General in California to the Scottish

date of next year's Observance. It was explained that the information

Public Schools Week luncheons in Shrine Clubs seem to have
become the rule rather than the exception, as ·they once were. The
programs are varied, but in almost every instance they include an address on some current school problem. The topic at one of the luncheons
this year was "Things You Didn't Know About Your School System."
The guests usually include members of the Board of Education, the
Superintendent of Schools, and frequently other representatives of the
school people. In one city, among the guests are always included one
or more of those in charge of the observance of Public Schools Week.
It was not only in the Shrine Clubs that Public Schools Week
luncheons were held,. There were others arranged by Service Clubs.
These, it would appear, were of two general classes. In one, the
luncheon was held where the members of the club regularly assemble;
· and it was the nature of the program which made it a Public Schools
Week luncheon. In the other, the luncheon was served in the cafeteria
of a public school; and the members of the club, either before or after,
generally after, lunch, were conducted about the school by pupils ap~
pointed for that purpose.
In one community they have what they call "An Inter-Service Club
Luncheon." All the service clubs in the city, with one of them as the
"host club" assemble in a joint session on some day during Public
Schools Week; and the luncheon is held in the cafeteria of a high
school. The clubs alternate as "host club."
The program consists (in addition to the usual introductory features
of a service club luncheon) of an address on an appropriate subject
with instrumental and vocal numbers presented by students. This year
the subject of the address was "A Complete Youth Program." .
There were several Lodges which this year furnished their members
with cards to be returned to the Master with a report of their participation in the observance by visits to the schools. In at least one instance,
the card was a printed U. S. Postal Card with only blanks to be filled
stating the school, or schools, visited, and the date, with any desired
comment. The return address was printed and all that was necessary
to be done (in addition to filling the blanks) was for the member to
sign his name and mail the card.
It is reasonable to assume that cards were returned by only those
who could report at least one visit; and it is perhaps also reasonable
to assume that (generally speaking of course) the return of the cards

As would be expected, after so many years, and with the dissemination of the information contained in these reports, it is not often that
there is now anything entirely novel in the arrangements. or in the program, of any particular observance. This year, however, there was a
real novelty reported in connection with the publicity of an observance.
Lapel ribbons on which was printed (by a high school print shop)
"Public Schools Week-April 26 to April 30-Visit Your School" were
worn immediately prior to, and during, the week, by the clerks in the
retail stores in that community. It was apparently very effective. In
passing, it may be said that there were forty-two organizations par-.
ticipating in the observance. They were referred to in the printed program as "Sponsoring Organizations."
There was another school print shop in another community which
took an active part in the observance there. Each visitor to the Union
High School received a souvenir in the form of a specially printed card
setting forth that the person whose name was printed thereon had
visited the Printing Department of that school during Public Schools
Week, April 26-30, 1948.
Akin to the old query "Which Came First-the Hen or the Egg?"
is the question of whether the amount of newspaper publicity is dependent on the extent of public interest in the subject covered, or if it
is the publicity which creates that interest. Whatever may be the fact,
there can be no question that this year both public interest and newspaper publicity reached a very high mark. There were editorials, news
stories, and special articles, with illustrations of all sorts-including
cartoons, individual and group photographs of participants in the programs and of those in charge of the observance, and graphs of various
sorts: and there were even reproductions of old photographs of the
days of "The Little Red School House." In some communities the
amount of newspaper space devoted to the observance of Public Schools
Week was such as to be literally amazing.
Some of the special articles must have been a revelation to those who
read them. Among others was one written by ·a reporter (with a "Byline") who went to school "For View of Classes as They Operate in

Information similar to that contained in this special newspaper piece,
but more of it and in greater detail, is set forth in the brochures and
booklets which were given to visitors at several "open house" functions
this year. Among the most ambitious of these was one which was practically a history of pioneer and early schools, not only in the city in
which the booklet was issued, but in the entire state.
Extensive as was the newspaper publicity this year (and never
before was there more of it) that received from the broadcasting stations was no. less so. And again this year the evident willingness, yes,
apparent eagerness, with which this fine cooperation was given by not
only local stations, but also by the statewide systems, was extremely
gratifying to those charged with the conduct of the observance, and
by whom it was greatly appreciated.
Again this year too, radio played an important part in publicizing
the observance, and in giving information concerning our public schools.
Indeed, because of a situation which could not have been guarded
against, it was in certain communities a very important part.
It will be remembered that in April of this year we had very unusual
weather in California, with torrential rains in certain sections of the
state: as a result, the radio programs were all that some people were
able to enjoy.

It is extraordinary, by the way, that there were such large audiences
in spite of the very inclement weather on certain days. Unfortunately
however, there were some outdoor events which, because of the weather,
were postponed, and in a few instances, completely abandoned.
It is extremely interesting to note that although there has been
marked progress everywhere in making the Observance a community
affair, rather than a purely Masonic event, the fact that it was instituted,
and continues to be fostered, by our Fraternity has been, in recent
years, more, rather than less. publicized.
Not only in the newspapers. but also in school publications, and in
printed programs, and by school people generally. Masonry's intimate
connection with Public School Week is repeatedly referred to and
emphasized.
Typical of this are the following excerpts from a printed "Welcome
to Public Schools Week" by a Superintendent of Schools:
"Under the sponsorship of the Masonic Lodge. Public Schools
Week has become a traditional time in which patrons of education
can better acquaint themselves with the school and its personnel.''

92

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

"The Masonic Lodge, through sponsorship of Public Schools
Week, is again exhibiting its notable service to American public
education." (This, by the way, was in a community in which
there were seventeen cooperating organizations.)
In another community on the back page of the program, the Superintendent gives "The Story of Public Schools Week"-and after reciting
its origin, concludes with_these words:
"Ever since, the Masons have unselflshly supported the schools
and the observance of this special week.-They deserve our appreciation."
A,nd on the inside cover of one of those booklets to which we have
referred-and, incidentally, a very attractively illustrated one depicting
"Steps to Leaming," appears the Proclamation of the Grand Master,
in full.
Reference has been made to the matter not boastfully, but for the
benefit of those of our Brethren, now happily fewer in number than
they once were, whQ are apparently fearful that Masonry will not
receive the credit to which it is entitled. Those Brethren have forgotten,
if they ever knew, that Public Schools Week was not instituted for
the aggrandizement of the Fraternity, but for the benefit of our Public
Schools.
Although, as has been said, it is seldom that there is now anything
entirely new reported, there are from time to time adaptations and
modifications of features which have proved particularly attractive in
other communities.
There was reported this year what was termed "An Appreciation
Banquet." It was held on the Saturday night preceding the beginning
of Public Schools Week: and while, in a way, it was similar to some
of the "pre-week" gatherings of which mention has been made in the
reports from this committee, it was for a different purpose.
The hosts were the members of the joint Committee of the Masonic
Lodges joining in the observance; and the ninety guests were principals
and teachers of the schools in the area. It naturally called public attention to the Week's activity, but its primary and announced purpose was
to "provide an expression of appreciation for the contribution of public
schools to the welfare and development of the community."
That this "Appreciation Banquet" served its avowed purpose, there
can be no doubt. But something more than this must have been effected.
Affairs of this sort are a recognition of not only the worth of our
teachers as such, but of their high place in the civic life of the community: and, incidentally, of their social status. They tend to make the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

93

profession attractive to those young people who now seem disin~lined
to prepare themselves for it. They also tend to create a different and
more intimate relationship between teacher and parent. It would be
strange indeed, if this did not result in a better job of teaching-of
teaching not only a child of the parent with whom the teacher had
become acquainted, but all the children in her classes.
Usually, and as would be naturally expected, practically all the
visitors to any school are parents of the pupils of that school. This
year, even in the very large communities, that was not so universally
the fact; although in one city where it was a case of "standing room
only" at almost all the evening affairs, parent attendance broke all
previous records.
There were several reports of visits by public spirited citizens who
had no children in the school. It was assumed that at least some of
them were desirous of ascertaining the truth or falsity of the arguments
being made for a proposed bond issue. They probably wanted to see
with their own eyes the over-crowded, obsolete and hazardous conditions which could be overcome only by the contemplated school construction program.
Whatever may have been the reason, a very interesting, and unusual,
situation was reported by one of the Lodges as showing the extent of
public interest. Visitors who had no children in school constituted more
than twenty-five per cent of the total number of visitors. There were
1200 visitors registered: and of these ·t here were only 841 with children
in school. Incidentally, the total pupil enrollment was approximately
1600.
Notable as was the increase in the number of visitors to the schools
and in the size of the audiences at the various functions, the success of
the Twenty-ninth Observance of Public Schools Week is not to be
measured by that alone; nor alone by the amount of publicity received
from the newspapers and broadcasting stations: or the fine cooperation
of the school people and of the organizations which join with us each
year. All must be considered together.
From every point of view, and in every aspect, of our latest observance, an extraordinarily high mark was set. Whether or not it will be
reached (and perhaps surpassed) next year depends entirely on the
effort which will be made. There is fair promise of it in the reports
from many places that preparations have been already started.
One Lodge reported that there is to be a preliminary meeting early
in December: and in another community there was a meeting held in
May, immediately after the close of this year's observance, to outline
plans for an even better observance next year.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Promising, too, is the fact that several of the reports make mention
of the organization of permanent committees for the annual observance
of Public Schools Week. Furthermore, this year's observance had
hardly come to its close before inquiries were being received from school
authorities who, in arranging their calendars, wanted to know the date
of next year's observance-April 25, 1949 (the fourth Monday in
April).
It is to be hoped that before that day arrives there will have been
a change for the better in the situation which, as stated in one of the
editorials quoted, "should never have been permitted to exist." But let
us as Masons have ever in mind, ( not merely in the fourth week in
April but in every week in the year, and on every day in the week), that
teacher shortage, over-crowded class rooms, double sessions, and obsolete school buildings are not the only danger threatening our public
schools. And let us as Masons not only have that in mind, but let us,
as citizens in our respective communities be ready to do something about
it. Let us be willing and eager to join with other friends of public education in meeting and overcoming that danger, whatever may be its kind
or nature, and from whatever source it may come.

CONDITION OF THE HOMES

Your Board of Trustees has repeatedly called the attention of
Grand Lodge to the work which should be done both at Covina and at
Decoto to keep the properties repaired and rehabilitated and in a condition of which the Fraternity may be proud. It has been possible now
to undertake this work of rehabilitation and reconstruction and, in the
case of Covina, at least, to complete it.
The Board reported last year that the contracts had been let to rehabilitate the Home at Covina and it is gratifying to be able to report
this year that all of that work has been done. All who have visited the
Home at Covina and inspected the completed job are enthusiastic in their
praise of the accomplishments. The buildings have been brought up to
a high state of repair, many things which have been planned for a long
time have at least been carried to completion both in new features and
in the beautification of existing portions of the buildings. The total
cost has been $200,153.11.
The work referred to in the last report of the Trustees with reference
to the work at Decoto, Page 115, 1947 Proceedings, is being carried
forward as rapidly as conditions permit. As of October 1st, the architect reports approximately 40% complete. The total contracts let to date
aggregate approximately $620,000.00. This does not include painting;
it is estimated that the painting will cost approximately $45,000.00.
Other work contemplated will be rehabilitating roadways, making certain changes· in all of the buildings, as a result of orders issued by th~
State Fire Marshall. The Board of Trustees is also considering the
construction of a home for the superintendent, away from the main
building. As soon as this has been accomplished, it is their intention to
employ an assistant to the superintendent, a need which has been recognized by all those familiar with the operation of the Home.

ENLARGEMENT OF BOARD

As presently constituted, the Board of Trustees of the Masonic
Homes of California consists of the Deputy Grand Master, the Senior
Grand Warden and Junior Grand Warden, ex Officio, and four trustees
appointed for four year terms by successive Grand Masters. Of the
appointive trustees, two must be from Lodges in the vicinity of the
Home at Decoto and two in the vicinity of the Home at Covina. The
three elected Grand Lodge officers usually are selected alternately from
the Northern and Southern parts of the state. Hence, the Board of
Trustees is composed of approximately equal numbers from the North
and the South.
While the full board meets together from four to six times each year,
the bulk of its work is transacted in meetings of the Southern half on
Tuesdays and the Northern half on Fridays and action taken by either
half is transmitted to the other before taking effect. No undue burden
is imposed when the Grand Lodge officers are residents of San Francisco
or Los Angeles or the immediate vicinities. There is a marked tendency,
however, to select regularly someone who resides at a distance from
these two metropolitan centers for the elective posts. This presents a
very practical problem for the sectional meetings of the Board. We
anticipate that it will not be lessened as time passes.
We therefore recommend that the Board of Trustees be increased
by the addition of one more trustee residing in the vicinity of each Home.
If the present term of four years was continued the result would be that
in some years there would be two vacancies and in other years only
one, but by shortening the tenure to three years, the terms of two trustees would expire each year.
We also recommend that our statutory provisions be modified to
provide that when a trustee shall have served nine years upon the
Board, he shall be ineligible for reappointment until the lapse of one
year. Such provision is to be found in other organizations and in practice
has been found meritorious.
.
To the several ends just discussed we propose an amendment to
section 79 of the Ordinances of the Grand Lodge and move that it be
referred to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes and on Jurisprudence. We propose that said section 79 be amended to read as
follows:
Sec. 79.
The Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California shall be
nine in number. The Deputy Grand Master, Senior Grand Warden
and Junior Grand Warden shall be Trustees ex-officio, the other
six Trustees shall be appointed by successive Grand Masters. The
term of appointive Trustees shall be three years from the close of

98

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

the annual communication of the Grand Lodge. Three appointive
Trustees shall be residents in the vicinity of the Home at Decato
and three shall be residents in the vicinity of the Home at Covina.
If a Trustee shall serve three consecutive terms after 1948, he
shall be ineligible for reappointment until the lapse of one year.
They shall be the successors of the Trustees originally appointed
under the resolutions adopted by the Grand Lodge in 1892 and
subsequently thereto.
Incumbent appointive Trustees shall continue in office for their
unexpired terms respectively and the Grand Master shall appoint
a Trustee residing in the vicinity of the Home at Covina to a
term ending in 1949 and another such Trustee to a term ·ending
in 1950. Their successors shall be appointed to terms of three years
each.

In the fiscal year ending July 31, 1937, there was a total of 151
women at Decato with an average age of 73.39, and during that yeaB
16 were admitted with an average age of 74.25. Ten years later, that
is to say, July 31, 1947, there were 172 women at Decato with an aver~
age age of 78 years and 32 were admitted with an average age of 76.87.
Again this clearly indicates that the average age of the women residents
at Decato is going up as is likewise the average age of the women who
are admitted.
This continued rise of the average age of the residents at Decato
is one of the reasons for the shortage of rooms. And because of the
shortage of rooms for women, it is not now, and during the entire year,
has not been, possible to admit a woman immediately whose application
has been acted upon favorably. But the completion of the building for
nurses and women employees now under construction will release rooms
in the main building which will relieve this shortage. Although not so
acute, there is likewise a shortage of rooms for married couples. But
there is nothing planned in the building program on which we are now
engaged to relieve that shortage.

POPULATION

It must be born in mind that the membership in the Lodges of Cali~
fornia is increasing, year by year, and we may reasonably expect that
there will be increased demands upon us both at Covina and at Decato
and we assume that it is the intention of the Fraternity to plan to meet
these demands.

The population trend at both Decato and Covina continues to pre~
sent an interesting situation as was stated last year. It is interesting to
note that the total applications to Decato for the year 1947 and for the
year 1948 are almost identical. The applications for Covina have been
accelerated somewhat but there is still not a very great population gain
there. It is interesting to note what has taken place in the last ten years
both in relation to Decato and Covina, and particularly in relation to the
average age of those admitted to Decato and those remaining there.
;Ten years ago, that is to say, at the close of the fiscal year in 1937,
there were at Decato 201 men with an average age of 74.61 years
and during the year there were admitted 37 men with an average age
of 73.72 years. During the fiscal year which closed on July 31. 1947,
just ten years Jater, the total number of men at the Home was 127
with an average age of 77.97 years, and there were admitted 42 men
with an average age of 76.92. This indicates that the average age of
the men at Decato is steadily rising as is likewise the average age at
the time of admission. The comparative figures for 1948, that is the
fiscal year closing July 31, 1948, are: total number of men at the Home
was 121 with an average age of 76.11 years; number of women at the
Home was 180 with an average age of 77.64 years. There were 27 men
admitted with an average age of 76.11 and 32 women with an average
age of 75.5.

We reported to you last year that the general finances of the Masonic
Homes were in excellent shape, but we pointed out that it was necessary
to spend in excess of a half million dollars for work contemplated or
actually under construction. As a matter of fact, it has been necessary to
spend two hundred thousand dollars at Covina and to contract for more
than a half million dollars at Decato with the prospect that there is
perhaps another one hundred fifty thousand dollars to be spent at that
location.
We pointed out last year that the Homes were being maintained with~
out any contributions from the Lodges except such payments as are made
for admissions in excess of the Lodge quota.
Your Board last year recommended that a provision for the constitu~
tional requirement of 50c for building fund be repealed and by action of
Grand Lodge that was repealed. Your Board had previously recom~
mended for two years that there be no per capita tax levied for mainten~
ance and therefore iJJ. the year which has just closed the Lodges paid no
per capita tax and no building fund levy.
We should like to refer again to paragraph four of last year's report
under the heading of Finances in which we explained the source of the
funds for the support of your Masonic Homes. It now becomes apparent

brings the 49th Superintendent's report of the operation of the Home
and the 8th of my stewardship.

not materially changed this year. At the beginning of the year there
were 172 women and 127 men who are comfortably housed, and who,
generally speaking, are quite contented and most appreciative of their

Masons throughout California. During the year, 32 women and 27 men
were admitted; and we lost by death 22 women and 33 men and 2 women
wE're withdrawn, leaving at the end of the year 180 women and 121 men,
a total of 301. Included in this total are 14 married couples.
The health condition of the residents of the Home has been very good
during the year. However, a very large percentage of the members are
well along in years. therefore it is reasonable to expect many of them
to be feeble and infirm. At present there are 54 men and women being
cared for in our hospital, and 16 semi-invalid women being cared for on
the fourth floor in the east wing. The hospital has been crowded most
of the time, while the east win-g as been full at all times, and several
women in the main building are waiting to be transferred to this department. The crowded condition. in these departments will be corrected

REPORT OF SUPERINTENDENT-COVINA HOME

To the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California:
It is again my privilege and my duty to present to you this my third
annual report for the year ending July 31, 1948.
During the past year much has been accomplished in the program of
rehabilitating the Home. The results obtained from this extensive work
have brought forth much favorable comment from visiting members of the
fraternity. All demands of the State Fire Marshall have been complied
with. The required steel fire stairways were worked into the plan with·
out seriously detracting from the appearance of the buildings. Color and
new fabrics have added greatly to the interiors of the children's build-

105

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

ings. To keep the program of the children on a normal basis as nearly as
possible during the alterations required great patience and understanding
on the part of all concerned. To those employed by the Home and to the
firms engaged in the contract work much credit is due.
HoME MEMBERSHIP: This year has brought no increase in Home
membership. The population now is 64. There are 45 boys and 19 girls.
During the year 15 children left us.two by graduation from high school
and ten to their homes to live with parents or relatives. Six of these were
to homes re-established by remarriage of mothers. 0 f the eleven admissions during the year there were ten boys and one girl.
A recent classification of the children under our care shows the following:
Percentage of children having neither parent living ........ 15.7
Percentage of children having one parent living ..............62.5
Percentage of children having both parents living ..........2L8
LODGE VISITATIONS: The interest in the Home shown by Lodges has
been most gratifying. An increase was registered both in number 'of
Lodges and individuals during the year. To these Lodges and to the
associated Masonic orlfclnizations we express our appreciation. Their
generosity in bringing gifts of jams, jellies and treats for the children is
recorded in other sections of the Home's report.
ENTERTAINMENT: During the year the children have enjoyed parties.
programs and movies through the generous thoughtfulness of our many
friends. The traditional Christmas party provided by Monrovia and Soujourners Lodges was again a highlight of the year. 'J'he Lodges of
Pasadena combined to provide facilities for the children to enjoy the
Tournament of Roses Parade. The weekly movies at the Home were
again provided by six of the major studios and were enjoyed more than
ever in the newly remodelled basement auditorium. If those who provided
these and other entertainments could have been here to witness the delight and pleasure of the children they would need no other expression
of appreciation to feel amply repaid for their gifts.
DONATIONS AND GIFTS: The many donations listed for the year have
added greatly to the fuller enjoyment and pleasure of the children.
Though each brings happiness not to be measured by the size or monetary value of the gift, we cannot pass the closing of the year without
special mention of a few. The television sets provided by Loyalty and
Los Cerritas Lodges have contributed much to the recreation program of
the children. The Westerners Masonic Club furnished the drapes and
curtains for the auditorium and have nearly completed the installation
of a 12-inch telescope. To these and all groups which have remembered
the Home we offer our sincere thanks.
SCHOOLS AND COMMUNITY ACTMTIES: The children have made
normal progress in the public schools of the community during the year.

Many have participated in the extra-curricular and sports programs of
their schools.
The Junior groups regularly attend the various Sunday Schools in
Covina. Regular attendance is not compulsory for older boys and girls
but some participate in Sunday school. church and youth programs.
Girl Scouts, Cub Scouts for boys and De Malay have met with favorable response and have provided means for the children to join with
other boys and girls in the life of the community. The Home will be
honored with one of its boys serving as Master Counselor of the local
De Malay Chapter next term.
HEALTH PROGRAM: The year has brought no serious problem in the
children's health program. Thirteen operations for tonsils and adenoids
are recorded. No other serious surgery or accidents occured. The children have been examined at regular intervals by Dr. W. P. Magan who
continues to supervise them closely. The average number of bed patients
during the year was 2.08 per day. Daily visits to the nurse at the Home
Cliinc are made by many children who have developed a good sense of
self-responsibility in helping to keep themselves in good health.
This health program requires of the doctors and nurses work and attention which must be motivated by a sense of duty and devotion to the
children's welfare. Of this service we are especially appreciative.
Dr. Ellwood Laine, dentist, examined and treated 118 cases during the
year. Two children began orthodentia treatment.
FARM AND GROUNDS: The grove, in common with many of this area,
has produced only a fair crop this season. Fruit sizes are small and the
market price therefore low. The portions of the grove in front of the
buildings have been put under a non-tillage method which makes it
unnecessary to work the tractor in these small plots. The borders are
being landscaped to add to the beauty of the grounds. New lawns and
flower beds are established in the front courts and along the main drive.
These are an addition to the general good appearance of the property.
A new tractor and new pick-up truck were purchased during the year
to replace old equipment.
To all who have helped in carrying the work and program of the Home
during the past year we wish to express our sincere thanks. It has been
a pleasure to receive at the Home the members of Lodges, Grand Lodge
Officers, Board of Trustees and others who assist in supporting and
maintaining the Home.
