Report of Committee on Homes Admissions and Applications

To the Most Worshipful Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Free and
Accepted Mason'S of the Jurisdiction of California.
Most Worshipful Sir:
At its annual communication in 1946 this Grand Lodge appointed a
Committee to survey and study the property, operation and management
of the Masonic Homes at Decoto and Covina. While engaged in that
work the committee was frequently urged to recommend changes in the
Rules for Admission to the Homes and to review the action of the
trustees in specific cases. The committee declined to take such action
upon ·t he ground that it had not been appointed for such purposes; but
in view of the urgency and frequency of such requests it did recommend
that a new committee be appointed to make a study of the rules and
the general policy of admission and make its report at this time. The
present committee was appointed for that purpose.
The Rules are printed in full in section 711 of the Ross Digest, but
the Craft, as a whole, are unfamiliar with them. Masons, as a general
thing, base their attitudes toward Masonic Relief. as administered by
the trustees of the Homes, upon the ritual and what they have assumed
to be the function of the Homes at the time of their raising. It is clear
that a broad campaign of education is needed to correct many misunder~
standings in that regard. Inspectors, masters, and other persons in~
terested in applications complain that they are not certain that the rules
mean; that when requested to advise prospective applicants as to the
possibility of admission they cannot give authoritative advice in advance
of formal action by the trustees; and that because of conflicting decisions
and inconsistent action in cases that appear to be based upon identical
facts, they cannot explain the reason for the rulings to the parties
directly affected or chart their future course by established precedents
One of the most frequent statements is that if a Mason ever needs help
it is when he is too ill to care for himself and must have immediate hos~
pitalization.
Before proceeding with a discussion of the criticisms mentioned, it
is desirable that we consider the historical background of Masonic
Relief as administered through the Homes in order that the Rules and
Practice of Admission may be viewed in their true light. For this purpose
we here incorporate a report made for this committee by one of its
members, Brother Frank Harwell Jr.:

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

107

"A Brief Sketch
of
The Historical Background and Development
of
Rules for Admission to Masonic Homes
"At the annual communication of Grand Lodge in October, 1890,
a special committee was appointed by the Grand Master to explore the
feasibility of erecting a Home for Masonic Widows. and Orphans.
"This committee made its report at the communication of 1891. The
report was referred to the Jurisprudence Committee which introduced a
resolution at this same communication to the effect that the Grand
Master be authorized to appoint a committee of nine brethren of the
Grand Lodge who would be empowered to act in all phases of the matter
of such a Home, their acts and decisions to be subject to final approval
by the Grand Master. The resolution was adopted by Grand Lodge.
"In accordance with this resolution, the Grand Master appointed
such a committee, and he reported to Grand Lodge in his annual message
in 1892 that the committee has submitted to him a plan which he had
approved. Following out the provisions of this plan, the Grand Master
reported that he had appointed nine Trustees with the general power,
among others, to adopt by~laws and rules, all subject to approval by
the Grand Master; that he had received written acceptances from these
nine Trustees, and that they had entered at once upon the discharge
of their duties.
"At this same communication of 1892 these nine Trustees made their
first annual report to Grand Lodge, covering their acts for the previous
nine months. Attached to this report and made a part of it was a copy
of the By~laws adopted by these Trustees. Articles IV and V, entitled
'Admission to the Home.' read in part, as follows:
'Section 1. The orphans, half~orphans and widows of deceased
Master Masons, who at the time of their death were members in
good standing of Masonic bodies within the jurisdiction of the
Grand Lodge of the State of California, shall be admitted to the
Home, under such regulations as the Board of Trustees may adopt.
As soon as the finances of the Charity will admit of it, the Board
may make provisions for the maintenance of the aged or infirm
Master Masons who may seek the protecting care of the Home.'
'Section 4. No orphan shall be received into the Home under
the age of 3 years, nor over 14; nor shall any be admitted who have
adequate means of support, nor any half~orphan, whose living
parent is able to support him, unless by special agreement, and

108

109

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

upon the payment of such sum as may be agreed upon with the
Board of Trustees.'
'Section 5. No person of unsound mind, or deaf and dumb, or
contaminated by any contagious disease at the time of application, shall be admitted:
'
'Article V. Section 1. These by-laws may be altered or amended at any regular meeting of the Board, by a majority of all the
members . of the Board, subject to the approval of the Grand
Master.'
"This entire report, including the By-laws, the first of its kind in
the history of Grand Lodge, was apparently received by Grand Lodge
and filed. The proceedings for that communication do not reveal that
any formal action was taken on the report.
"The reports of the Trustees for the next six annual communications
had to do with administration of funds for relief, appeals for contributions to a building fund and accounts of its growth, and preparations
for obtaining a site for the Home and the erection of the first building.
"At the communication of 1899, the Trustees made their report and
included in it, 'Regulations for Admission to the Masonic Home,' subheads 1 to 17 inclusive. Certain of these read as follows:
'8. A Master Mason in good standing in a Lodge of this jurisdiction who is unable to support himself or earn a livelihood, is
of good character, and free from disease, of temperate habits,
not addicted to the use of narcotics, and without relatives who
by process of law can be compelled to support him, may, if
his admission does not interfere with the demands of orphans
and widows applying for admission, be admitted to the Home.

free from any chronic disease, either physical or mental. may
also be admitted.'
'17. The Board of Trustees may admit to the Home Masons.
their wives, widows or orphans, not covered by the foregoing
regulations, upon such terms as they may deem best.'
'Adopted by the Board of Trustees September 14, 1898.'
"In succeeding years we find in the annual reports of the Trustees
many references to problems confronting them incident to the administration of the rules for admission, and appeals to the Lodges for a more
careful scrutiny of applicants for admission. Certain portions of these
reports have a particular bearing on the matter of Rules for Admission,
and their interpretation and application.
"In the Trustees' report for 1918, we find the following:
'Admissions. * * * There has been but one disputed point in
eligibility. A ruling was made by a Grand Master that a female
orphan of a Mason was always an orphan, regardless of age, and
regardless of how many times they may have married outside the
fraternity, and were entitled to relief. Our regulations provide for
admission of orphans under 16 years of age, and we have not
recommended any change. We received 2 applications this year
for orphans 70 years of age. who by the ruling of the Grand Lodge
were entitled to Masonic relief, but by our regulations not entitled
to admission to the Home. Unless otherwise instructed, the Board
will contin.ue under our present regulations.'
"In the Trustees' report for 1919, the following is pertinent and enlightening:
'It not infrequently happens that an application is made for
admission to the Home at Decoto for a person who is not indigent
in the sense governing admissions to the Home, but who is so
situated that he is without a home-( describes a case). Under the
rules and regulations governing the Home, the Trustees were compelled to deny the application.'
'The situation with reference to children is even more embarrssing. In the event of the death of the father, if the mother
is compelled to seek employment and therefore unable to care for the
child, it is admitted to the Home at Covina. In the event of the!
death of the mother, however, the child is not admitted if the
earnings of the father are sufficient to provide for the support of
the child.'
'Under the discretion vested in the Trustees, if the earnings of
the father are not sufficient to pay for some one in whose care
the child may be placed while the father is absent from home, the
child is admitted. 1£, however, the earnings of the father are suffi-

'The theory of course upon which the Homes are maintained

"We find the first reference to the ·authorization for and use of
Outside Relief' in the report rendered in 1922:
'At the last annual communication of the Grand Lodge the
Trustees were authorized to ·assist Lodges in the care of those

'Responsibility of Lodges * * * We have steadily adhered to

"The Trustees' report for 1929 contains the following interesting
statement of policy:
'A matter of policy. In the booklet that was mailed to all
Lodges in April last, giving rules for admission and general information respecting the Masonic Homes, the following paragraph
appears: "The welfare of the child should be the first consideration of the Lodge. No child should be sent to the Home until every
effort has failed to find a place in a private home." * * * Therefore,
very careful investigation should be made not only by your Trustees but by Lodges in every case to ascertain so far as possible if

Masonic Home.'
"In the report for 1934 we find the first reference to the resolution
adopted by the Board governing the reappointment of children to the
Home at Covina, which reads in part as follows:
'Reappointment of Children. In 1931 your Board of Trustees
adopted a resolution providing that the continuance of any child
in the Home beyond the age of 16 must be authorized by special
action of the Board. The superintendent notified each child coming
within the rule to make written application for reappointment,
which applications are considered by the Board at the May
meeting.'
"This brings us the Trustees' report for 1935, in which they stated
they were submitting to Grand Lodge 'a revision of our rules and regulations governing admission to the Homes. * * * with the hope and
desire that Grand Lodge will specifically indicate the policy which should
be pursued by the Trustees with respect to any rule which does not meet
with its approval, we submit the following revision of the rules heretofore in force.' Here follow 'Rules governing admission' substantially
as found in Ross Digest, Section 714, and as revised February 3, 1940,
which are the Rules presently in force.
"It is interesting to note the following which is found on Page 501
of the Proceedings for 1935:
'The report of the Trustees was approved * * * excepting the
report as to the rules adopted by the Board, which were ref erred
to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes. and consideration of the rules was made special order for 2 o'clock Wednesday.
At that time the matter of policy as to rules adopted by the Board
was postponed for .final consideration until the next annual communication.'
"The matter was not taken up or mentioned at the next annual communication.
"One other amendment to these rules was made in 1937, which is
covered in the Trustees· report, as follows:
'Rules for Admission. Amendment to rules as follows: For
each additional applicant (in excess of the quota) admitted to the
Home, or to whom outside relief is given, a charge will be made in
an amount to be fixed from time to time by the Board of Trustees.'
"This concludes the historical review. From a search of the records,
it is apparent that the Trustees at all times, both prior to and subsequent to incorporation of the Homes, have been empowered to adopt
such By-laws for their guidance and for the management of the charity
as they deemed proper and best, subject to the approval of the Grand

112

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Master. This is the law as stated in Section 81, Ross Digest. It therefore follows that the Trustees may adopt such Rules and Regulations
governing admissions to the Homes as they may aeem proper and best.
"Furthermore, when the Trustees, in 1899, adopted the first formal
and comprehensive set of 'Regulations for Admission to the Masonic
Home,' they wrote into these Regulations Section 17 which gave them
the authority to admit certain applicants not covered by the Regulations
upon such terms as the Trustees deemed best. From that day to this, the
Trustees have always held and operated under such discretionary power.
The record does not disclose that Grand Lodge or the Grand Master
at any time has questioned or objected to this policy.

from the historical report, for example, that the original plan inaugurated
in 1890 was to provide for a selected group of widows and orphans.
Subsequently, the plan was expanded to provide for certain Master
Masons and their wives. The purpose at all times was to provide a
home for those who were not in immediate need of actual or continuous
hospitalization. The obvious reason for many restrictions was that
sufficient money was never available to furnish adequate hospitalization for all who might apply. The initial responsibility still rested upon
relatives, if any, and upon the subordinate Lodges. It became apparent,
however, as time went on, that Lodges were often unable to grant
adequate relief in such cases and in 1922 Grand Lodge approved the
trustees of the Homes to grant Outside Relief.

"The record also clearly shows that the Trustees, on various occasions, have asked Grand Lodge for formal approval of Rules for Admission adopted by the Board, and on many occasions have appealed to
Grand Lodge for guidance in the interpretation of the Rules and their
application to perplexing cases. Grand Lodge has seen fit, at times, to
approve--never to guide."

It is at once apparent from a consideration of the foregoing extracts
from our official proceedings since 1890, that if this committee recommends specific changes in the Rules, and if the Grand Lodge at this time
adopts such recommendations, it will be the first time in our history that
Grand Lodge has taken the initiative in such matters. As said in the
report, "Grand Lodge has seen flt, at times, to approve-never to guide."
Without direct suggestion of any kind from this Grand Lodge the trustees ~ave formulated rules based upon practical experience jn the administration of such relief and the rules have been approved either by the
Grand Master or Grand Lodge.
Some ~f the confusion arises from the wording of the rules. In the
interests of clarity, some of them should be modified and the terms
defined. After a discussion of this question with the members of this
committee, the trustees have signified intention to undertake to make
appropriate changes.
The great majority of the Masons of California have never read the
Rules and are entirely unfamiliar with their origin and purpose. Masons,
in general. get their ideas of Masonic Relief from the ritual or from
others who assume that the full burden of providing relief rests upon
the homes in cases where applications can be filed. Whatever California
Masonry may undertake to do ab~ut these problems in the future, there
is no justification historically for such assumptions at the present time.
The prima~ responsibility for Masonic Relief always has rested upon
the subordinate Lodges and the true function of the Masonic Homes of
California, as originally planned and consistently followed ever since
is to supplement such relief within a limited sphere of activity and to th~
extent permitted by the use of such funds as are available. It appears

113

If anyone questions the necessity for such restrictions on admission.
he need only consider the fact that when the present program of modernization of the physical plants is completed approximately $800,000.00
will have been spent within a period of two years and the Homes will
then have only such limited hospital facilities as were contemplated in
the original plans. It is interesting to note, in this connection, that the
State and Federal governments now estimate that it requires nearly
$12,000.00 per bed to build and equip a modem hospital. In spite of the
great strides in financing made in recent years, it is obvious that the
Masonic Homes of California cannot accept everyone who wishes
to apply.
·
It is frequently said that the rules should be so specific and definite
that under any given set of facts anyone could determine in advance
exactly who is eligible for admission. All will agree that this is highly
desirable and the trustees should seek to meet such standards in the
formulation of rules so far as they may be practicable. But experience in
the administration of the Homes, and in the decision of many cases
presented, demonstrates that this is not always desirable. Every lawyer
is familiar with the fact that from the beginning of recorded history
when laws and rules became too rigid undue hardships resulted and
someone had to be given the power, with reasonable limitations, to make
exceptions when the facts justified them, or, as a famous English writer
once put it, to make corrections in the laws "wherein they were defective
by reason of their universality." To permit the trustees to do equity in
passing upon applications, the rules seek, so far as possible, to set up
general standards but they also recognize the power of the trustees to
exercise a wide discretion in cases where peculiar facts appear to justify
an exception to the general rules.
The exercise of this discretionary power leads occasionally to apparently conflicting decisions that are confusing when viewed as precedents,
but it is the opinion of this committee that the right to exercise such
power is salutary and necessary to avoid hardships in exceptional cases.

115

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

As an illustration, cases have arisen where an applicant. otherwise
qualified, could be provided for by compelling relatives to receive the
applicant into their homes. In cases where the relatives are required by
. law to provide for the applicant and where it appears that the applicant
can be reasonably happy, it is the policy to deny the application so
that other more pressing applications can be approved. There are cases,
however, where the facts appear to be identical. but the confidential
reports of investigators or members of the Lodges reveal the fact that
some unfortunate condition prevails in the homes of the relatives and
t~at under the circumstances the applicant should not be required to
live there. In such cases the application is granted but to the casual
observer who has no access to the reports or case histories the action
of the trustees seems to be arbitrary, discriminatory. and inconsistent
with other decisions. Such intangibles frequently dictate the course to
be followed and, in our opinion, demonstrate the need for such discretionary powers.
. Since the initiation of the Masonic Homes Program in 1890, our
ideas concerning relief have changed materially. This is a reflection of
the changed attitude of society generally toward the care of children
and of the aged. Many new factors. such as pension plans and social
security must be considered. The recent increase in the rate of divorce
has raised new and complex problems concerning the children involved.
Old i~eas regar.ding the responsibility of children for their parents have
gone mto the discard. Throughout the nation individuals and the smaller go~ernmental units are seeking constantly to shift the heavy burden
of relief to larger and richer units. It is natural that such a tendency
should affect our attitude toward the problems of Masonic Relief and
the administration and functions of the Homes.
It is our opinion that the plans as originally conceived we~e sound
and suited to the ends to be attained: that although certain minor
change~ could he made by the trustees of the Homes to clarify the rules
a_nd bnng greater certainty into the practice of passing upon applications. the great need at present is for an active program of education
to acquaint the craft with the principles involved. The time has not
yet arrived for a radical departure from established procedures.
Respectfully submitted,

Report of the Board of Control
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The report of the Board of Control must detail not only the activities
of that body but also must contain a complete outline of the work of our
Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus.
It should be pointed out that the Board of Control was created by
the Grand Lodge in 1929. In its hands is placed the authority of main, taining Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus and it is its responsibility to control. supervise and so direct their affairs that they may be
managed efficiently and economically.
This report. like those previously presented to Grand Lodge by the
Board of Control. is another testimonial to the sincerity of effort on the
part of those men who are actively engaged in the work of Masonic
Relief and Employment and represents further proof that they justify
the trust reposed in them.
We are pleased to report close harmony and cooperation existing
between the Board of Control and Boards of Relief. We believe that
there is now a more active interest within Boards of Relief and the working affairs of their organizations. That this is partly due to our frequent
meetings with them, can seem to be of little doubt. The personal contact with the members of these bodies has developed into many close
ties of friendship and understanding. Mutual problems have ·been dis.cussed and decisions reached with the complete cooperation of all.

BoARDS OF RELIEF

The Grand Lodge of California permits lodges having concurrent
jurisdiction to form Boards of Relief for _the purpose of properly relieving the distress of sojourning Masons, their widows and orphans. under
a compact to be agreed upon among themselves and approved by the
Grand Lodge or the Grand Master before becoming effective. Grand
Lodge requires that they provide a method of paying for the expense
of the work in such a manner as shall seem proper. Boards of Relief are
required to report annually showing in detail their work for the year
together with their receipts and disbursements, specifying separately
what, if any. has been expended for relief of non-affiliated Masons.
their widows and orphans. therein sojourning. of this or other jurisdictions and how much thereof. if any. has been repaid.
Such detailed reports have been made and are now on file with the
Board of Control. They show the activities and financial condition of
each of our seventeen Boards of Relief.
Our Boards of Relief are made up of 263 Lodges with a Masonic
membership of 110,600. Each Lodge is represented on the Board of Relief by Trustees selected from among their own membership. The delegates select a secretary whose duty it is to manage, under their direction.
the active operations of the Board of Relief. In matters of relief. only
temporary relief is contemplated, however, they are not restricted in

116

117

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

affording such relief as in their judgment the circumstances may warrant.
Boards of Relief are maintained by a per capita assessment agreed
upon by the trustees which is limited by the maximum set up within
their compact. They may establish employment bureaus and are required
to visit the sick, investigate and administer relief applications, and supervise all Masonic funerals of sojourning brethren in their district.
The statistical records show that they have conducted 792 funerals
during the past year, have made 3466 calls upon the sick, administered
relief or investigated 2481 cases. and handled 1380 cases involving other
types of relief, or a total of 7327 service calls.
$43,718.54 was disbursed for relief during the year.

Your attention is directed to the fact that while Grand Lodge is
committed to the policy of assisting Boards of Relief financially in the
support of Employment Bureaus, in order that they may be done on an
equitable basis, the Board of Control has set up a formula for the allocation of Grand Lodge funds for the Employment Offices. This formula
requires that receipt and expenses allocated to Employment Bureaus
roust be in like ratio, i. e., whatever percentage of total expense of a
Board of Relief is charged against Employment Bureaus, a like percentage of the total receipts shall be devoted to the Employment Bureaus,
and that Grand Lodge will not contribute an amount greater than the
local per capita allocation to Employment. excluding the revenue from
endowments, bequests, gifts, etc. The Board of Control will determine
the proportion of time and effort devoted respectively to relief and employment activities in the several Boards of Relief operating Employment Bureaus, and the operating receipts and expenses shall be allocated on the prescribed percentage basis. T hese percentages are subject
to adjustment by the Board of Control from time to time after adequate
survey demonstrates that such a change is warranted.

EMPLOYMENT BUREAUS

Under the terms of the uniform compact adopted many years ago by
Grand Lodge, Boards of Relief may. with the approval of the Board of
Control, organize and operate Masonic Employment Bureaus.
Seven such offices are now operating in this jurisdiction, five under
the management of secretaries of the Boards of Relief and two, East
Bay and Los Angeles, employing a separate employment manager.
In the employment bureaus, there are 218 Lodges representing a
Masonic membership cf approximately 92,000.
During the past year our employment officers have placed 3064 in
jobs. Were we to operate our offices as commercial employment agencies,
the total fee that these people would have had to pay wuuld have
amounted to $184.665. We, therefore, believe that we can justly say
that our employment offices have saved the Masons and their families
nearly $185,000 in fees.
10,308 applications for employment were received by our offices "during the year and we had 8541 inquiries from employers seeking help.

Every reasonable effort has been made to secure repayment through

During the year, as already mentioned in the report, approximately
$44,000 was paid out by our Boards of Relief. Of this amount, all but
$145 mentioned above was repaid to the Boards by the individual
Brother, who had received aid, his lodge or his Grand Jurisdiction.
The recommendation for reimbursement by the Board of Control is
not to be interpreted as indicating that our cases of financial assistance
are made in the form of a loan. Boards of Relief do not operate in that
manner. When relief is needed and the applicant has established his
Masonic affiliation, then relief is granted willingly, wisely and kindly
and no mention, directly or indirectly, is made as to the return of the
amount advanced. No notes are signed. no promises accepted. Should
the Brother choose voluntarily to return the amount of the relief extended, he simply returns that which, at some future time, will be
available for some other worthy Brother, his widow or orphans.

119

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

When relief is extended to a Brother of another jurisdiction, it is our
interpretation of our obligation that we are acting on behalf of that
Brother's lodge and, therefore, we communicate with his lodge, giving
all of the details of the case and ask that they reimburse us in the amount
advanced. In most cases, we actually receive the lodge's authorization
prior to advancing the money needed. This proceedure is also true in
relief cases involving lodges within our own jurisdiction.
With Grand Lodge standing behind our relief program in returning
uncollectible items, to lodges and Boards of Relief, we feel that we
have thus eliminated the possibility of anyone administering relief in a
niggardly manner or in amounts not sufficient to the occasion. ·

BOARD OF CONTROL

The Board of Control, as established by Grand Lodge, is made up
of five members, each appointed for a term of three years. Your present
Board, as has been the custom, were appointed from all sections of the
State, from San Diego, Los Angeles, Fresno, San Francisco and Sacramento. This territorial selection is not accidental but is a part of the
overall plan whereby the Board can work in dose contact with the
Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus. By this plan, there is at
least one member of the Board of Control accessible to every Relief and
Employment office. The value of this form of selecting members for the
Board has proved the farsighted wisdom of our Grand Lodge and its
Grand Masters, in that important decisions can be made without loss
of time.
Since last Grand Lodge, the Board of Control has met in San Diego
and Sacramento. The Board is in session during this Grand Lodge in
Room 414, which is the Board of Relief and Employment office of San
Francisco. We invite you to bring your relief and employment prob·
lems to us.
The meeting in San Diego was held on January 16th, 17th and
18th and all Boards of Relief and Employment Offices of Southern California were invited to attend with their delegations. Specific times were
set on our agenda for each Board of Relief and sufficient time alloted for
an adequate hearing. Six Boards of Relief attended the meeting and
three employment offices were represented. The members of the Board of
Control were the guests of the San Diego County Masonic Officers
Association at a dinner meeting at which they were given the opportunity of hearing M. W. Claude H. Morrison explain some of the work
done by Boards of Relief and the San Diego Board of Relief in particular.
The chairman of the Board of Control was afforded an opportunity to
address the gathering on the functions and responsibilities of the Boards
of Relief and the Board of Control.
On May 14, 15 and 16, the Board of Control met in Sacramento.
All _Boards of Relief and Employment Offices of Northern California

One year ago, the Board of Control decided upon a uniform method
of handling the records of our Employment Offices. This system proved
simple, efficient and economically sound and lends itself to rapid and
accurate audit. Realizing the value of reports that are comparable, the
Board of Control continued its study of record keeping and on August
1st, 1948, extended the system to all Boards of Relief. A complete set
of instructions covering the method to be used under the new system
was prepared in pamphlet form which is called "Standard Practice
Bulletin for Masonic Boards of Relief and Employment Service." When
the proceedures as outlined in this folder are followed, the financial data,
statistics on employment . accumulated at each office and the reports
therefrom will be uniform and comparable. The data recorded and the
substantiating documents will be maintained in a manner which will
make it feasible to audit the transaction of each office with a minimum
amount of work. The folder containing the instructions and explanatory matter is made up of twelve bulletins of twenty-five pages and
contains twenty-one illustrations of required and optional forms to be
used. The Board of Control feel that this is an important step in the
direction of efficiency and economy.
For the past several years, the Board of Control has recognized
the fact that the uniform compact and by-laws under which Boards of
Relief operated were not meeting the requirements of present day usage.
Over a period of time, minor changes had been approved so that they
were no longer uniform. Some Boards of Relief were operating under
compacts and by-laws drawn up and approved long before the adoption
by Grand Lodge of the Uniform Compact and By-laws. Two years
ago, the Board of Control began to give serious thought to this problem.
Committees were appointed and after many meetings and volumes of
correspondence a complete new "Uniform Compact and By-laws" has
been prepared for the operation of Boards of Relief and Employment
Bureaus. An effort has been made to retain all the desired provisions
which experience has indicated will make them more comprehensive
under present conditions. Additional study of this matter is planned
and it is hoped that it will be completed during the coming year.

with that of any other Grand Jurisdiction.

Report of Special Committee on
George Washington Masonic National Memorial
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
This special committee begs to report as follows :
The Grand Master appointed this special committee to assist him,
among other things. in executing Recommendations 1 and 4 of the Report of the Special Committee on George Washington Masonic National Memorial in 1947. which were adopted at the Niney-eighth Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge.
Resolutions were prepared and, in the presence of all members of
this committee except Arthur S. Crites, P. G. M., who was confined to
his hotel room because of an infected ear, were ably, carefully and
earnestly presented by our Grand Master at the Thirty-eighth Annual
Convention of the George Washington Masonic National Memorial
~ssociation at Alexandria, Virginia, on February 23, 1948, with provisions and results as follows:
1.
Resolution to Amend the Articles of Incorporation of said association so as to admit to active, voting membership the following bodies :
(a) The General Grand Chapter of Royal Arch Masons.
( b) The General Grand Council of Royal and Select Masters.
( c) The Grand Encampment of Knights Templa~.
( d) The Supreme Council of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish
Rite of the Southern Jurisdiction.
( e) The Supreme Council of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish
Rite of the Northern Jurisdiction.
( f ) The Imperial Council of the Ancient Arabic Order Nobles of
the Mystic Shrine.
This resolution required a two-thirds vote, but it was defeated on
roll call by a vote of 24 in favor of it to 25 against it.
·

2.
Resolution to Amend the By-laws of said association to increase
the members of the Board of Directors from 21 to 27, by adding one
member from each of the Brand Bodies listed in (a) to ( f) . inclusive.
under Paragraph 1 above, and to provide for zoning the United States
into 21 districts. with a member of the Board of Directors to be selected
from each district by the Grand Lodges.
In ·t he light of the vote on the resolution under Paragraph 1 above,
wisdom dictated that this resolution be withdrawn, and our Grand
Master, after counseling with this committee, withdrew it.

130

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

3.
Resolution to add a new section to the By-laws of said association
to provide for the selection of a Si:ate Chairman by each Grand Jurisdiction for the term of one year, whose duty it shall be to actively represent said association in his jurisdiction and promote its interest therein.
This resolution was adopted by acclamation.

4.
Resolution providing that the funds and monies of the Endowment
Fund of said association be invested only in bonds issued by the United
States of America.
This resolution was adopted by acclamation.

Brother Richard A. Kem, Past Grand Master of Masons in Pennsylvania, chairman of a committee, presented a resolution providing
as follows:
That a Central Ways and Means Committee, over which the President shall preside, be established, consisting of one member, to be
appointed by the President, from each of the ten regional districts
listed below: that a representative from each Grand Lodge in each
regional district be appointed also by the President to serve for one
year, constituting a Regional Ways and Means Committee; that each
member of the Central Ways and Means Committee be the Chairman
of the Regional Ways and Means Committee in the regional district
from which he was appointed, and that the latter committee in each
regional district meet at the call of the respective chairman: that the
function of the Regional Ways and Means Committee shall be to conduct a publicity campaign in its area for the purpose of raising funds
with which to complete, maintain and endow the memorial; and that
the Central Ways and Means Committee shall meet annually in Washington, D. C., on the day preceding the annual meeting of the association to receive reports from its members and make future plans.
The ten Regional Districts are as follows:
I. Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, Massachusetts, Rhode
Island, and Connecticut.
II. New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware, Maryland,
District of Columbia.
Ill. Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia.
IV. Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, T~nessee.
V. Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, West Virginia, Kentucky.
VI. Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico.
Vll. Missouri, Arkansas, Kansas, Colorado.

VIII. Minnesota, Wisconsin, Iowa, North Dakota, South Dakota,

On roll call, this resolution was adopted by a vote of 36 to 11.
The California resolution under Paragraph 3 above was later
adopted, which has the effect of changing the foregoing (Kern) resolution to the extent that the Grand Master in each Grand Jurisdiction
will appoint the State Chairman (not representative) instead of the
President of the association.
The President of the association has appointed William B. Ogden,
P. G. M., a member of the Central Ways and Means Committee and
designated him as Chairman of the Regional District No. X. Our Grand
Master has appointed John R. Moore, P. G. M., as State Chairman of
the Grand Jurisdiction of California.
From the foregoing report, it will be observed that this committee-as the California Delegation at Alexandria, Virginia- was not completely successful in executing the recommendations of this Grand
Lodge, although the delegation labored diligently with the Board of
Directors collectively and individually, and campaigned at length among
the Grand Masters from the several states. Originally, the Grand
Bodies listed in (a) to ( e) under Paragraph 3 above were active members of this association and have made large contributions toward the
memorial, but for invalid reasons or for no reason at all they were
dropped from membership at the time of reorganization. To correct this
injustice we earnestly 1:ontend that ·they ought to be restored to active
membership and that we should continue our campaign to restore them,
believing that their reinstatement would further stimulate their interest
in the memorial resulting in material financial assistance from them and
their subordinate bodies.
One of the purposes of our Resolution No. 2 above was, of course,
to change the members of the Board of Directors of the association by
having them selected from zones throughout the United States and
thereby acquire new members with virility, stamina and enthusiasm. But
we still have the same old board, albeit some members do possess the
qualities above mentioned and even more and better ones. We believe
that the newly created Central Ways and Means Committee and the
Regional Ways and Means Committees will have a salutary effect upon
the Board of Directors and will either move them to active and effective performance or do their work for them.
Work has been done on the memorial. In 194 7, the Mystic Shrine
Rooms were finished: the room of the Mystic Order of Veiled Prophets
and the Cryptic Lodge room were almost completed: the dining room
and kitchen were completed and the kitchen equipped: and extensive

grading was done on the grounds. On these additions and some smaller
ones, the sum of just under $147,000.00 was expended in the year 1947,
while less than $100,000.00 was spent toward the erection of this memorial during the 5-year period from 1942 to 1946. Plans for the curren·t
year call for the expenditure of some $321,000.00 on the following installations and work: Elevator; assembly halls; bronze statute of Washington and marble base: granite steps, north and south; bronze memorial doors: stairways: Memorial Hall windows and murals: roof on
part of building: and so on.
The architect, Brother Corbett, estimated that the Memorial Building could be completed at a <:ost of $1.000,000.00, excluding landscaping, endowment and maintenance.
The architect has estimated that more than $400,000.00 will be
required to complete landscaping of memorial grounds. This committee
believes that this sum is excessive and that the Board of Directors
should give serious consideration to a substantial reduction.
Contributions to the building fund announced at recent annual conventions have been as follows: In 1946, $93,069.85: in 1947, $120,169.41: and in 1948, $208,907.54.
California, in the last two years, has raised its share of "Cain"
about the stagnancy of the memorial and the fund-raising campaign.
It is the opinion of this committee that California's activity has contributed materially to the progress indicated. It is also our opinion that
this favorable tide ought to be increased to flood by every effort possible. As a means to this end, we make the following recommendations:

I.
That a levy of fifteen cents ( l 5c) per capita be made and the proceeds placed in the George Washington Masonic National Memorial
Fund and to be remitted to the George Washington Masonic National
Memorial Association as and when authorized by this Grand Lodge,
or by a committee comprised of the Grand Master, the Grand Treasurer,
and the Chairman of the Committee on Finance.
·

That ·t he committee comprised of the Grand Master, Grand Treasurer and the Chairman of the Committee on Finance give careful consideration to withdrawing all accumulated funds in the George Washington Masonic National Memorial Fund on January 15, 1949, and
paying them to the George Washington Masonic National Memorial
Association on or before February 22, 1949.
III.
That the Grand Master advocate by appropriate means that a substantial reduction be made in the costs of landscaping the memorial
grounds.

urge an amendment to the Articles of Incorporation of the George

under Paragraph 1 above.

Report of Special Committee on Retirement Plan
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
In order that there may be a clear understanding as to the purposes
of your Committee on Retirement, we are reviewing the activities of the
Committee since its appointment.
In his message to the Grand Lodge in 1946, Grand Master Brouillet
recommended to the Grand Lodge that some consideration be given to
setting up a retirement plan for the employees of the Masonic Homes
and other Grand Lodge employees. This recommendation was approved
by the Grand Lodge, and in accordance with that recommendation a
special Committee on Retirement was appointed' by Grand Master Moore
in 1947. This Committee consulted a well known actuary who prepared
an insurance company plan, and at the 1947 Communication of the
Grand Lodge your Committee recommended the adoption of this plan
which provided for the retirement of eligible employees of the Masonic
Homes and also employees of the Grand Lodge office staff. Owing to the
fact that in the opinion of the members of the Finance Committee the
proposed plan represented a considerable initial outlay of the funds
of the Grand Lodge as well as the funds of the Masonic Homes the
plan as proposed was not adopted, but the Board of Trustees of the
Masonic Homes was c>uthorized to adopt a retirement plan suitable to
the needs of the employees. The continuation of the Committee on Re- ·
tirement was also authorized, and the members of the Committee were
reappointed by Grand Master Warlow.
Inasmuch as the Grand Lodge had rejected the plan which seemed
to the members of your Committee to be the most feasible and practical,

135

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

it was felt that the Committee this year could best function by assising
the Trustees of the Masonic Homes in perfecting and adopting a plan
covering the eligible employees of the Homes and by making it sufficiently broad so that other employees of the Grand Lodge, either direct
or indirect, could be covered eventually if it seemed feasible in the
judgment of the members of Grand Lodge. Accordingly. your Committee working in collaboration with the members of the Board of
Trustees has again consulted an actuary and a new plan has been prepared and is now being considered for adoption by the members of the
Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes.

given us by Brother Ralph L. Low who has been very patient and painstaking in working out the various plans to fill the needs of the Grand
J..odge.
Respectfully submitted,

134

However, your Committee does not feel that the purpose for which
it was appointed has been completed with the adoption of a retirement
plan only for the employees of the Masonic Homes. By authorizing the
adoption of a plan for the employees of the Homes in the 1947 Communication, the Grand Lodge recognized the principle of providing for
retirement for eligible employees to be right and just and in fact approved
such a policy. If such a policy is right and just for the employees of the
Masonic Homes, your Committee feels that it should apply with equal
force to other employees of the Grand Lodge. In addition to the employees in the Grand Secretary's office, there are employees of the Grand
Lodge in the Club Houses at Berkeley and Los Angeles and there are
employees of the various Employment Services and Boards of Relief
who could be considered to be at least indirectly employees of the Grand
Lodge. It might be possible also to supplement the retirement plan by
receiving contributitons of the various Lodges for the retirement of their
Secretaries.
The members of your Committee are not prepared at this time to
recommend an extension of the pension plan to any of the employees
of these various classes of employees until the plan has been adopted by
the Board of Trustees and is in operation so far as the empolyees of the
Masonic Homes are concerned. However, we do believe that the Grand
Lodge has a definite responsibility so far as the other employees are
concerned, and therefore we recommend that the incoming Grand Master
be authorized to appoint a Committee on Retirement for the purpose of
giving further study with a view to supplementing the retirement plan
now under consideration by the Board of Trustees of the Masonic
Homes by broadening it to include such other employees of Grand
Lodge, either direct or indirect, as may seem suitable and practical.
While Brother Walter _Scheffauer is not officially a member of the
Committee we have considered him as one, and he has rendered us invaluable assistance and this is acknowledged gratefully by the members
of the Committee. We acknowledge also the constructive assistance

G. TAYLOR

Report of Special Committee on Masonic Magazines
To the Most Worshipful Chester H. Warlow
Grand Master of Masons in California
and Members of Grand Lodge:
The subject of whether the Grand Lodge of California should
publish a regular magazine or bulletin for the information and education
of the membership of the constituent lodges has been under discussion
for a number of years. Also various Grand Lodge committees have made
preliminary investigations. Following the 1947 session of the Grand
Lodge, the Grand Master appointed a committee to culminate this
series of investigations and bring in a definite report and recommendation.
Your current committee has examined reports of former Grand Lodge
publication committe~s and has inspected and analyzed the publications
of the Grand Lodges of other jurisdictions. Most of these publications
appear to be of interest to the membership and of considerable value in
promoting the interests of Masonry. Also they provide an avenue by
means of which to inform the membership of the Grand Lodge concerning matters of which they are entitled to be informed-and also of matters
concerning which it is to the advantage of Grand Lodge to have the
members know.
In its investigation, this committee first considered whether it is desirable for the Grand Lodge of California to have a means of communication with the membership. The answer is obvious. Such a means of
communication through regular bulletin or magazine publication definitely would be desirable.
Secondly, if such a publication is issued by the Grand Lodge, should
it be a commercial venture including advertising, or should it be strictly
an informative bulletin. This committee is definitely of the opinion such
a venture should not be commercial and should not contain advertising,

136

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

but rather should adhere to the central purpose of providing a published
contact between the Grand Lodge and the membership.
The magazine business is a separate, highly specialized enterprise,
requiring considerable capital to install and operate, and calling for a
highly skilled staff in the advertising, editorial, business and mechanical
fields. This should not be the function of the Grand Lodge. Furthermore,
it is felt that members of the fraternity who are in business should not
be solicited for advertising support because of their connection with the
order. It is easily seen that aggressive solicitors could provide a source of
embarrassment for members and bring discredit on the craft.
After eliminating a magazine venture for the reasons stated above,
the committee determined that the proper publication vehicle would be
an eight page bulletin, six by nine inches in size, and printed monthly on
white paper stock.
The editorial content would be varied, and suited to the occasion
from time to time. It would contain summaries of Grand Lodge actions,
me!lsages from the Grand Master and the Grand Secretary, news of the
activities of the Grand Lodge and its officers, news of outstanding
Masonic events throughout the state, articles on Masonic education, and,
in fact, running the entire range of matters of mutual interest.
The costs of such a bulletin have been obtained in estimate form.
The committee has the detail on this from printing firms in Los Angeles
and San Francisco, but roughly they average $10 per 1,000 copies-the
equivalent of one cent per copy. To do a s:rood job it is estimated that the
editorial work should be figured at $250 per month for part time reportorial, editing and office help. A sizeable item of expense, which would
require actual operation to determine, would be the matter of postage.
This committee believes the postage expense could be held to a minimum by the Grand Lodge bulletin being sent in bundles to the constituent lodges which have regular lodge bulletins and the two bulletins
being mailed in the same envelope by each such lodge. Those lodges
which do not have bulletins may wish to cooperate by handling the mailing of the Grand Lodge bulletin, or in the event this is not forthcoming
the Grand Lodge would have to handle the mailing direct from San
Francisco. It is noted, however, that lodges without bulletins of their
own usually are in the less populated areas and thus represent a small
portion of the total membership in the state. It is believed, therefore, that
distribution to the vast majority of the membership can be accomplished
economically through the cooperation of the lodges.
In conclusion, we are aware of the wide departure from past usage
this would involve for the Grand Lodge of California, but are of the
firm belief that the expenditure, although large. would have corresponding benefits to the advancement of Masonry in California. We are grateful for the opportunity of having served, and recommend that matters

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

137

contained herein falling within the jurisdiction of other committees be
referred thereto.
Respectfully submitted,
HAMILTON L. HINTZ
JOHN M. SERVER, JR.

Report of the Committee on De Molay
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on De Malay welcomes this opportunity to present
to the Inspectors, Masters and Wardens attending this annual Communication of the Grand Lodge, our report of past activities and to
solicit your continued interest.
Our second year of operation finds the work started last year progressing satisfactorily, that of endeavoring to acquaint the members of
the Lodges with the fact that there is such a thing as the Order of De
Molay and that it is e>ntitled to their full support and that this Grand
Lodge has recognized the possibilities for good inherent in such an organization by forming a Committee whose duty it is to co-ordinate the
activities of the various Lodges with those of the Chapters of De Molay
and to carry information to the membership as to the needs of the Order.
Visitations and talks to the Lodges of the jurisdiction have been continued and have in many instances resulted in the volunteering of assistance in the way of Advisors and the stimulation of interest in the
work of De Malay. If the Masons of California generally, knew of the
grand work which this Order is doing among the youth of today your
Committee would not be compelled to ask for support but would be
overwhelmed by offers to help.
The communication issued by the Grand Master to the Inspectors
and Lodges of the jurisdiction was of great value, it having the direct
result of influencing a number of the members of the various Lodges to
call upon the committee for information relative to De Malay, the steps
necessary to be taken in sponsoring a Chapter of De Malay, the methods
used in selecting Advisors and other pertinent information. In this connection be it noted that it is the custom of committee members, in every
instance, to call to the attention of the inquiring member or members the
fact that the Lodge, as such, may neither sponsor a Chapter or accept
any financial responsibilities either in the formation or continuance of
its activities.
To bring the work of De Malay more strongly to the attention of the
membership: your Committee strongly recommends to the Officers of

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

the Lodges in the jurisdiction that they arrange to have a Chapter of De
Molay exemplify one or more of their degrees, preferably at a Stated
Meeting at which dinner is served, a greater numbers of members will
be present. Any member of the Committee will be glad to make the necessary arrangements.
The Lodges in the San Diego area have given the Committeeman
in that district very .fine support, in that, by virtue of his hard work,
practically every one of them has set up a committee of its members
to work with him. An opportunity was given the San Francisco representative of the Committee to address the Master and Wardens association
on the subject of De Molay, which opportunity was much appreciated,
as is every invitation to deliver our message to the Officers and members
of the various Lodges.
Chapters in Cailifomia are in a healthy .financial condition and a
very substantial increase in membership would seem to indicate that the
messages brought to members having eligible sons making them aware
of the .fine work that De Molay is doing is. in part at least, responsible
for some of the increase. Although the increasing of membership is not a
part of the duties of your Committee we feel that each boy added to De
Molay membership is one more started on the road to good citizenship.
Many expressions of appreciation for the interest the Grand Lodge
has taken in De Molay as shown in the formation of your Committee
have come from the Deputies of the Grand Council of the Order and
Officers and members of the Chapters. They request that we convey
their thanks to the Grand Officers and members attending this Communication.
Based on our experience ·during that past two years. we .find that it
is physically impossible: for one man to adequately cover as large a territory as the San Francisco and Los Angeles area where so many Lodges
are placed and we therefore recommend that the Committee be increased
by the addition of two members. one additional for the San Francisco
area and one for the Los Angeles area.
Your Committee recommends that an appropriation in the sum of
$750.00 be made to cover the necessary expenses for the ensuing year.
Respectfully submitted:

Report of Committee on Masonic History

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Masonic History begs leave to submit the
following report.
.
At the last Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge your History
Committee was authorized to prepare the manuscript of a comprehensive
history of Masonry in California. The Chairman of this Committee w_as
given supervision of the preparation and writing of the ~aid manuscript
and, pursuant to that authorization, obtained the services of Brother
Clyde Arbuckle of Liberty Lodge, No. 299. of Santa Clara. and Brother
Samuel Steelman, Senior Warden of Hollywood Lodge. No. 355, ~f
Hollywood. Brother Arbuckle was a ~embe~ of y~~r Hi~tory Committee for eight years and is well experienced ID wntlDg history. Brother
Steelman, an attorney-at-law and also a member of your History Committee. is likewise highly competent in the same field.
Before your Committee could begin the actual writing of the manuscript, however, it was necessary to catalog and index the vast amou~t
of material that has been gathered over a period of twenty-years. This
work alone took very close to three-months and has been subject to no
small amount of subsequent supplement.
The resultant indices consist of three large volumes of standard
typewritten pages. The .first, covering Major Edwin A. Sherman's Fifty
Years of Masonry in California, consumes sixty-three full pages. The

140

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

second covers the voluminous material taken from Lodge minutes, general records, trial records. bills. and correspondence by Brother Charles
Ingram over a period of two years, during which he was continuously
employed for that purpose. It consumes two-hundred pages. The third
is a general index of two-hundred and eighteen pages covering over
one-hundred printed volumes (including the Grand Lodge Proceedings).
seventy-five scrapbooks, the numerous published and typewritten histories of individual Lodges, thousands of letters and notes, and a large
volume of miscellaneous memoranda.
In indexing this material your Committee found literally hundreds of
gaps. omissions. and errors that needed filling and correction. It also
found in published works gross inaccuracies that have long been accepted as fact-statements that did not even remotely agree with Lodge
minutes and records .. This has necessitated an inordinate amount of
time-consuming correspondence with Grand and Subordinate Lodges
and individual Masons throughout the entire United States, to say
nothing of the meticulous double checking of almost every item in order
to insure a strict adherence to truth. As a result. your Committee has not
progressed so rapidly toward completing its manuscript as it at first
anticipated. But it does feel that once the work is complete, it will stand
the most critical examination.
The collection of this material began in 1928, when Grand Master
Will H. Fischer revived the virtually dormant Committee on Masonic
History for the purpose of perpetuating the story of Masonry in California. Today the objective of this Committee is about two-thirds
achieved. Besides gathering and indexing all the necessary data. it has in
its files completed manuscripts of the following chapters:
Seafaring Men-the story of the first Masons to come to California
-11,000 words.
Wayfaring Men-the story of the pioneer Masons who came across
mountain, plain. and desert to California before the American Conquest
-50,000 words.
"But the Greatest of These"-a comprehensive account of Masonic
relief and charity before the coming of the Widows and Orphans Home
-30.000 words.
In addition to these are the Sacramento Valley District and the
Southern California District. Both of these are chronological histories of
the Lodges in their respective parts of the State. are practically complete,
and will run about 120,000 words each. Morever. work is progressing
rapidly on the Lodges of the Mother Lode District, whose intensely interesting stories come down to us from the Gold Rush days.
In order to facilitate this work, your Committee has divided the State
into nine great districts. each with a Masonic background almost peculiar
unto itself and ranging from three to eleven counties apiece. Besides the

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

141

previously mentioned Sacramento Valley, Southern California, and
Mother Lode districts, they are:
The Northern California District, extending northward from the
Sacramento Valley and the Mother Lode to the Oregon line.
The Northern Coast Countie-s, extending southward along the coast
from the Oregon line to Sonoma County.
The San Francisco Bay District, embracing the six metropolitan area
counties on San Francisco Bay.
The Central Coast Counties, extending southward along the coast
from Santa Cruz County to San Luis Obispo County.
The San Joaquin Valley District, embracing all the counties of the
San Joaquin Valley.
The Eastern Central Counties, which includes only Alpine, Inyo. and
Mono counties.
Chapters in tentative outline, but yet to be fritten, include those
on the Northern California, Northern Coast, San Francisco Bay, Central Coast, San Joaquin Valley, and Eastern Central districts as well as
the following special chapters:
The Conquest of California, showing how Masons participated in
conquering California and annexing it to the United States.
The Constitution Convention, wherein Masons were most influential
in organizing the government of this State.
The Organization of Grand Lodge.
The Gold Rush Days, during _which Masons helped to establish
civilization and law and order from one end of the diggings to the other.
The Civil War Period, showing how Masons saved California for the
Union.
The Reconstruction Period, in which Masons helped to rebuild the
nation and rekindle the spirit of brotherly love between Northerner and
Southerner.
Masonry Among the Indians, revealing how the Redman acquired
Masonic lore and understood the use of Masonic signs and symbols.
Mcrsonic Humor, amusing accounts of such humorists as Mark
Twain, John Phoenix, and innumerable other droll characters with
Masonic connections.
Colorful Characters, portraying such unforgettable brothers as William Bull Meek, John Adolphus Fisher, Judge William B. Almond,
"Mountain Charlie" McKiernan, etc.
Morals and Conduct, showing how Masonry restrained the transgressor and improved the morality and behavior of brethren in a wild,
new country, particularly in the gold region.
Evolution of the Ritual, the story of how the California Ritual, starting with a hodgepodge of work from several jurisdictions, gradually
evolved to its present form.

143

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Special Degrees, outdoor degrees, unusual ceremonies, etc.
Native California Masons, the stories of Spanish Californians who
joined the Craft, and how one of them, Romualdo Pacheco, became
governor of the State.
Sojourning Brethren, relating how m'a ny distinguished brothers from
other jurisdictions such as Mark Twain, William Tell Coleman, Samuel
Addison Bishop, and Will Rogers contributed much to California's culture and welfare but for reasons best known to themselves did not affiliate
here.
Long Tenure, a record of faithful brethren continuously serving their
Lodges in one or more offices over a long period of years.
Long Membership, stories of brethren wh~ have been Masons over
fifty years and upward to sixty and seventy-five years.
Lodges of Other Jurisdictions, an account of Lodges in Oregon,
Nevada and Arizona organized under the jurisdiction of the Grand
Lodge of California prior to the organization of the Grand Lodges of
their respective States.
Territorial Lodges, a study of the establishment and growth of Masonry in the Hawaiian and Philippine Islands under the jurisdiction of
the Grand Lodge of California.
·
California Brethren Abroad, the record of California Masons who
have distinguished themselves as Grand Masters, Grand Secretaries, etc.
of other states and territories.
A good deal of this material is already in rough outline, but its conversion to manuscript would be greatly facilitated if all later day Lodj:Jes
that feel they have little of interest in their histories would send it, what
little they do have. As it is, your Committee estimates that the finished
work will comprise four volumes of 500 pages each, averaging 325 words
to the page, with one-hundred and twenty-five 5 x 7 inch cuts and an index of not less than one-hundred pages.
At the last Annual Communication of Grand Lodge, $11 ,000.00 was
appropriated to this Committee to defray the costs of writing and preparing the manuscript of this work for publication. Of this sum approximately $7,767.00 will have been expended by October 15 of this year,
leaving an unexpended balance of $3,233.00. ( $457.00 of the expended
sum was for office equipment, furniture, etc.-a non-recurrent capital
expenditure.) But judging from its experience, progress, and necessary
costs incurred to date your Committee is now certain it will take to the
middle of 1949 to complete its work and that another appropriation will
be necessary. It estimates that approximately $6,720.00 will be needed to
carry on its work during this extended period beginning October 17,
1948, to June 30, 1949--which will allow ample time for publication
before the Centennial Odservance of the organization of the Grand
Lodge of this State in 1950.

Therefore, your Committee offers the following resolution and moves
its adoption:
Resolved:
( 1 ) That the work of the Committee on Masonic History in compiling the history of Masonry in California be continued.
( 2) That the sum of $6,720.00 be appropriated and set aside for the
use of the said Committee for the completion of the manuscript of the
aforesaid history.

SPECIAL NOTICE
The correspondence report, 306 pages, is too
long for inclusion in this Book of Proceedings.
The table of contents and the statistics are
being included here on the following pages.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Early in this Masonic year our Most Worshipful Grand Master,
through the agency of our M. W. Grand Secretary, sent summons to
seven members of the Craft, and bade them travel. some east, some west,
some north and some south, in search of the most recent word regarding
Masonic labor and its welfare.
Accordingly we met by appointment, using the correspondence route
as the means of travel, arranged our calendar in six divisions, in order
that the Foreman of the project, might accompany each severally on his
journey about our American domain.
Each traveler was given certain sections or states to cover, figuratively speaking, in his month's sojourn among friendly people.
When this commandment of our Grand Master had been accomplished, the Foreman or Overseer of the enterprise, set out alone to visit
foreign parts. His travels took him from the far frozen recesses of Canada to Mexico and even to the Antarctic regions where he found Brother
Masons in earnest convocation.
The long arm of Freemasonry carried him to Guam, Okinawa, the
Philippines, China and Australasia. India and the western European
countries were visited.
We reached the United Grand Lodge of England to mourn with our
British Brethren, the passing of their M. W. The Grand Master, the
Earl of Harewood, and to witness the installation in his high office of
the new Grand Master, His Grace, the Duke of Devonshire, by His Majesty The King, Past Grand Master of the United Grand Lodge of England. We marked with sorrow, the passing of our M. W. Bro. H. M.
King Christian of Denmark, Past Grand Master, and noted with profound regret the tragic death of R. W. Bro. H. R. M. Prince Gustaf
Adolf of Sweden, who held high office in that country as Deputy Grand
Master.
This globe encircling journey has been one of high privilege. Our
acquaintanceship has flourished. We have basked in the radiance of
Masonic luminaries from shore to shore of almost every land, as we
sought to lift our vision in the vast outreach. We have formed a rich
value of the new found friends as they extended the hand of Masonic
companionship, in the bond of mutual service and understanding.
True it is, that we have shuddered at times because of the lack of
proper precautions in spreading upon the printed page the esoteric teachings so dear to the Masonic heart. It was and is, our earnest hope that
the eyes of the profane behold not what our eyes have seen.
Our confessed inexperience as a reviewer of affairs Masonic, has
caused our mediations to query the source and usage of such words as
"Sister Lodges," and "Sister Jurisdictions." As much as we cherish our

147

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

own beloved sisters. we would enjoy much more the substitution of the
word "Brother." -Custom becometh usage, as ~e all well know.

Our story is told. Our preface is ended. Had we said that, had we
done this, so might we gain, so might we miss. We leave our diary, so
filled with the richest of morsels, in your hands. The overseer greatly
is indebted to the travelers who accompanied him on his way. Over land
and sea we figuratively followed the course plotted by our Grand Master
and Grand Secretary.
We trust that each of you will derive as much pleasure and food from
its pages as came to us during its several months of preparation.

Among our newly found and valued friends are certain ones who
stretch a scornful finger at California's style of "topical review," much
preferring their own effective style of editorial comment. So rich in
philosophical wealth are many of these Correspondence reports that we
regret our lack of time and space to bring them to you. We are tolerant
enough to ~e~ their value-but we prefer best our own established style
of presentation.

To go back a moment to "Sister or Brother Jurisdictions or Lodges,"
our avid reader~students will note that we have forgone the usage of
either of those words, substituting in their place the word "other;" let
the chips fall where they may!
May we ask your gracious pardon for a moment while we lock rhetor~
ical horns with our distinguished neighbor and co~reporter, Most Wor~
shipful Otto C. Hagmeier, P. G. M. of Oregon Jurisdiction. The emin~
ent Doctor, in his 1947 review called the attention of the Masonic world,
that we in California still persist in saying "compass" instead of "com~
passes.''
·
Now, the Book of The Entered Apprentice used by this Grand
Lodge, in speaking of certain inheritances states:
" .... the source of some of these particulars, the following may be
cited f;l'om old pre~Grand Lodge rituals of the 17th century:
'What makes a just and perfect Lodge?'
.
'A Master................... with Square, Compas and Common Gudg.'"
"Please. Dr. Watson, spare the need(e."
We found the scars from the holocaust of war, some slowly healing,
others still in need of the relief and aid to be given best by Masonic
hands. Close study of our account will indicate their urgency.
Again and again we noted with sorrowing heart the passing from
the wide Masonic universe, of some long. well~laboring Brother. Would
that our chronicle could list their names and their distinguished service
record.
These few lines from Whittier's immortal poem, marks their lasting
·
·
place in our fraternal brotherhood:
"How strange it seems, with so much gone
Of life and love, to still live on!
Yet Love will dream and Faith will trust
That somehow. somewhere. meet we must.
For who hath not learned in hours of faith
That Life is ever Lord of Death,
And Love can never lose its own!"

Report of Committee on Memorial Temple
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The San Francisco members of the Committee have been engaged in
activities largely exploratory. This is enforced by circumstances-building costs which may be inordinate, appropriate location, and financing.
Requirements of Grand Lodge are obvious to everyone who attends
the annual communication. Representatives are packed in to such a
degree that they are uncomfortable. The discomfort of those on the floor
and the remoteness of those in the galleries interferes with and suppresses, without doubt, many who desire to participate in discussion of
Grand Lodge problems. It is not necessary to comment upon the misfortunes of those who are forced to be seated in the adjacent room and
are limited to loud speaker transmission.
There is not ample or suitable accommodation for committees whose
studies, reports and recommendations are an integral part of the transaction of business of Grand Lodge. There are not sufficient facilities
for social intercourse, which is important and particularly when limited
to an annual occasion.
A survey of the temple now accommodating Grand Lodge is convincing that it will not lend itself to remodelling sufficient for the purposes.
The possibilities of the fourth floor have been mentioned and considered
in the afore-mentioned survey. If remodelling that floor were feasible
even for the purpose of accommodating Grand Lodge in session, it would
not satisfy everything that is desirable, and would probably be an unsatisfactory temporary expedient. We must not be without concern of
the dangers involved under crowded conditions, particularly in event of
catastrophe. Consideration must be given to the adequacy of elevator
service, as under ordinary conditions during the Grand Lodge session it
is not always sufficient. Incidentally, a remodelling program would not
satisfy the Memorial objectives.
An ediS.ce is contemplated that will serve the purpose of Grand
Lodge and at the same time be appropriate for a memorial and also be
productive of income. The selection of location to complete the pattern
will require adroit real estate experience. Manifestly, there are problems
for experts. Building costs need not necessarily prove an obstacle. It
is not unlikely that building costs will continue in a high bracket and
that delay on that account would be unfortunate.
San Francisco, as is generally the case in metropolitan communities,
is undergoing revision of its transit and traffic, involving street improvements, arterials and free ways, possible intrusion upon real property encompassed in projected programs. There is a problem of parking and a
very deS.nite requirement that hotel and restaurant facilities shall be
reasonably easy of access.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

,
I

153

Locations will not be divulged until the interests of Grand Lodge may
be protected, for obvious reasons. At the moment, two seemingly satisfactory locations are being investigated, either one of which, depending
on financial requirement, seems to fit the pattern.
The study of the Committee is requiring time, and may defeat the
objective of completion during the Centennial year. Notwithstanding
past and prospective delay, we are not convinced that the objective may
not be accomplished. If the Committee is successful in developing the
project according to the pattern, financing should not be an insurmountable problem. It may be essential to provide a reasonable proportion of the required financing by means of a per capita. This added to
available funds, taking into consideration prospective income, will be
essential to obtaining an adequate loan. There is nothing to be gained
by any speculation as to S.nancial requirement until the essential facts
have been developed.
Based upon the foregoing it is the recommendation of the Committee
that a Memorial Building Committee be continued.
Respectfully submitted,
