Centennial Arrangements Committee Report
To the Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Centennial Arrangements has made some
progress during the year, but the real work of the Committee remains
to be done in the next two years. At the last Communication of Grand
Lodge it was determined that we would celebrate the hundredth anniversary of the founding of the Grand Lodge during Grand Lodge week
in October, 1950, in San Francisco. That it might be a celebration worthy
of Grand Lodge a per capita tax of 25c was levied on the Lodges, and
expected to continue for three years, in order to S.nance the celebration.
Since only general plans could be formulated, we make this preliminary report in the hope that it will aid the committee hereafter in the
tremendous task that lies ahead of it. Your committee has held several
meetings. Since no funds have yet been made available, we have not
made any S.nancial commitments, but we have explored some of the possibilities and make certain suggestions that we think appropriate to submit
to Grand Lodge for approval. All we have done is preliminary and your

155

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

committee awaits authority to incur expense and to prosecute its duties
until the fulfilment of a task that will redound to the credit of Grand
Lodge and merit the approval of the brethren.

The invitations shall be personal and not transferable, except with
the approval of your committee, and other distinguished Masons may
be invited by your committee with the approval of the Grand Master.
We estimate that the special guests who accept our hospitality will be
not less than 250.
In addition to our special guests we hope and expect many thousands
of California Masons will attend the celebration and the program will
be arranged for their pleasure and entertainment. Much thought is being
given to doing something for our own members because it .is th~ir celebration and the centenary of their Grand Lodge and California never
does anything by halves.
5. PROGRAM
A tentative program, subject to alterations and future consideration.
would be as follows:

154

1. AUTHORITY OF THE COMMITTEE

A Centennial Arrangements Committee should be appointed to serve
for three years, with full power to arrange for and conduct the celebration and to close up the business affairs connected therewith. The
committee should be authorized to expend the whole, or any part, of the
special fund accumulated for the celebration; to appoint a general manager; to appoint appropriate sub-committees; to arrange entertainment
and do whatsoever is necessary or expedient for the celebration-all with
the consent and approval of the Grand Master.

2. RESERVATIONS
Through the kindness of the Grand Secretary, and by the authority
of the Grand Master, a contract has been signed for the use of the
entire San Francisco Civic Auditorium with a seating capacity of
10.560 for October 9th through October 15th, 1950, and a deposit has
been made thereon. Through the Tourist and Convention Bureau of San
Francisco, 2000 rooms in Class A Hotels have been reserved for October
8th through October 15th, 1950.
3. GENERAL MANAGER
The committee has tent~tively employed a General Manager who has
had convention experience and who will serve under, and subject to, the
direction of the Centennial Arrangement Committee. It will be his duty
to maintain an office and to correlate the work of all the sub-committees
and to attend to all the details of the celebration. It is also tentatively
agreed hat he shall receive a salary of $650 per month for the year 1950,
and will employ such office help as shall be required.

4. GUESTS
It is contemplated that Grand Lodge shall invite as its special guests
for the Grand Lodge meeting in October, 1950, and pay their expenses
from the time of their arrival in San Francisco until the close of Grand
Lodge, the following distinguished persons: The President of the United
States, the Vice-President of the United States (if he is a Mason), the
Governor of the State of California, the Grand Masters of all Grand
Lodges with which we are in amity, the Grand Master of the Grand
Encampment Knights Templar, the Grand Commanders of the Supreme
Councils of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite for the Southern and
Northern Jurisdictions of the U.S. A ., the Grand High Priest of Royal
A'rch Masons of the U . S. A .. the Grand Master of Royal Select Masters
of the U.S. A., the Imperial Potentate of the Mystic Shrine, the Grand
Secretaries of the several Grand Lodges of the United States, together
with their wives.

SUNDAY:

An informal dinner for special guests.
MONDAY:

Opening of Grand Lodge.
Banquets in the evening for guests and all delegates. ·

Grand Lodge Session.
Visit to Decoto in the afternoon.
Cavalcade in the evening.

Grand Lodge Session.

Woods, or tour of San Francisco including Golden Gate Park,
Cliff House and thirty mile drive). ·
Cavalcade in the evening.
THURSDAY:

Grand Lodge Session.
Trips and entertainment in the afternoon.
Cavalcade in the evening.
FRIDAY:

Grand Lodge Session and installation of officers in the morning.
Afternoon for shopping and go-as-you-like.
Evening, Centennial Ball.
As an alternate for the Cavalcade in the evening, arrangements will
be made for a Twilight Cruise on San Francisco Bay, a tour of Chinatown After Dark, theatres, etc.
6. CAVALCADE
We hope to have written and produced a play giving in dramatic
form some aspects of the history and experiences of the Grand Lodge of

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

156

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

California. The history of California has a most colorful background and
in the hundred years of California Masonry there are many periods and
episodes that lend themselves to dramatic presentation. If our expectations are realized, the play will be presented to our brethren on three
successive nights. A strenuous effort will be made to present the play by
motion picture, or otherwise, to as many of the Craft throughout the
State as may be possible.
7. DINNERS
An informal dinner to our special guests and a sumptuous banquet to
the Grand Lodge delegates and other guests will be given. Arrangements for the latter will be difficult, but it will be worked out. Private
dinners and other entertainment will probably be offered by the local
Commanderies, Scottish Rite Bodies and Lodges. To avoid confusion,
all such functions must be cleared through the Centennial Committee.
8. HOTELS
The policy regarding distribution of special guests and other guests
will await a time when we have more information regarding the needs,
but a suitable arrangement for the comfort and convenience of our guests
will be worked out. Advance publicity will be complete and informative.

9. SUBCOMMITTEES
Many subcommittees will be appointed by the Centennial Committee
to be responsible thereto, who will be coordinated by the General
Manager, who will have the direction of all their work. Among such
committees will be the following:
Protocol. Finance, Housing, Registration, Police, Information, Greeters, Badges, Souvenirs, Program, Cavalcade, Dinners and Luncheons,
Printing and Publicity and Women's Activities.
10. WOMEN'S ACTIVITIES
There will be committees of women to assist in entertaining the
ladies who will attend the celebration, either as wives of special guests
or as wives of delegates.
11. BUDGET
It is too early to make a budget for the manifold activities of Centennial Week. Your committee is not yet advised of the cost of living,
transportation or entertainment in 1950 and it would be idle to try to set
a budget at this time. However, the per capita tax being levied on the
Lodges will produce not less than $135,000 and this will be the limit set
for our expenditures. There will be no deficits because we intend to
spend the money appropriated and no more.
The chief items in the budget will be hotels, transportation, Caval-

f

157

cade, dinners, ball~ entertainment, General Manager's expense and Convention Hall cost.
We. therefore, recommend that the Centennial Arrangements Committee be continued for three years and that said committee be authorized:
. .
1. To expend such money, within the limitations of the appropriation,
as is necessary to conduct and manage a Centennial Celebration that
will be creditable to Grand Lodge.
2. To draw warrants which shall be paid by the Grand Secretary out
of the special fund.
3. To employ a General Manager and such office assistants a~
necessary, to appoint subcommittees and take whatever steps seem to
them necessary and proper to accomplish its purposes.
Adopted.

Report of Conunittee on Jurisdiction

At the suggestion of the Grand Master, on motion, the entire matter
was referred to a special committee to be appointed by the Grand Master
after October 15, 1948, which committee was instructed to report at the
next Annual Communication.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of
Free and Accepted Masons of California:
Your Committee on Jurisdiction, to whom there has been submitted
several matters of importance, has devoted considerable time and thought
to what we consider the two most pressing problems pending before our
committee, and we offer the following resolutions and move their adoption:
1. That the Grand Lodge of California Free and Accepted Masons
of California take immediate steps to incorporate as a non-profit
corporation under the corporatiton Code of California to the end
that our name be not appropriated by clandestine organizations.
2. That the incoming Grand Master be authorized and directed to
employ counsel for the formation of such corporation in which the
Grand Master, the Deputy Grand Master, the Senior and Junior
Grand Wardens, the Grand Treasurer and Grand Secretary be
the officers, and their successors in office as elected or such other
officers as the Grand Master or Grand Lodge may direct.
3. That the incoming Grand Master be authorized to employ
counsel to appear on behalf of the Grand Lodge as a friend of
the court and set forth our prior right as the Supreme Masonic
authority of this State in the appeal now pending wherein the
"Sons of Light et al" are plaintiffs and "Hiram of Tyre et al" are
defendants.
Respectfully submitted,
ARTHUR w. BROUILLET
LEO E. SIEVERT
OTTO ROHWER
HENRY C. MACK

Report of Special Taxation Committee
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The Special Taxation Committee composed of Walter Perry Johnson, James E. Hammond and R. P. Wisecarver, Chairman, was reappointed for the current Masonic year.
During the year Brother Walter Perry Johnson passed away, and
the Committee and this Grand Lodge and Masonry in general has lost
by his passing a man of the highest character and erudition, who has ever
given freely and generously of his time and money to all good causes.
As we reported for the year 1947, all outstanding problems taxwise
have been ironed out and during the past year there has been no new
legislation passed by Congress nor by the State affecting seriously the
· tax structure of Grand Lodge. There were numerous tax bills introduced into Congress, but we have found none that passed which seriously
·
affect the status of Grand Lodge.
Some of the unpassed bills might fundamentally alter the tax structure of Grand Lodge and it is the understanding of this Committee that
some, if not all of the bills, will be presented for passage at the next
Congress.

Report of Committee on Grievances
To the Most Wor.shipful Grand Lodge of California:
Forty-nine records have been referred to your Committee on Grievances for study and report to Grand Lodge. Thirty~ne of these will be covered by this report and the remaining
eighteen will be presented to you with individual opinions by various
members of the Committee.
As is not unusual, we have again encountered several trial records
in which the Master has permitted nominations for trial commissions.
We are not unmindful of the fact that by two rulings made in 1892,
reported in paragraph 974 of Edicts and Resolutions of the Grand
Lodge, it was held that nominations of Trial Commissioners might be
permitted. However, it seems to your Committee, and we have so stated
to Grand Lodge, that the nomination of Trial Commissioners is out of
harmony with the language of Section 299 of our Ordinances and that
the better practice is for such nominations not to be permitted. The packing of a Commission, is, of course, a Masonic offense. If nominations
of Trial Commissioners is permitted, the packing of .the Commission
might be a very simple matter. Section 299 of our Ordinances provides
in part as follows :
"Each member present will write the name of as many members
of the Lodge upon one ballot as shall correspond with the number
of Commissioners determined upon,".
If this procedure is followed without the making of nominations.
the packing of a Trial Commission would be a virtual impossibility.
Again, therefore, we recommend to Masters presiding at Masonic Trials
that the nominations of Trial Commissioners be not permitted.
Each year, and this is no exception, we encounter a number of trial
records in which the accused has been convicted of a crime in the courts
of the land. In many of such cases, the specifiations charge this conviction rather than setting forth the commission of the crime itself. We
again emphasize that being convicted of a crime is not a Masonic
offense-it is the commission of such crime which constitutes the offense.
Therefore, the specifications contained in a charge of Unmasonic conduct should be that the accused had committed a crime, specifying the
nature and date of same and not that he had been convicted of committing the offense.
Considering the records before us as a whole, we are impressed
by the sincerity with which Masonic Trials are handled by the constituent Lodges and the Trial Commissions selected by them. The fact
that many of such trials are presided over by Masters who are unskilled in law sometimes result in errors being committed which require
a retrial of the matter. Frequently such errors could be avoided if
Masters who are called upon to preside over trials would devote more
study to the Ordinances and decisions under them. If in doubt, they
should not hesitate to seek the advice and assistance of those who are
skilled in Masonic law,

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

..

161

In one of the cases covered by this report, we encountered a situation in which a Master directed the Junior Warden to prefer charges and
thereafter presided at the trial. In accordance with previous rulings of
Grand Lodge, this would ordinarily compel a reversal. However, in
this particular case the accused did not appear at the trial and the
proof of guilt is so clear that your Committee feels the conclusion of the
Trial Commission should not be disturbed. We call this particular case
to your attention in the hope that such errors will be avoided in the
future.
This report deals with the following trial record:
No. 108~(Retrial) A member of San Bernardino Lodge No. 348.
Suspended March 7, 1946. Retired and found not guilty
February 13, 1947.
No. 1088-( Retrial) A member of Willow Glen Lodge No. 676. Expelled October 2, 1946.
No. 1121-A member of Blackmer Lodge No. 442. Expelled October
6, 1947. (See also Trial Record No. 1143.)
No. 1122-A member of Mount Moriah Lodge No. 44. Expelled November 5, 1947.
No. 1123-A member of Porterville Lodge No. 303. Expelled December
11. 1947.
.

7, 1948.
No. 1126-A member of University Lodge No. 394. Expelled January
5, 1948.
No. 1127-A member of Santa Barbara Lodge No. 192. Suspended
January 8, 1948.
No. 1128-A member of a Lodge in Washington. Expelled January
7. 1948.
No. 1131-A member of Woodland Lodge No. 156. Expelled February
6. 1948.

Section 341 of our Ordinances reads as follows:
"No judgment of a trial commission shall be set aside, or new
trial granted, for any error of any sort as to pleading, procedure,
or introduction of evidence, unless, after an examination of the
entire case, including the evidence, the Grand Lodge shall be of the
opinion that the error committed has resulted in a miscarriage of
justice.''

Lodge has been complied with. This section requires an expelled Mason
desiring to petition Grand Lodge for restoration to notify in writing the
Lodge which expelled him of such intended petition at least sixty days
before the annual communication at which the petition is to be presented.
The section further provides that proof of the giving of such notice to
the Lodge must be shown before the petition can be considered by
Grand Lodge. In the absence of proof of giving such ·notice to the
Lodge which expelled petitioner and in the absence of a further show~

Trial Record 1087
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
To your Committee on Grievances has been referred TRIAL REC~
ORD NO. 1087 from Golden Rule Lodge No. 479.
This record was before Grand Lodge at its meeting in 1947. The
accused was charged with a conspiracy to operate slot machines and
other gambling devices in Santa Clara County while he was acting as
the duly elected and qualified Sheriff of that county. As a trial held late
in 1946, the accused had been acquitted by his Lodge. This matter was
reported to Grand Lodge by the Grievance Committee in 1947 in its
omnibus report, with the recommendation that the acquittal of the
accused be affirmed by Grand Lodge. Upon motion made from the floor

170

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

of Grand Lodge, this record was removed from the 1947 omnibus report
of your Committee on Grievances. Thereafter, and by further action of
Grand Lodge, the case was reversed and remanded to the Lodge for a
retrial.

We now have the matter before us again. Both trial records are in the
hands of Grand Lodge. In the interests of justice we feel that Grand
Lodge. in disposing of this case, should take into con.sideration all that
is disclosed for our information from both of these trial records.
Considerable publicity was given to the trial of the accused when
he was before the Superior Court. The situation involving the accused
is doubtless well known to all of the members of his Lodge. The Trial
Commissions of that Lodge have now twice found the accused not guilty
of unmasonic conduct, the total vote of the two commissions being fifteen
in favor of not guilty and one in favor of guilty.
From a consideration of this entire record as it has come to Grand
Lodge over a period of two years, your Committee does not find that
there has been a miscarriage of justice sufficient to warrant Grand Lodge
in again reversing the finding of the Trial Commissio~s.
Grand Lodge has heretofore declared: "A judgment of acquittal by
the subordinate lodge, of which the accused is a member, should not be
reversed or disturbed by the Committee on Grievances, or by the Grand
Lodge, except in a case of gross violation of Masonic law by the trial
commission or by the lodge acquitting him."
In view of the foregoing, your Committee offers the following resolution and moves its adoption:
Resolved, that the action of the Trial Commission in finding the
accused not guilty of the specification and the charge be and the same is
hereby ratified, affirmed, and approved.
It was moved, seconded and carried that the recommendation of
the committee be not adopted and Grand Lodge then, on motion, reversed the recommendation of the committee and remanded the case for
retrial in a lodge to be designated by the Grand Master.

Such a retrial has now been had and by a vote of seven to one, the
Trial Commissioners found the accused not guilty of the specification
and by a vote of eight to none, found the accused not guilty of unmasonic conduct. The accused has therefore been acquitted for the
second time by a Trial Commission of his Lodge.
On this second trial, the only evidence introduced by the prosecution
was a certified copy of the record of the Superior Court of Santa Clara
County evidencing a finding of guilt of the accused of a similar charge.
No evidence was introduced by the accused. However, his counsel urged
upon the Trial Commission that the accused had been once acquitted
by the Trial Commission of that Lodge and that this served as an offset
to the finding of guilt by the court. Counsel for the accused further
erroneously urged upon the Trial Commission that this second trial
amounted to tv:ice placing the accused in jeopardy for the same offense.
Such was not the fact since Grand Lodge had reversed the previous
finding of not guilty and had ordered a new trial. Thereafter, the second
trial did not involve a situation where the accused was being charged
for the second time with the same offense. Instead, it was merely a retrial
of the first charge pursuant to an order by Grand Lodge. If your Committee were considering this record for the first time and solely on the
basis of this second trial. we would be constrained to recommend to
Grand Lodge that the finding of not guilty be reversed. This would be
our recommendation for the reason that the certified copy of the conviction of the acccused in the courts of the land constituted a prima facie
case and no defense having been offered by the accused to offset this
prima facie showing, no finding other than one of guilt would be permissible.

Section 341 of our Ordinances reads as follows:
"No judgment of a trial commission shall be set aside, or new
trial granted, for any error of any sort as to pleading, procedure, or
introduction of evidence, unless, after an examination of the entire
case, including the evidence, the Grand Lodge shall be of the opinion
that the error committed has resulted in a miscarriage of justice."
Your Committee still adheres to its views that the finding of not
guilty by the Trial Commission on the trial held in 1946 should have
been affirmed and still feels that under the provisions of section 341 of
the Ordinances just quoted the action of Grand Lodge in reversing the
finding of not guilty and remanding the cause for a new trial was not
warranted.

Trial Record No. 1125

Trial Record Nos. 1101, 1129 and 1130

The accused, A. P. P., was charged with unmasonic conduct on the
ground of drunkeness and intoxication. On October 23, 1947, a special
meeting of Palms Lodge was held at which nine commissioners were
duly elected to try the accused. The Master named November 24, 1947,
as the time for the first meeting of the commissioners, and directed the
secretary to prepare a summons to the accused to appear at said time
and place. The record shows that on November 24, 1947, six of the
nine elected commissioners were present for the trial, together with
one past Master, not elected as a commissioner, and who is referred to
as "Chairman." The record further shows that the summons to the
accused, although dated October 30, 1947, was not served on the
accused personally, but was "forwarded by mail" by the Secretary to
the accused at his last known place of residence on November 18, 194 7,
just six days before the trial. The accused did not appear at the trial
either in person or by attorney. The trial then proceeded with the socalled "Chairman" conducting the trial as the presiding officer, and the
accused was suspended. The Master of the lodge was present, appearing
at the first hearing as a witness against the accused, and at the continued hearing in the role of prosecutor or counsel for the accuser, conducting the examination of the witnesses.
Section 308 of the Ordinances provides:
"If the accused be within the jurisdiction of the Lodge, the summons
and copy of the charges shall be issued and served upon the accused
at least ten days prior to the day appointed for the trial, and shall be

This is a report concerning two trial records, record No. 1129 and
record No. 1130, and also trial record No. 1101, No. 1101 being a
duplicated number.
The facts have to do with a real estate broker, a real estate salesman, the owner of real property, and a dummy. The broker and the
salesman were both Masons of this jurisdiction. The salesman was
an employee of the broker. The owner employed the broker and the
salesman to sell the property. The broker and the salesman caused title
to be conveyed by their client, the owner, to a dummy, and represented
to the owner that the sales price was $1219.75 less than what the
property was really sold for. In truth and in fact the sale was to a purchaser (to whom title was conveyed by the dummy) for $1219.75 in
excess of the purchase price the two Masons told their client they had
received.
Then they collected a commission of 5% from the owner on the
purported purchase price, and the salesman kept the $1219.75 "profit."
The broker was highly incensed at the salesman for keeping the whole
sum of $1219.75: claimed that half of it belonged to him. Finally he
fired the salesman, and preferred charges of unMasonic conduct against
him.
These charges were heard last year by a trial commission which
reprimanded the salesman. When the record of this case came to Grand
Lodge, it was returned for further trial because the trial commission
had made no findings on the specifications of unMasonic conduct. From

175

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

this record it was apparent that the broker and the salesman were
each guilty of unMasonic conduct ·and should both be tried therefor.
Obviously they were both guilty ·of fraud and deceit as to the owner of
the real estate, whom they represented and to whom each of them owed
the duty of a fiduciary. Grand Lodge therefore ordered the broker to
be tried and the salesman to be retried.
Upon the trial of these two cases this year, the broker was found
guilty of unMasonic conduct, ·and the penalty fixed at suspension; the
salesman was likewise found guilty of unMasonic conduct and the
penalty fixed at expulsion.
A brief has been filed in behalf of the salesman, arguing that the
penalty as to him is unduly severe compared with that fixed for the
broker; that the salesman was a young man who looked to the older
broker as a mentor; and that the fault was primarily that of the broker,
who should have set a better example for his employee. There is merit
to this argument.
Your committee has given serious consideration to these cases. We
are of the opinion that the charges of unMasonic conduct as to both
parties have been amply proved, and that the proceedings are all regular
and sufficient. But we think we should recommend to Grand Lodge that
the penalties be the same and fixed at suspension.
Therefore, we offer the following resolutions:
Resolved that in trial record No. 1130 the findings and judgment
of suspension of the trial commission be approved.
Resolved that in trial record No. 1129 ( No. 1101 ) the findings of
the trial commission be approved, but that the penalty be reduced from
expulsion to suspension.

the saloon business, either as owner, agent or employe, except in
connection with and as a part of the operation of a bona fide hotel
or restaurant, or who shall become a barkeeper. shall be deem~d
guilty of unmasonic conduct, and shall, upon due trial ?~d conv~c­
-tion of said offense, forfeit all Masonic rights and privileges. mcluding membership in any Lodge."
.
In this case the Commission fixed the penalty at suspension.
In the opinion of your Committee, the language of Section 210 of the
Ordinances to the effect that one found guilty of being a barkeeper
shall "forfeit all Masonic rights and privileges, including membership
in any Lodge," does not permit of the penalty of suspension and commands the penalty of expulsion.
.
From a realistic point of view, there may not be a great deal of difference between our penalties of suspension and expulsion. It is true that a
suspended Mason may not enjoy any of the rights and privileges of a
Mason during the period of such suspension. However, a ~omplet~ forfeiture of such rights and privilege as contemplated by Section 210 m the
opinion of your Committee can only be accomplished by expulsion.
We therefore offer the following resolution and move its adoption:
Resolved. that -the action of the Trial Commission re trial record
1134 in finding the accused R. M . guilty be and the same is hereby ratified, affirmed, and approved but that the fixing of the penalty of suspension be and the same hereby is modified and the penalty fixed at
expulsion.
·

174

Adopted.

Trial Report No. 1145
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The accused presented his petition for the degrees to a lodge in
Marshalltown, Iowa. Objection was made and he was rejected. Shortly
thereafter, he came to California and presented his petition for the
degrees to Whittier Lodge.
..
..
.
In his petition to Whittier Lodge, he answered No to the question
whether he had ever applied for the degrees to any other lodge; he also
answered "No" to the question whether he had ever been rejected by a
Masonic Lodge.
In his trial by Whittier Lodge. the accused admitted the falsity of
his answers to these questions and to the further question in the petition whether all of his answers were true. He was convicted of unMasonic conduct and adjudged to be expelled.
In these cases, it has been the policy of Grand Lodge to adjudge
suspension rather than expulsion because Section 345 of our Ordinances

176

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

requires the accused should he hereafter desire to be restored te the
rights and privileges of Masonry, first to petition the Lodge which
heard the case, thus the Lodge which tried him is required to formally
consider and pass upon the petition for restoration.
Therefore, your Committee offers the following resolution:
Resolved: That the action of Whittier Lodge in finding the accused
guilty of unMasonic conduct be approved but that the penalty be fixed
at suspension.
Adopted.

Trial Record No. 1149
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
From East San Diego Lodge No. 561 :
The accused, a Fellowcraft, was charged with unmasonic conduct
supported by a specification charging that he was in the saloon business.
A sharply contested trial was had, the main question being whether the
place of business, of which the accused was a part owner, was a saloon
or a bona fide restaurant. The trial commission found against the accused.
In the opinion of your Committee, there is sufficient evidence to support
the finding. The penalty was fixed as suspension.
As previously reported to this Grand Lodge in Trial Record No.
1134, your Committee feels that Section 210 of the Ordinances of Grand
Lodge does not permit of the penalty of suspension but compels expulsion when the accused is convicted of engaging in the saJoon business.
Accordingly, we offer the following resolution and move its adoption:
Resolved, that the finding of guilt by the Trial Commission in the
Trial Record No. 1149 be and the same hereby is affirmed and approved
but that the penalty of suspension be and the same hereby is changed to
expulsion.
Adopted.

Report of Committee on Constitution Month Observance
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
I have the honor to submit a report of the Committee of the Grand
Lodge, Free and Accepted Masons of California, on Constitution
Month Observance.
We are pleased to advise you that more interest has been demonstrated throughout the Jurisdiction in the matter of this Observance
during the year just concluded than has attended the efforts of the
Committee during any former year. 332 of the subordinate Lodges of
the Jurisdiction joined in presenting a suitable program and in 120
instances the public was invited to be in attendance. The Brethren
throughout the Jurisdiction have responded well to the various requests
directed to them by the Committee, and we take this opportunity to
thank them for their support and interest. The Inspectors of the various
Districts were also of considerable assistance, and we thank them for
their help. The Committee has worked in exceptional harmony and
the utmost assistance and cooperation was apparent at all times. I wish
to take this opportunity to express my sincere thanks for the efforts
which they have expended.
The Committee was particularly fortunate this year in the amount
and kind of publicity which attended our efforts, and a considerable
degree of credit in this regard is due to Brother Harry Hammond Beall
of Los Angeles.
The Committee wishes to thank those members of the Craft who
responded so well to our plea for speakers. On several occasions it was
necessary for a speaker to travel approximately four hundred miles for
the purpose of addressing a subordinate Lodge on the subject of the
Constitution.
Constitution Month observance in California has become an accepted
tradition and this is due in large part to the efforts of this Grand Lodge.
For many years we were the only fraternal organization in this state

178

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA
PROCEEDINGS OF THE

committed to an observance of the birth of the Constitution, and by
reason of the activities of the subordinate Lodges throughout the state
other fraternal organizations and societies have joined in a general
observance of the natal day of the Constitution. This is a healthy
situation to note and augurs well for the observance of the future.
I wish to commend our Most Worshipful Grand Master, Chester
H. Warlow, who during the entire Masonic year impressed upon Mason
and citizen alike the necessity for a strict observance of this sacred
document, and may I likewise express my deep appreciation as well for
the cooperation and assistance of our Grand Secretary. Lloyd E. Wilson.
We of California may well feel proud of our splendid accomplishments in this regard, for Masonry throughout the Jurisdiction has made
a substantial contribution to the cause of good government and in
renewing our commitment to the worthy principles espoused by this
immortal document.
The Constitution of the United States is an American document.
Its antecedents are to be found in the heritage of English political history and liberty. Historic incidents which forced Magna Carta from
the King at the point of the sword, the suffering and oppression which
brought the Petition of Right, and the final achievement of the inalienable right of Englishmen in the Bill of Rights, all formed background
for the fifty-five framers of the Constitution who met in Philadelphia
for the purpose of drafting a new charter. Steeped in the philosophy of
Locke, Blackstone, and Montesquieu, they knew what governmental
structure would best preserve their concept of life. liberty. and property.
No nation in the world can in war or peace match our production
under our system of free enterprise, with its incentives and rewards for
effort. The United States has emerged from the war as the most powerful nation on earth. A system of government that has made all this
possible, that has given us the highest standard of living ever known,
that has opened the way for our amazing progress and has provided
opportunity, happiness, and blessings not enjoyed anywhere else in the
world,-such a system of government certainly is worth saving. And it.
must be saved.
To accept the substitute, a planned society, it is necessary to surrender the right to think. to surrender the mind which controls the free ·
actions of men. In a planned society education is controlled. freedom of
speech is abridged, freedom of the press is abridged, freedom of assembly is abridged. The control of the mind of man for the maintenance
of the plan is not economic democracy. It is not social justice. It is
tyranny-blind tyranny-the darkest, blackest tyranny that the human
race has ever seen.
Under the American Constitution the cause of human freedom has
been served. Human rights-the right to life, freedom of thought, re-

ligion, residence, press, assembly, petition and act~on, civi~ li~rty, ~~~
roperty-are promulgated and perpetuated by this Constitution w _ic
~romotes the welfare of the individual as one of many individuals making
up the nation.
Government exists for only one purpose-the prot~cti?n ~f these
rights. Its exercise of power is limited by a written consbtut:on. m ~~der
that it may never curtail these rights. As long as the Con~titution ives,
America need not dread the heel of the dictator or the disorder of anarchy.

As America faces the future, let us pause to recollect t at t e arseeing vision of our constitutional fathers resulted in an instrum~nt of

formidable fortress of defense in time of stress still remams the Constitution of the United States.

The Uni_versity Masonic Club at the University of California in
Berkeley enJoyed a very successful year during the fall and spring
semesters of 1947- 48. The club membership for the fall term was 837
and 587 for the spring term.
'

~eetmg place for t~e many students living in homes in the Bay Area and
1~ the ~any boarding houses surrounding the campus. It is used extensively m the evenings for study purposes and is one of the few places,

The special interest groups within the club assisted the club materially in many of the functions, and others supplied services to the club
as a whole. During the spring semester, the club newspaper came to life

Report of Board of Directors Masonic Club House
at Los Angeles
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of
Free and Accepted Masons of California:
Your Board of Directors for the Masonic Club House at Los Angeles
herewith presents its annual report.
At the board meeting on October 4, 1948, the resignation of Brother
Oscar Lawler, P. G. M .. from the chairmanship of the board was submitted and reluctantly accepted. He had served in that capacity since
May, 1946, to the satisfaction and gratification of the board. We regret
that the press of activities has compelled him to take this step, but we
are happy that he will continue as a member of the board. We value his
wise and calm counsel based as it is upon his broad experience in professional, business and civic affairs.
During the academic year which ended in June, 1948, the number
of Masonicaily affiliated students from the Westwood campus of
U. C. L. A. who joined and paid dues to the student organization at the
·club house was 651. Instruction on the southern campus of the university
starts a month later than at Berkeley, hence the present semester started
less than a month ago, but it appears that the number of paid up members
will equal or exceed the number last year.
You will be interested to know that the number of ex-G. l.'s has declined almost to the vanishing point in the student group. The present
student body is almost entirely composed of those who were in high
school during the war years. For the past several years it seemed strange
to visit the club house and have the men there introduce you to their
wives and talk about their children who were themselves near school
age. But they brought a maturity and determination to the affairs of the
dub house which contributed to the success of aII endeavors.
Last year the Board of Directors granted permission to the students
to establish a "snack" counter and tables in a part of the building. This
was the first time that meals had been served in the dub house on a daily
basis. The undertaking was and is entirely the responsibility of the
students. It met an urgent need because the more than 14,000 students
in the student body sorely taxed the restaurant facilities of the vicinity.
It began as a comparatively smaII co-operative undertaking of a few but
grew like "Topsy" and soon required full time help. During the seven
month period from October, 1947, to June, 1948, althouSJh meals were
served at cost, receipts totaled $11,173.05 or an average of $1.596.15 per
month.
From dues and revenues the students have purchased and donated
to the plant a Coca-Cola machine, a mimeograph. a smaII and a large

186

($315.00) ice cream cabinet. They have also done commendable work
of a charitable nature'. Food has been donated to the children of Europe,
sports equipment to a local Boy Scouts' Council. a Christmas party given
for the boys in the Ho11enbeck Center, an Easter party for the boys of
the McKinley Home and a dinner party for certain high school students.
Each Friday evening the students held an informal dance and each
Sunday an open evening supper. Attendance at the Friday informals
averaged between 200 and 300. Among the special occasions we may
note a few as follows:

carried a notice relative to these two institutions in their trestle boards.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Lodge Financing has been called on during the
current year to pass judgement and consent or disapprove on some fifty.seven applications presented pursuant to Sections 78 and 152 of the
Constitution and Ordinances.
While building projects and necessary repairs to buildings now
owned have been held in abeyance due to high costs, the point has been
reached in many instances where further delay in building would impair
the well-being of the Lodge, and in the case of repairs be detrimental
to property. Your Committee has taken these factors into consideration
in analyzing the various applications and inquiries presented.
After your Committee has given an answer on an application, in
each instance, a complete flle on the case, including the details of the
request, necessary Lodge or building corporation resolutions, financial
statements, comments by Committee members, together with copy of
written consent is filed in the Grand Secretary's office as a part of
the records of this Grand Lodge. In view of this procedure and the
fact that many requests follow the same pattern we are listing them in
our report by Lodge or building corporation, as the case may be, with
the amount of expenditure involved and the method of financing briefly
stated, under an appropriate statement covering the nature of such
cases. However, the requests of an individual nature and those we feel
may be of particular interest have been listed separately with additional
detail.

It is observed in the past two years four Masonic Temples have
been destroyed by fire. In each case the fire insurance carried is only
a small proportion of replacement cost. Your Committee is therefore
prompted to suggest to Lodges and Temple Associations that they carefully examine the insurance coverage for fire and other hazards on
buildings with the view of securing adequate coverage commensurate
with present day appraisals and costs.
Although the task of the Committee during the past year has been
arduous, as Chairman, I can report to you that all problems presented
have had our unbiased and sympathetic attention in an endeavor to
carry out the purpose for which the Committee was appointed. I would
be remiss if I did not express my appreciation to the members of the
Committee for their willing cooperation in accepting assignments and
giving many hours of time in carrying out the responsibilities of Committee membership.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Columbia Temple R-estoration begs leave to
submit the following report :
At the last Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge, the Committee on Finance in its report withholding recommendation of an appropriation for the proposed rebuilding the old Temple at Columbia, in part
stated as follows:
"Your Committee on Finance is in sympathy with the plan to rebuild
the old Temple."
"However, in its judgment the information now on hand is not sufficient to warrant the recommendation of an appropriation."
"The following information should be furnished to the Committee:
1. Complete information as to the plans of the State Park Commission
for the restoration of the old community together with information
as to progress already made.
2. Complete plans and specifications of the proposed building, so that
further check might be made on the probable cost.
3. List of the proposed furnishings of the building, together with an
estimate of the cost of same.
4. The proposed plan for the future use and occupancy of the building
together with an estimate of costs of operation."
No. I-HISTORY AND PLANS OF PARK COMMISSION FOR RESTORATION
OP COLUMBIA AND PROGRESS ALRBADY MADE

In 1928 Frederick L. Olmstead, an architectural engineer of national
reputation, was retained by the State to make a comprehensive survey
throughout the Mother Lode Country and report on the old mining town
which, in his judgment, was more nearly representative of the mining
communities of the '50's and which was best suited to be constituted a
State Historical Park and incorporated into the State Park System of
California under the jurisdiction and control of the California State
Park Commission.
In 1932 Mr. Olmstead filed his report setting forth his reasons for
choosing the town of Columbia, Tuolumne County, as the one town best
suited, from present state ·of preservation and historical background, to
the declared policy of the State to establish a historical park in California
somewhat along the lines of the Williamsburg, Virginia project where
an entire city, much larger than Columbia is being reconstructed and the
existing old time buildings are being rehabilitated to take on the identical
appearance they originally had. This rebuilding of Williamsburg, Virginia up-ta-date has cost 20- million dollars and there are approximately
100 more buildings to !'ecreate.
In 1945 Mr. Ol:Mstead filed a supplementary report on the Columbia

199

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

project recommending the extention of the original area of the Park.
The recommendation was adopted by the State Park Commission.
The California Legislature in 1945 appropriated $50,000.00 for the
purpose of acquiring property in the town of Columbia, and the act sets
forth the plan of acquisition for the area. A copy of the Act accompanying this report is marked Exhibit "A". A copy of the original Olmstead
map outlining the Park boundaries is attached to this report and made a
part hereof and marked Exhibit "B".

In 1947 Dr. Aubrey Neasham, Regional Historian for the National
Park Service, was given a leave of absence and was retained by the
California Park Commission as Special Consultant on the Columbia
Park project and is now compiling a historical summary and recommendation preparatory to the creation of a Master Plan for the preservation
and development of Columbia Historical State Park. It is anticipated that
this Plan will be completed during the early part of 1949.
The California State Park Commissioners' meeting in San Francisco,
September 17, 1948 approved Dr. Neasham' s recommendation to the
extension of the boundaries for Columbia Historical State Park. These
recommendations for extension of the boundaries were vital for the
proper administration, protection, development and interpretation of
Columbia State Park. This Master Plan will assure the preservation of
the lot upon which it is proposed to reconstruct the old Masonic Temple.
As soon as the Master Plan is completed and adopted by the Commission, work on the restoration of the old buildings will be pursued as
rapidly as money is available. It is impossible to estimate how long it
will take to fully complete the present program of rehabilitation and reconstruction. It will probably take several years. But the State is definitely pledged to the restoration of this historical Park and its future
maintenance.
Attached to this report and marked Exhibit "D" is a photostatic map
prepared by Dr. Neasham of the part area showing in black the principle
buildings now standing. In addition, outstanding historical structures no
longer in existence, including the Masonic Hall, are shown with dotted
lines. A key to said map accompanies it.
Also, there is attached hereto a map in colors marked Exhibit "E"
repared by Dr. Neasham protraying the areas within the Columbia
project to be acquired by the State of California. The proposed acquisition will be acquired in the order of their priority as follows:

In 1947 the State Legislature appropriated the further sum of $40,000.00 for acquisition of property in Columbia. A full summary of the
several appropriations up-to-date toward the establishment of the Columbia State Park is also attached to his report and marked Exhibit "C".
On July 15, 1945, Governor Earl Warren signed the Mayo Bill
creating Columbia a State Park.
On December 24, 1946 the Columbia Historical Park Association,
a non-profit corporation, was duly incorporated under the laws of California. This Corporation was authorized and required to act in an advisory capacity to the California State Park Commission in the matter
of the Columbia Park.
·

It has also been recommended by Dr. Neasham, in addition to the
area acquired, that Tuolumne County pass zoning laws to protect the
setting of old Columbia. Such zoning would be effective at least one mile
on all sides of the boundaries as set forth in Exhibit "E". It is also proposed that all approach highways and roads leading into Columbia be

There are eleven ( 11 ) blocks included in the central area covered
by priority No. 1, and in this particular section there are approximately
thirty-six ( 36) outstanding historic structures including store buildings, hotels and residences which date back to the 1850's and 1860's.
The so-called central area has a present population of approximately
one-hundred ( 100) persons and there are within the vicinity of Columbia five-hundred ( 500) persons.
Forest Park Ranger, Al Beck, who resides in Columbia, is in immediate charge of the Park and according to his records there have been
during the present year 58,285 visitors from all sections of the United
States.

the Columbia Park, but is entirely too lengthy a document to be set out
in full herein. This statement was issued by the Commission to aid
in clarifying public understanding of the· purposes and policy of the
Commission in regard to the Columbia State Park.
Attached to this report and marked Exhibit "G" is a list of business
houses, public buildings and some residences in Columbia to be restored
and preserved.
The plans of the Commission call for the elimination, not only of
automobile parking in the streets, but also prohibition of the use of
automobile by visitors and sight-seers within the Park. It is proposed to
provide parking space outside the area where historic structures are
predominant.
.
The College of the Paciflc purchased the old Fallon Theatre m
Columbia which is situated across the street from the site of the Masonic
Temple. The College has given the Commission title to this property
and is leasing the theatre and 'the Fallon Hotel. Dr. Robert Bums,
President of the College, informs us that the College will put on plays
of the "Fifties" during the summer months and house its Little Theatre
players in the Fallon Hotel.

Mr. E. E. Powell of Stockton, District Superintendent, will be in
charge of the restoration work. Said work will be done in accordance
with th~ Master Plan. He will have available a sufficient force of men
from the Division of Parks and Beaches to carry on his work.
It has been suggested that the following buildings. no longer standing, be fully reconstructed from the ground up because of their historical importance and need for them.

The policy of the State Park Commission relative to rebuilding of
structures within the Park limits is in part set forth in a letter your
Committee received from Mr. A. E. Henning, Chief Division of Beaches
and Parks as follows:
"The Odd Fellows and the Native Sons of the Golden West
are two fraternal type of organizations who intend doing restoration work. The State Park Commission, if "funds are available. will no doubt finance some of the rebuilding of structures
within the Park limits but not for any fraternal organizations."
It is proposed by Dr. Neasham to rebuild the old Broadway Hotel
which adjoins the Masonic Temple on the east, on Broadway. This
would be reconstructed by the State for the purpose of furnishing
visitors to the Park accommodations overnight, and otherwise, for
compensation. This system was also inaugurated in Williamsburg,
where one of the old historic Inns was fully restored and where visitors
may study during their visit to the project paying for meals and room
accommodations.
Preliminary discussions have .been held with some of the San Francisco Chinese to flnance the rebuilding of the famous old Joss House in
Columbia.

The erection of the Temple of Columbia Lodge No. 28 was completed in 1855 and was occupied by the Lodge until the gravels gave
out and the old Lodge was forced to surrender its Charter in 1891, and
consolidate with Tuolumne No. 8 at Sonora.
The title to the lot upon which the Temple stood is now vested in
the State of California.
In 1947 the Chairman of this Committee wrote the Hon. Joseph R.
Knowland, Chairman of the State Park Commission, inquiring as to the
policy of the Commission with respect to leasing property in Columbia, ·
and the following is the reply addressed to the Chairman:
Aug. 22, 1947
"Leon 0. Whitsell,
Burlingame, Calif.
My Dear Mr. Whitsell:

It has been understood by the State Park Commission that the
Grand Lodge of Masons of the State of California will be given premission to erect a replica of the old Masonic Temple on the ground
which they have acquired, upon which the old building stood, in the
town of Columbia, now owned by the California State Park Commis-sion. A satisfactory lease will be made by the State to whatever body
may desire to enter unto such a lease representating the Masonic
Fraternity of California.
Fraternally yours,
J. R. Knowland, Chairman
Park Commission."
Your Committee has also written the Park Commission as to its
attitude and policy toward granting permission to rent the lower story of
the proposed Temple at Columbia and the following is the reply from

205

Commission in its official meeting on June 11th and 12th, 1948.
Division of Beaches and Parks,

May 24, 1948
"Mr. Leon 0. Whitsell.
1565 Newlands Avenue,
Burlingame, Calif.
Dear Mr. Whitsell:
If you should be given a lease on the property and agree to maintain
it then I would recommend to the Commission that any rental you receive from the ground floor should go to your organization. We can
make a satisfartory lease at a nominal rate.
I feel that the Grand Lodge will have made a great contribution to
Columbia by re-erecting this building.
Fraternally yours,
J. R. Knowland."
RESOLUTION OF CALIFORNIA STATE PARK COMMISSION ADOPTED
AT !Ts MEETING JUNE 11 AND 12, 1948

Columbia Histric State Park
Chief Henning presented correspondence relative to the reconstruction of the Masonic Temple in the Columbia Historic State Park,
in which it was stated that the Lodge desires to lease land from the State
of California for the reconstruction of the Temple and wherein permission was asked to rent the lower portion of such building in order to use
rental moneys for the maintenance of the building. It was moved by
Commissioner Waldner that the Staff enter into negotiations for lease
satisfactory to the Grand Masonic Lodge of California to this Commission. Seconded by Commissioner Carrillo and approved.
The Mother Lode will be the great magnet drawing our visitors to
those localities in the mountains where Masonic romance flourished and
where the Masonic Temple was in reality the religious center for those
hard working and hard playing miners in the early days.
If the Temple in this "Williamsburg of the West" is rebuilt and
properly maintained it will be a Masonic Shrine to which the history
hungry California Masons will visit and revisit and it will stimulate a
healthy interest and pride in our past-a pride, not only in the minds of
the older members of our Fraternity but also in the minds and hearts
of the young, virile new members who must be prepared and equipped

206

207

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

to carry on so that Masonry in California may ultimately reach that
high destiny to which its glorious past entitles it.
California Masonry needs the stimulating influence of the years
that are gone; it needs to again commune with the strong Masonic
spirits of the Mountains-the spirits of men who in the long ago had
visions and in those visions saw and foretold the great part which Masonry was destined to play in this State and its ever expanding institutions.
Let us rebuild the old Temple in the Mountains.
Let us provide under proper supervision that Degrees may be conferred therein, that the members of our Lodges may gain inspiration in
that atmosphere redolent with memories of the men who so many years
ago held high the banner of Masonry in those old hills until the gravels
were exhausted and they were compelled to seek the illusive metal
elsewhere.
Columbia will be to the West what Williamsburg is to the Easta historical Shrine. When the old buildings now standing are fully restored in structure and appearance as in the "Fifties". and the buildings
which have heretofore been torn down and destroyed are rebuilt, this
old erstwhile ghost town will be the pride, not only of the Mother Lode
but the pride of the entire State of California.
This old Masonic Temple should be rebuilt as it was in the "Fifties"
and should be so maintained that the Lodges of California, that desire:
may sojourn to that historic spot and confer Degrees on their candidates,
upon appropriate and convenient occasions.
Th~ lower story should at a later date be prepared as a Masonic
museum.
I have no doubt that then within a reasonable time, sufficient Masonic items of historical interest will be forthcoming and a museum
could be established and maintained which would be of tremendous
interest to members of the Craft and the layity as well.
./
The year 1950 will be a red-letter year in California history as well
as Masonic history. That year will mark the centennial of the admission
of California into the Union, and the beginning of Grand Lodge Masonry in California.
Thousands of history minded people from all over the United States
will visit our State. Men and women from the Eest will come seeking
the localities and scenes where their relations worked ancf'labored and
met with either success or failure, during the hectic days of the greatest
search for gold in the history of the world.
Masons from all sections of the Union, as well as from foreign countries will come to join with us in celebrating our first century of Masonic
existence. Masonry should be ready for them.
Approved of the following resolution by this Grand Lodge shall not

become effective until Plan "B" and Specifications accompanying it shall
have received the approval of the California State Park Commission as
required by law.
Your Committee on rebuilding the Temple at Columbia submits
the following Resolution and moves its adoption.
I-That it is the policy of the Grand Lodge to rebuild the old Masonic Temple at Columbia on the site last occupied by Columbia ·
Lodge No. 28.
2-That the sum of $38,204.00 be appropriated and set aside for that
purpose.
3-That a Committee be appointed by the incoming Grand Master
to enter into a contract in the name of the Most Worshipful
Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of California for
the rebuilding of the old Temple in Columbia for a sum not to
exceed $38,204.00.
4-That said Temple be constructed in accordance with Plans and
Specifications made and prepared by Brother Wm. Mooser of
San Francisco. A copy of said Plans accompany this report
marked Exhibit "H'' and a copy is filed in the office of the Grand
Secretary.
5-That upon the completion and acceptance of said building by the
said Committee that there be filed by them with Grand Lodge a report
setting forth complete Plans for the future, care, operation and maintenance of said building, together with the necessary rules and regulations to govern same.
Respectfully submitted for the Committee

We have also carefully examined one hundred twenty·eight Reso·
lutions affecting Life Membership. Most Lodges secured from the Grand
Secretary the form complying with Section 253 of Ross Digest. Eleven
Resolutions have been continued to next year because of additional in·
formation needed before our Committee can approve same. The entire
Resolution as amended should be sent in, and not only the paragraph
amended. In one case the original resolution was lost, and had not been
spread on the minutes of the lodge. (We recommend the resolution al·
ways be incorporated in the minutes). The lodge this year passed an
amendment raising the amount charged for Life Membership. We could
not approve it because neither we nor they knew what was in the origin·
al resolution, and it also could not be ascertained as to whether or not
it conformed to Section 253. They are going to pass a new resolution.
When in doubt as to any point, we would recommend that the Secretary
or Master write to the Grand Secretary. Correct information is always
available from him. The Life Membership provision is now handled by
a standing Resolution, and it should conform to Section 253 of Ross
Digest.

Report of the Committee on Masonic Information
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Masonic information reports as follows:
In its last annual report your Committee went to some length in reviewing the history of Masonic Education or Information in this Grand
Jurisdiction over the past thirty years, quoting conclusions reached
and reported in prior years, analyzing the problems presented, and
concluding with an outline of principles applicable and with a proposed
program to be followed. Your Committee has not, in the main, changed
its views, so that, for a fuller understanding of the course to be followed
and of the objectives to be attained, the 1947 report of your Committee
should be consulted.
With that report, your Committee tendered manuscripts for two
booklets, one called "Address to the Candidate" to be presented to the
applicant for degrees immediately after his election to receive them,
and the other called the "Book of the Entered Apprentice" to be delivered to the candidate upon his initiation. These books having been
authorized by Grand Lodge, 15,000 copies of each were printed and
distributed to the lodges, in quantities as nearly as could be estimated
equal to the number of candidates to be initiated during the year. Regretably and, perhaps, necessarily, there were underestimates in some
instances, or some Lodges accepted more candidates this year than
they did last year. Before the year was past, at the request of the Grand
Secretary, who had obligingly undertaken the distribution of the booklets, an additional 5000 copies of each were run off the press. This increment will probably not carry much beyond the present Communication of Grand Lodge.
Widespread, unsolicited and hearty commendation followed the issue of these pamphlets. Your Committee has received many letters of
approbation and the Grand Secretary received many more. While these
booklets were intended primarily for candidates, as stated in last year's
report, a number of Lodges have ordered supplies to be sold or given to
their existing membership. or these extra copies for such use, your Committee was forced, by the limitation on its appropriation, to exact a price
of ten cents each, the money to be remitted to the Grand Secretary for
credit of the Committee's fund, which had been almost wholly consumed by printing expense.
Feeling certain that the first two publications had filled a need, your
Committee has prepared and presents with this report, the manuscripts
for two additional pamphlets, one called the "Book of the Fellow Craft,"
and the other the "Book of the Master Mason." The former is much of
the same character as that for the Entered Apprentice, differing, of

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

215

course, to the extent the two degrees differ. This distinction is pointed
out in the booklet and the Fellow Craft Degree is presented in what is
believed to be its true character as the operative degree, or, at least, the
most operative of the Three Degrees. This Degree, by reason of its
position between the First and the Third, possessing neither the surprise
which attends the one nor the sense of completiori and accomplishment
which accompanies the other, has lost emphasis and suffered some loss
of influence. Your Committee has attempted to explain it in a way which
restores it to the proper rank and gives it a character all its own, which
neither of the others exemplify.
In preparing the Book of the Master Mason, your Committee was
confronted with a larger task, for the Master Mason, besides being the
recipient of a degree, is vested with certain privileges and charged with
certain duties which do not pertain to the Entered Apprentice or Fellow
Craft. The Master Mason is, so to speak, endowed with full Masonic
citizenship; he becomes a voter and a taxpayer; and, upon him depends
·the conduct, welfare, purity and prosperity of the Craft. Therefore, it
is necessary, if the newly raised Master Mason is to take his place and
perform his functions as a Mason, that he be informed of many particulars outside of and beyond those relating to degrees, ceremonies and
ritual. As they have appeared to your Committee, these subjects are:
A survey of the broad question of what Freemasonry is and what its
teachings and purposes are; a succinct statement of the privileges and
duties of the Master Mason; advice on the important matter of applicants for degrees and how the portals of the Fraternity are to be guarded; the paramount importance of peace and harmony; and explanation
of the positions and prerogatives of the Master of the Lodge; the Inspector, and the Grand Master; an outline of the organization, composition, and functions of the Grand Lodge; a brief treatise on the customs
and laws of Freemasonry; a word about the Masonic Homes and other
examples of Masonic relief: and, finally, through all of these, to bring out
the different phases of Freemasonry and the several fields of activity
or endeavor open to the Master Mason.
Although this booklet contains about 18,000 words and may, at first
glance, appear to some as too extended, it is not perceived how less
would suffice if instruction of value is to be communicated. Moreover,
it is not intended to be the fate of this booklet to be read once and laid
aside, but rather that it will serve as one to which future reference may
be made until the holder has undertaken further study or has received
additional instruction by his lodge. For purposes of comparison attention is directed to the Manual published by Grand Lodge in 1938, which
ran to some 68,000 words or almost four times the volume of the proposed booklet. Although the Manual of 1938 was subsequently abandoned, it is instructive to observe, that ten years later copies of it have

been found in the ·possession of brethren who use it for information
which they desire and which that publication undoubtedly contained,
notwithstanding its faults. It is belie.v ed that the proposed Book of the
Master Mason contains all of the useful parts of the former Manual.

otherwise would stray? Does it create veneration for the Society and
make Masonry appear something different from the ordinary fraternal

Your Committee recommends:
1. That the two manuscripts accompanying this report be referred
to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes for approval: that,
with such amendments as that Committee may recommend, such manuscripts be approved by Grand Lodge; and that the Grand Secretary be
authorized to print and distribute the same to the Lodges:
2. That your Committee be continued for the ensuing year;
3. That there be appropriated, for the printing of said pamphlets,
the sum of $5,000 and, for the general expense of the Committee the
sum of $500.
Respectfully submitted,

Your Committee points out that it has deliberately refrained from
any attempt to interpret, explain, or enlarge upon the symbolism or
allegory of any degree, believing that, while that may be a proper and
instructive occupation for individual Ma5ons, the place for the official
comment, if any, by Grand Lodge is in the ritual, and that, when, if
ever, elucidation is deemed necessary, it will be accomplished by agencies
other than this Committee.
Your Committee reiterates what was said last year, that a program
of Masonic Information is not to be quickly or easily accomplished.
It is, in itself, a small revolution, and, in such experiments, it is best to
proceed slowly. consolidating each position before moving on to the next.
The value and effect of the work is best judged by the actual effect
wrought in the Lodges and by what the Masters and other officers observe and feel about its usefulness. Thus far, your Committee is reasonably satisfied that it is on the right course.
With the complete publication of the four booklets herein mentioned, your Committee will not consider that its resources are exhausted,
but will then consider the matter of committees in the Lodges to carry
on the educational work. It is hoped that, by these pamphlets, your
Committee will secure the confidence of the Masters and other officers of
the Lodges in the program and, thereby, command their earnest and
whole hearted support. Already, there is evidence of added interest
shown by candidates, some of whom inquire when the other ·booklets
are to be delivered to them.
We cannot be too oft reminded that, while the Grand Lodge is the
center of Masonic authority in this jurisdiction, it is not the center of
Masonic activities; that center is in the Lodge. Unless the Lodge selects
the proper candidates and inculcates in them a full understanding and
appreciation of the principles, policies, and purposes of Masonry, then,
all of the hopes and aspirations, all of the orations and addresses, and
all of the plans and projects of Grand Lodge will be futile. A stream
can rise no higher than its source, and the source of all Masonic material is the Lodge. The Masters, Wardens, and Secretaries of the Lodges
are on the firing line, so to speak: it is they who know the candidates,
their characters, abilities, and personalities; and it is they who can appraise the effect that Freemasonry is having upon those candidates, what
interest they show, and what part they will probably play in the Craft.
We want those opinions. Is this program doing any good? Does it
awaken more interest in the candidate? Is it arousing his curiosity? Is it
calculated to induce further study? Will it probably hold some who

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
During the past twelve months your Grand Master has seen fit to
grant dispensations to form new Lodges as follows:
Meudell Lodge at Bakersfield
Crossroads Lodge at San Diego

Crossroads Lodge was granted a dispensation on January 31st, 1918
and instituted by the Grand Master May 29th, 1918.
This Lodge is an outgrowth of the North Island Masonic Club
formed in June, 1915, which Club had held regular monthly meetings.
In addition they formed several degree teams which conferred degrees
at the invitation of the Lodges in San Diego County.
Among the twenty-five Charter members, fourteen are members of
the San Diego district Lodges and nine ( 9) members of foreign juris·
dictions.
The San Diego Lodges have given wholehearted support to the new
Lodge, evidencing the need therefor and t~eir satisfaction with its composition. Further evidence of this fine spirit is noted by donations
received from Masonic Bodies in the area, totaling nearly five hundred
dollars ( $500.00).
Their financial condition is excellent, the record showing a cash
·
balance in excess of $3,000.00.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that a Charter be granted
to Crossroads Lodge No. 696 at San Diego in the County of San Diego.

SAINT ELMO LODGE

Your Committee is impressed by the ardor and enthusiasm of the
entire group, and with the progress they have made and we feel that
the brief life of the Lodge holds bright promise for the future. However,
your Committee is of the opinion that a Lodge under dispensation
should work a reasonable period of time to prove to Grand Lodge that
the granting of a Charter is entirely appropriate. We feel that this group
has not been functioning a sufficient length of time to meet this qualification.
We suggest that the brethren of Bixby Knolls Lodge possess themselves of that cardinal virtue "patience" and your Committee recommends that Bixby Knolls Lodge be continued under dispensation.

Saint Elmo Lodge in Oakland was granted a dispensation March
29th, 1948, and Instituted by the Grand Master May 18th, 1948.
This Lodge was formed principally by Brethren in Maritime occupations.
Although they have received fifteen ( 15) petitions since their Institution, they have adhered to their original plan of conferring only one
degree a week and it is the observation of this Committee that they are
making Masons who will be a credit to the Fraternity.
The Lodge is out of debt and has a cash balance of approximately
$1,000.00. Most of their equipment has either been donated or made
by their own members.
The Committee feels that while this Lodge may never be one of
the larger Lodges, it will be a credit to Grand Lodge and we, therefore, recommend that a Charter be granted to Saint Elmo Lodge No. 697
at Oakland in the County of Alameda.
WILLIAM D. STEPHENS LODGE

William D. Stephens Lodge in Los Angeles was granted a dispensation June 7th, 1948 and Instituted by the Grand Master June 19th, 1948.
While this Lodge has been operating only since June 19th, 1948 an
Inspector was assigned to them, at their request in August 1947, and
since that time they have regularly met as an organized group and
perfected their proficiency in the work.
Since their Institution, they have conferred seven ( 7) degrees and
your Committee is ·pleased to note that their first consideration is to
make Masons rather than members and to that end they have inaugurated a plan for welcoming their candidates which merits the attention
of other Lodges. When a candidate is to receive a degree, he is met at
his home or place of busines by a member-taken to dinner and then to
the Lodge room and introduced to the brethren, thus he is made to feel
that he is a part of the organization. While this plan probably could
not be carried out in all Lodges, William D. Stephens Lodge is to be
complimented for their enterprise in this respect.
This Lodge is renting an adequate meeting place in the Masonic
Temple at Pico and Figueroa Streets in Los Angeles and is in a sound
financial position. There is ample room in Los Angeles for this Lodge
as the seventy-four ( 74) existent Lodges have an average membership
of 429.
We, therefore, recommend that a Charter be granted to William
D. Stephens Lodge No. 698 at Los Angeles in the County of Los
Angeles.
BIXBY KNOLLS LODGE

Bixby Knolls Lodge in Long Beach, was granted a dispensation on
July 21st, 1948, and was Instituted July 31st, 1948.

PONDEROSA LODGE

Ponderosa Lodge in Fresno was granted a dispensation August 1st,
1948 and Instituted August 5th, 1948, by the Grand Master.
This Lodge has had an auspicious start and your committee commends the Masons in the Fresno area for their efforts in the formation
of this new Lodge.
However, due to the short time these brethren have been working
together the Committee feels that it would be to their interests and that
of Grand Lodge for them to work a time with patience under dispensation.
We are confident the enthusiasm of these brethren will not suffer
and that at the next communication of Grand Lodge they will have
demonstrated by their works that they should have a Charter.
We, therefore, recommend that Ponderosa Lodge be continued under
dispensation.
