Report of Committee on Freedom Train
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Freedom Train was appointed by the Grand
Master pursuant to a resolution of Grand Lodge. This resoultion was
presented to your Committee on Policy and General Purposes by
Brother Arthur Joel. Inspector of the 48-A Masonic District. Brother
Joel is now deceased, but his alertness and thoughtfulness lives in the
activity which resulted from bringing the matter to the attention of
Grand Lodge.
The Committee's mission was to assist in carrying out the nationwide Freedom Train project. The broad objective was to awaken our
citizens to a keener appreciation of the rights and responsibilities
inherent in American citizenship. Your Committee felt that our California lodges on behalf of the Masonic fraternity could serve this great
cause by recalling to the minds of our brethren, and in turn to our
citizens, how dearly the political rights they now enjoy were won, how
carefully they must be guarded, and how completely lost they would
be in a totalitarian world. It was further felt that especially at this
time should our fraternity, always preeminent in the cause of freedom,
assist in stopping alien ideologies and try to make misguided converts
see that their ultimate end must be inevitable chaos and conquest.
An example in point appeared in a recent Congressional hearing
on Communistic espionage activities in the United States. A star witness was a former member of the Communist party and, according to
her own statement, she had been a war-time spy for a Communist ring.
In her testimony she candidly confessed that she was attracted to
Communism because "I grew up to womanhood without becoming
acquainted with the American government * * * this fault, I think,
runs all through our educational system." If this is true, then it was
not because the witness was not "educated." She went through grammar school. high school. a fine woman's college in the East. She also
took a master's degree at Columbia University. Apparently, however,
at no point in her education did she become acquainted with the American government. She never understood the basic assumption of our
government otherwise she would not have become a Communist.
In keeping with the broad objectives of the Freedom Train project
and the desires of the Grand Master, your Committee kept in close
touch with representatives of the American Heritage Foundation. This
is a privately financed, nonprofit organization, representative of all the
major groups in our American system, including industry, labor and
the professions. It has for its purposes the program of the Freedom
Train. The Committee received and passed on to our 590 lodges the
schedule of stops of the train in California, recommended to the lodges
that local sub-committees in the lodges be appointed to inform their

members and others in order that all persons possible might take advantage of the great opportunity to visit the train, and to make contacts
with various local groups similar to our activities during Public Schools
Week so that school organizations, officials and publicizing agents in
the respective communities would participate in the project and to conduct programs in our lodges, including talks on the precious documents
in the train. Later, your Committee divided the State into sections of
inspectorial districts and assigned a section to each of the members of
your Committee for supervision. Follow-up letters were sent to the
masters of all the California lodges giving pertinent data and recommendations. In order to get maximum results other recognized organizations were included in the general program.
Since it appeared quickly that the train could not accommodate all
who desired to make the visit, your Committe arranged with those in
authority to take a 16 mm. movie film of the exhibits for later distribution throughout the State. M. W. William B. Ogden presented to the
Grand Master the idea for these films. Thereupon, your Committee,
with the assistance of R. W. Ellsworth Meyer, got in touch with
Brother Ernest W. Miller of North Hollywood, who was appointed
to take the movies. Great credit is due Brother Miller and his assistants
for their volunteer work in recording on sound track 16 mm. movies
the priceless documents and the pictures of the Freedom Train at stops
throughout California. They did yeoman work and in a truly professional manner they overcame problems of getting access to the exhibits
when the crowds were not in attendance and in the problems of lighting. An example of their professional touch is that those in charge of
the Freedom Train project now greatly desire a copy of the film. It.
perhaps will be of great value, since it is the only one in existence.
Another reason for taking the pictures was because your Committee
felt that while the train itself was a dramatic incident, it was merely a
spark to rekindle throughout our nation the fire of real old fashioned
Americanism. This initial emotion to be of maximum value should be
followed through and continued. Hence, your Committee recommended
that activities extend beyond the mere arrival and departure of the
train and that the films be made available to the California lodges for
the purpose of conducting continuing programs, talks and discussions.
We are happy to say that while unavoidable delays have occurred, the
films are now in the process of completion. You brethren, especially
those who were unable to visit the train, will be glad to know you soon
can sit and see pictures of the train and its exhibits. Programs can be
built around the event to show the meaning and relation of the documents to the historic fundamentals of our form of government. Thus,
we can dedicate ourselves anew to our priceless heritage and to the
importance of the continual care and devotion necessary to preserve
our freedom.

22i

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Those of you who saw the train may remember there was also
evidence of the necessity of this continual alertness, for some alien
organizations distributed subversive literature and tried to impede the
program at the stops in California.
Your Committee is most happy to teJJ you that the response of the
California lodges to the entire Freedom Train project was, if anything,
over-enthusiastic. Some 155 of our California lodges made written
reports to your Committee of programs they conducted. These are
available for your examination. You will be interested to know that
Union Lodge No. 58 of Sacramento commemorated the visit of the
Freedom Train to that city on March 20 by the preparation of this
elaborate permanent bound volume. It comprises an inspired historical
article, the publicity attendant upon the event, and resolutions by
members of the lodge. Thus, each member pledged themselves to
renewed awareness of their American citizenship. The volume was
presented to the Grand Master and will be a permanent reminder here
in Grand Lodge of the event.
Under the continued leadership of our lodges throughout California,
therefore. your efforts and influence were exerted toward the objectives
of the Grand Lodge resolution of last year.
So, on the 1948 anniversary of George Washington's birthday. the
Masons of California were on hand when the Freedom Train, brightly
painted red, white and blue. roJJed across the Southern border of the
State and into the City of San Diego, and continued throughout the
length of our great State.

Jin and Silas Dean, an early draft of the Constitution of the United
States with handwritten annotations by George Washington. You also
saw the original official manuscripts of our Bill of Rights and of
Abraham Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation.

If you were so fortunate as to get inside the train, you saw treasured
sheets of parchment and paper. many of them yeJJowed with age. which
told graphically the story of the birth and development from 13 littleknown struggling colonies of the mighty nation now known the world
over as the United States of America. You saw a letter printed in Rome
in the year 1493 in which Christopher Columbus described to a friend
his discovery of the new world, a copy of the Mayflower Compact
published in 1622, under which the Pilgrims of Plymouth Colony governed themselves for a number of years-perhaps the first seed of
democratic government in our country, a copy of the Treaty of Paris,
signed by Great Britain in 1783, recognizing the independence of the
original 13 colonies. as well as printed public documents, handwritten
manuscripts, or authentic informal letters, recording every event of
historic importance through the 165 years since the winning of American independence. You saw also documents preceding the history of
the American nation, such as the 13th century copy of the Magna
Charta, signed by King John of England at Runnymede in 1215, the
protest of the American colonists against the British Stamp Act in 1765,
a copy of the Declaration of Independence attested by Benjamin Frank.-

we understood better that we are the heirs and the guaraians of these
liberties, and that we,, should pledge ourselves anew, "they shall not
perish from the earth.

The poet has said that the leaves fall fast in Vallombrosa, but they
are nothing compared to the human leaves that fall daily from the tree
of life. Life is so uncertain that every poet, every philosopher, every
~ol~ book of every g~eat religion has dealt with the mystery, attempting in some way to give comfort and consolation to those who remain.

In the past year 231 Masters and Past Masters, members of this

Grand Lodge, have been called to that "spiritual building, that house
not made with hands. eternal in the heavens."
The losses have been in 176 lodges, 133 have lost one, 33 have lost

most heavily upon Santa Cruz Lodge No. 38, which has lost five: Percy

brethren of this lodge in their great loss.

PROSPER ALBERT SAINGES

On May 12, 1947 death claimed Prosper Albert Sainges, Inspector
of La Parfaite Union Lodge No. 17 of the City of San Francisco. This
Lodge conducts its meetings in the Frenc~ langu~ge and compris~s t~e
1l3th Masonic District. Brother Sainges Masoruc career began m his

by King Soloman's Lodge No. 260 of San Francisco. He was mitlated
April 13, 1908, passed June 8, and raisea August 17. the same year.
He dimitted from this lodge in 1935. He applied for affiliation to La
Parfaite Union Lodge No. 17. The petition was received July 6, 1935,
and his election to membership occurred August 2, 1935.
A thorough knowledge of French and -his enthusiastic interest in
Masonry deeply impressed his brethren, and in 1936 he was appointed
Junior Deacon, which office he heia for three years. He was elected
Junior Warden in 1939; Senior Warden in 1940, and served the Lodge
as Master in 1941-42.
Appreciating his qualifications as a leader in Masonic work Grand
Master Gilbert C. DeForest appointed him Inspector April 1O. 1945.
The presentation of the Certificate was made in the presence of the
Grand Secretary and eight Inspectors May 4, 1945, in one of the most
pleasant and enthusiastic meetings ever held in this lodge. He was also
a member of Golden Gate Commandery, and for ten years was a member of the Patrol of Islam Temple of the Shrine.
Brother Sainges was born in 1885 in the village of Villesgure,
France. As a boy he was fascinated by what he read of the wonderful
City of the Golden Gate in the great State of Califo~nia, in far awa!
America. He was determined that some day that city would be his
home. His hopes were realized earlier than he expected and traveling
alone he arrived in San Francisco in 1900.
The beauty and fascination of the city far exceeded his fondest
dreams, and he immediately dedicated his efforts to her interests. He

applied for papers of naturalization upon reaching the proper age, and

HENRY CLAY MC MASTER

Henry Clay McMaster, Inspector of the 101 st Masonic District,
was called from labor Easter Sunday, March 28, 1948, at his home in
Fullerton, California.
Brother McMaster was ·born in Cleveland, Ohio, June 17, 1888. He
received his education in that ctiy. Coming to California in his 25th
year he settled in Fullerton, and passed the remainder of his life in that
beautiful community. Entering the service of the Union Oil Company
he was a salesman in the salvage department for 38 years. He is survived by his widow, Mabel McMaster, one daughter, Mrs. Phillip
Pippiatt of Brea, California, four brothers and four sisters, one granddaughter, Ellen Louise Pippiatt.
On February 18, 1920 he-was initiated in Fullerton Lodge No. 339,
passed March 18, and raised to the Sublime Degree April 9. Elected
Master of his Lodge he served in that capacity for the year 1924. In
1936 Brother McMaster was appointed Inspector of the lOlst District,
comprising the lodges in the northern half of Orange County, and
served faithfully in that exalted position until his death.
Other branches of Masonry appealed to his sense of the beautiful
and he devoted much of his time to the York Rite, being Past High
Priest of Fullerton Chapter No. 90 Royal Arch Masons; Captain of
the Guard of Santa Ana Council No. 14 Royal and Select Masters;
Commander of Fullerton Commandery No. 55, Knights Templar.
The esteem in which he was held was most fittingly expressed by
the brethren of his lodge: "In the passing of Worshipful Henry C.
McMaster Masonry in Orange County has lost its most distinguished
and loyal member. Known throughout the county for his devotion to
the ideals of Masonry, for his extreme tolerance and kindness to his
fellow man, for his readiness to aid and assist a distressed brother or
his dependents, and to instruct with rare indulgence the ritualistic and
secret work of our Order, his passing creates a void which no time can
fill."
The example set by Henry McMaster is a pattern of love and devotion for the Fraternity. We ask God's blessing upon him.

JAMES BERTRAM MC LEES

Death from a heart ailment from which he suffered for more than
50 years ended the long and useful career of J. B. Mclees at his home
in San Diego. December 16, 1947. "Bert," as he was most affectionately
known. was born in Edenburgh, Scotland, June 9, 1877, and brought
to the United States by his parents at the age of 1. His family settled
in Lock Haven, Pennsylvania, where he received his early education.
He was graduated from Franklin and Marshall College with the
degree of master of arts, and went to San Francisco in 1901. He moved
from San Francisco in 1904 and established himself in San Diego, becoming associated with the San Diego Railway, leaving that company
to enter the County Clerk's office as a deputy in 1906. He served as
deputy for 11 years before he was appointed to head the department
in 1917. He was elected each succeeding 4 years and served San Diego
County in this responsible position until his death.
Loyal and devoted service to his adopted country was one of Bert's
most outstanding qualities. He enlisted from Lock Haven, Pennsylvania, in the Spanish-American War. serving as Sergeant and Company
Clerk of the 12th Pennsylvania Volunteers, but was invalided out of
the service when the doctors discovered he suffered from a heart ailment. His attempts to enlist in World War I were unsuccessful for
the same reason.
On November 5, 1907 Bert married Maude Loretta Clark, a native
of Kentucky, in San Diego. They have five children, all of whom survive. His other survivors are his wife and a brother, Howard Mclees
of Corry, Pennsylvania.
The Masonic career of our beloved brother began in San Diego
Lodge No. 35 when he was initiated, passed and raised, all within the
month of November 1917. He held various offices in the Lodge and in
1923 held the highest office, that of Master. Following the installation
of his successor Bert was appointed Inspector of District No. 109. His
work was so outstanding that each succeeding Grand Master reappointed him, and he was most active until the last. The night of his death he
attended Normal Heights Lodge No. 632, where he installed his son,
Winfield Scott McLees, as Senior Warden.
- Branches of Masonry other than the Blue Lodge excited his interest
and he became a diligent worker in both the York and Scottish Rites.
He was Past High Priest of San Diego Chapter No. 61 Royal Arch
Masons. and Past Grand High Priest, Royal Arch Masons of California, and was coroneted a 33rd degree Mason December 18, 1943 by the
Supreme Council Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite of the Southern
Jurisdiction of the United States, Past Potentate Al Bahr T~mple, Order of the Mystic Shrine, and a charter member and organizer of the
Royal Order of Jesters, and recorder of San Diego Conclave No. 62,
Red Cross of Constantine.

229

Other civic and fraternal organizations received his support. He was
a member of the Fraternal Order of Eagles, Aerie No. 244: Benevolent
and Protective Order of Elks No. 168, Knights of Pythias. In civic
activities he was a member of the San Diego Club, Chamber of Commerce. and the San Diego Advertising Club.
The attendance at his funeral was one of the largest of any similar
gathering in the history of San Diego County. The Masonic service
was conducted by Past Grand Master Claude Morrison, and was followed by cremation.
_
In the passing of Bert McLees California Masonry has lost one of its
greatest and most beloved members, and the city of San Diego has lost
a citizen who was a vigorous foe to monopoly, an immense force for good
government, and a clear thinking defender of liberty under law.
SIDNEY KRAMER LEHMAN

\

Friendships are acquired in many different ways-business, college,
aocial contacts, and in military service, but none are more lasting nor
more binding than those made in the unselfish service of love and devotion to the interests of Free Masonry where men of like thoughts,
like interests and similar goals, combine their efforts and without thought
of personal gain or self-aggrandisement work for the accomplishment
of an ideal world. It was Sidney Lehman's unswerving belief in these
tenets of Masonry and his efforts in their behalf that endeared him to
men in every part of this Grand Jurisdiction. Sidney Lehman's record is
a pattern for those who would contribute more to making this a better
world for good men, gentle women and little children to live in. There
is no event in his life story that shows where any person was injured or
caused to shed a tear because of any act of his.
As a Master of his Lodge, as an Inspector, and as Assistant Grand
Lecturer he gave of his time and of his substance that the pathway of
others in this uncertain and troubled world might be made smoother.
One of the happiest events of Sidney's life occurred on the evening
of June 2, 1947, in Los Angeles Lodge No. 42. At that meeting Sidney
raised his son, Sidney Jr. to the sublime degree of Master Mason. Each
station was occupied by an Inspector of the Los Angeles area. Following
the degree he addressed the gathering, and the understandable emotion
of his fatherly feelings was communicated to all present, and there
were few dry eyes among the brethren.
He answered the final call April 12, 1948 at his home in Beverly
Hills. His death came suddenly and unexpectedly. He is mourned by
untold numbers of friends both in and out of Masonry. A more fitting
tribute will be paid to his memory later this morning by the Most
Worshipful Leslie E. Wood, Past Grand Master, who will deliver a
special eulogy to this splendid character.

FRANKLIN DAY CALDWELL

became most active, serving as Venerable Master of the Lodge of Perfection, Wise Master Chapter Rose Croix, Commander Council of
Kadosh, and Master of Kadosh of the Consistory. In 1919 he was
coroneted a 33rd degree Inspector General Honorary by the Supreme
Council of the Scottish Rite of the Southern Jurisdiction of the United
States. He was also a member of Islam Temple of the Mystic Shrine,
and for many years secretary of the Board of Directors of the Shriner's
Hospital for crippled children in San Francisco.

After a lingering illness death relieved the suffering of Franklin
Day Caldwell on August 22, 1947, in Artesia, California.
Franklin Caldwell, son of Boyd E. and Elizabeth Caldwell, was
born September 20, 1881, at Mount Pleasant, Iowa. In 1889 the family
moved to Central City, Nebraska, where he received his education,
specializing in agriculture. Believing that his talents could be put to more
productive use in the fertile valleys of Southern California he moved
in 1913 to the southeastern section of Los Angeles County. For many
years he operated farms in that area. When his health began to fail he
transferred his activities to lighter work, and became associated with
the Los Angeles County Board of Education. He served as Custodian
of the Union High Schools at both Norwalk and Artesia, until illness
forced his retirement in 1945.
His Masonic light began in Lone Tree Lodge No. 36, Central City,
Nebraska. On July 17, 1913 he was received by dimit into Artesia Lodge
No. 377 at Artesia, California, and was elected and served that lodge
as Master in 1919. Following his retirement as Master he was appointed
Inspector of District No. 95, at a time when Lodges in that area were
few and far apart. The District covered most of that section of Los
Angeles County and also included the town of Whittier.
Franklin Caldwell was a loyal and faithful worker, greatly loved
and admired. His death leaves a vacancy in the hearts of his brethren.
ARTHUR M. JoEL

The Great Architect of the Universe has in his infinite wisdom seen
fit to call from our midst another of our beloved brethren, Arthur M.
Joel. Arthur was born in the City of San Francisco July 25, 1882, educated in the public schools of that city, attending Hastings Law School
for two years, and finished his legal education at Stanford University.
At the outbreak of hostilities in 1898 he enlisted in the United States
Navy that he might do his share in defending his country in the war
against Spain. He served as an officer aboard the U.S. Transport Sumner. seeing action in the Far East. At the close of the war he returned
to his native city and spent the balance of his life in civilian activities.
His Masonic career began in Doric Lodge No. 216 in San Francisco,
but in 1918 he dimitted to become a charter member and first Master of
Lincoln Lodge No. 470. He was appointed Inspector of District No.
48-A in 1919 and served in that responsible position untin 931. In 1935
he was reappointed and served faithfully until his death.
He was captivated by the great moral teachings of the Scottish Rite
of Freemasonry, and immediately after his initiation in those Bodies he

devoted friend, a true Mason. The Fraternity mourns his loss. We
commend his soul to Almighty God, and comfort ourselves in the knowledge that he is happier in his Father's house.
EZRA

w. DECOTO

Ezra William Decato, former Grand Orator of the Grand Lodge of
California, died August 6, 1948. He was 72 years of age.
Son of Ezra and Janet Lowrie Decato, he was ·b orn at Decato,
Alameda County, California, February 6, 1876. His education was obtained in the vicinity in which he was born. After graduating from the
Decato Grammar School and the Centerville HitJh School, he attended
the University of California graduating in 1900 with a Ph. B. degree.
Then followed two years in Hastings Law School from which he graduated with a B. L. degree. He was admitted to the Bar in 1902.
He began the practice of law in association with J. B. Richardson in
the City of Oakland. From 1906 to 1918 he served as Prosecuting Attorney, City of Oakland, was District Attorney for Alameda County
from 1918 to 1925. In 1925 he became a member of the California Railroad Commission, served as its President in 1929, an'd re-entered priVate
practice in 1930. Governor Earl Warren appointed him Judge of the
Superior Court in 1943 where he served in the Juvenile and Civil courts
until his passing. As a member of the Alameda County Bar and the
State Bar Association he was one of their most highly regarded aiid
respected members.
Brother Decato served Masonry well. He was Master of Live Oak
Lodge No. 61, F.&A.M. of Oakland in 1915; a 33rd degree Honorary
of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite, receiving the honor December 2, 1947; Potentate of AAmes Temple of the Shrine in 1928. He was
also very active in the Benevolent and Protective Order of Elks, and
was Exalted Ruler of the Oakland Lodge in 1915.
Brother Decato is survived by his widow, Gladys Girard Decato, two
daughters, Mrs. James Nordahl, and Mrs. Webster Jessup, also four
grandchildren.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

His passing is deeply regretted. His work in Masonry is his monument. He will be remembered long and favorably by this Grand Lodge.
' Man's belief in the immortality of the soul. his constant struggle
for the light above, and his continual effort to withstand the trials. tribulations and vexations of life, are all influenced to a large extent by his
religious experience.
From the dawn of history the religions of the world have been roughly divided into two groups-those founded by persons of strong spiritual
convictions, and the so-called leaderless religions. The leaderless religions comprise the' Egyptian, Babylonian and Assyrian, Hindu, Greek,
Roman, Shinto, and others, and most remain far behind the path of
progress. These leaderless religions were the least ethical and most
immoral. holding firmly to animism or nature worship. A few reached
the next stage, polytheism. Their prayers were principally incantation
and divination. When things went wrong incantation was used to set
them right. When it was feared that evil was approaching divination
was used to keep it away. Their principal desire was safety and security
in this world.
Most of us are follow~rs of the two great ethical religions, Christianity and Judaism, which were founded by the greatest religious teachers
the world has ever known, Jesus of Nazareth, and Moses of the Hebrews. Their tea<'.hings were predicated upon the fatherhood of God and
the brotherhood of man.
These ethical religions do not lay great stress upon security in this
life, but emphasize mans responsibility to his God and his obligations
to his fellow creatures; that man by his own acts is responsible for most
of the suffering and unhappiness of humanity; that man's spiritual
strength is within himself, and the individual conquering of anger,
hatred, intolerance, envy. greed and covetousness, should be his highest
goal. In the Book of Proverbs we read: "He that is slow to anger is
better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than 'he that taketh a
city." By this mastery of self and he love of God he need have no fear
of the world to come.
Our departed brethren have dedicated their lives and actions to the
beliefs of the great ethical religions, and in so doing have left the world
better because of their having passed this way. Their influence rests
upon us and their examples guide our ways. We will see them here no
more but it will not be long, "and the wisest know not how soon" when
we shall greet them in our Father's house for they are not far away.
As the poet Robert Freeman has said: "They are in the other room":

To a bigger, brighter room?

Shall I sit enswathed in gloom,
When I know my love is happy,
Waiting in the other room?"

SIDNEY KRAMER LEHMAN
by .Leslie E. Wood, Past Grand Master
It is fitting that, amidst the rejoicing and recounting the blessings of
the year just closing that we pause in our labors to testify our regard and
sincere affection for a brother who has laid aside the working tools of
the. craft, and to pay a tribute to his fine character as a man and as a
Mason.
Were it not for our belief in the immortality of the soul. and the
knowledge that death is not the end of life, there would be nothing to
allay our fears of death or to assuage our sorrow, but we realize that
death is but the drawing of a curtain, the extinguishing of a light and the
preparation for a fuller and better existence, where there shall be no
more death, neither shall there be sorrow or pain, but only peace and
life everlasting.
Sidney Kramer Lehman was a native Californian, having been born
May 19, 1889 in the city of San Bernardino, where he attended the public schools. At the age of 17 years he moved to Los Angeles where he
resided the balance of his life. After attending business college, he
started his business career with the Los Angeles Gas and Electric Company. Twelve years later we find that he was in the wholesale electric
business for himself. In 1929 he entered the insurance field as Agency
Supervisor for the Guardian Life Insurance Company and continued
in that capacity until 1942 when he opened offices as an insurance
broker, which business he conducted until his death on April 12, 1948.
On March 22, 1916 he was united in marriage to Elizabeth Cohen
in the city of San Francisco and two fine sons were born of this union,
Sidney Kramer, Jr., and John Malcolm.
Brother Lehman's masonic career began October 14, 1912, when he
was initiated an Entered Apprentice Mason in Los Angeles Lodge No.
42. He was raised to the sublime Degree of Master Mason on November 18, 1912. Two years later he was given his first appointment as
Junior Steward and progressed through the several stations to that of
Worshipful Master in 1918. In 1921 he was appointed Inspector and
served his district with distinction until 1934. He was appointed Senior
Grand Deacon of this Grand Lodge in October 1933 and served until
October 1934.
After the death of Very Worshipful Thomas J. Baker, Grand Lecturer in 1934, it was the decision of the Grand Master, Most Worshipful James Black Gist, to try out a new system of teaching the ritual and
brother Lehman was chosen as Assistant Grand Lecturer for the southern district of the jurisdiction. On being requested to accept this appointment he asked the Grand Master if the position carried a salary
and when told that it did not, he replied that he would accept. His long

235

Sidney Lehman has passed beyond our sight, as we too shall pass;
but he has left with those who knew and loved him a cherished memory
that will live on through the years. His warm friendship, his cheerful
smile and his genuine good fellowship will be remembered and few wiU
forget his many virtues, particularly that of never saying an unkind
word about another. Others will take his place in Grand Lodge and time
will heal the sorrow of his passing, but as long as memory remains, we
will remember him as a loving husband, a proud father, a true and faithful friend and an ardent Mason, who believed in the teachings of our
institution and lived according to its principles.

l

Sid., we shall miss you: but we part with abfding faith in the hereafter and the firm belief that there is a life after death. We pray that
you may be happy in that Celestial Lodge above and that, when our appointed time shaII come, we may again clasp hands in a continuance of
that brotherhood and fraternal love we cherished. We know that life
goes on beyond this existence and that, like the flower that withers and
dies, it will spring to newness of life with the coming of the spring, as
best expressed in the words of the poet when he spoke of the rose:
"Onward it crept with towering strength
With never a thought of fear and pride,
Until it reached the light in the crevice length
And unfolded itself on the other side.
The light, the dew, the broadening view,
Were just the same as they were before,
But it lost itself in beauties new,
Breathing its fragrance more and more.
Shall claim of death cause us to grieve
And make our courage faint and fall,
Nay! Let us hope and faith receive,
The rose still grows beyond the wall.
Scattering fragrance here and there,
Just as it did in days of yore,
Just as it did on the other side,
Just as it will for ever more."

Distinguished Guests

8TEREOPTICON EQUIPMENT

Three distinguished guests-John I. Preissner, Past Grand Master
and Grand Secretary of Washington, 0. C. Hagmeier, Past Grand
Master of Oregon, and C. G. Patterson, Past Grand Master of Oregon,
were received by Grand Lodge and escorted to places in the East.

There has been referred to the Committee on Ritual the following
resolution:
"Whereas, the Most Worshipful Grand Master of Free and
Accepted Masons of the State of California has issued an order
to all Masonic Lodges under his jurisdiction prohibiting the use
of stereopticon equipment in connection with the Lodge degree
work: and

Most Worshipful Lloyd K. McRae, Grand Master of Masons in
Oregon, was invited to address Grand Lodge which he did with great
interest to the Brethren, laying particular emphasis on the high standard
of our Masonic Home which he had visited.

"Whereas, after due and proper consideration the members
of Oceanside Lodge Number 381 Free and Accepted Masons
of the State of California have concluded that the use of said
equipment is of value not only to those who are now members of
the Fraternity but also of great and distinctive value to those who
are receiving their first steps in Masonry: now therefore

Most Worshipful John I. Preissner, Past Grand Master and Grand
Secretary of the Grand Lodge of Washington, and official representative of M. W. Delos Shiner, Grand Master of Masons in Washington,
at the invitation of the Grand Master addressed Grand Lodge, and his
remarks were received wtih enthusiasm.

Be It Resolved, That the Worshipful Grand Master be and
is hereby respectfully requested to reconsider his order prohibiting the use of stereopticon equipment and that said order be
recinded."

Report of Ritual Committee
OFFICERS' COACH

There has been referred to the Committee on Ritual the resolution
of Brother Joseph F. Hogan proposing that Section 53, Subsection 3-A
be amended to read as follows:

Your Committee wishes to point out that the manufacture, possession or use of stereopticon slides or any other medium which portrays
visually the esoteric work of the degrees of Masonry is a violation of
Masonic obligations.

"To appoint in each Lodge within his District an Officers'
Coach, who shall be a qualified Past Master of the Lodge, and
who shall be acceptable to the Officers thereof. The Officers'
Coach shall serve at the pleasure of the Inspector and shall assist
in teaching the ritual to the Officers of his Lodge, and assist in
preparing them to qualify for advancement."
The effect of this proposed amendment will be to provide that the
selection by the Inspector of an Officers' Coach shall be limited to one
who will be acceptable to the Officers of the Lodge.

We therefore recommend that the aforesaid resolution be not
adopted.
Adopted.
MASONIC INFORMATION BOOKLETS

The Committee on Ritual has made a hurried examination of the
proposed booklets prepared by the Committee on Information covering
the Second and Third Degrees. This report was placed in our hands on
Wednesday afternoon of this week.

With this proposal your Committee is not in agreement. From long
association with, and observation of, men who become Past Masters
of Lodges, the Inspector is the best qualified individual to select the
Officers' Coach.

The material contained therein is too complex and voluminous to
permit a careful study during this Communication. We recommend that
copies be furnished to each member of the Ritual Committee, who will
made a careful examination and thereafter report to the Grand Master.

Experience proves that too much difficulty is encountered in arriving
at an agreement among a group of men. It too often results in a compromise which fails to select the best qualified.

Respectfully submitted,
ARTHUR M. WARREN
MERVYN E. HANSHAW
WALTER H. E. VONKONSKY
OBED
CARR

We feel that no limitation should be placed upon the Inspector in
the discharge of this important function.
We therefore recommend that the proposed amendment be not
adopted.
Adopted.

FRANK HARWELL, JR.

The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes respectfully submits the following report on subjects submitted to it for consideration
and recommendation:
RECOGNITION OF FOREIGN GRAND LoDGES

Tests of Recognition
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has been guided
by the tests for extending fraternal relations to other Grand Bodies
provided for by the resolution of Grand Lodge set out in the Proceedings
of 1913 at page 163 and the Proceedings of 1918 at page 159. The
Grand Lodge applying for recognition must show to this Grand Lodge
that it complies with the following requirements:
1. A belief in God.
2. That the Three Great Lights of Masonry, the Bible, the Square
and the Compasses shall always be on the altar of the Grand Lodge
and its subordinates when at work.
3. Secrecy.
4. That men only shall be admitted to membership.
5. That the Grand Lodge shall be independent of any other body or
bodies and shall be the sovereign and supreme authority over the three
symbolic degrees and shall exercise undisputed control over its constituent lodges.
6. That it teaches the Third Degree Legend.
7. That such Grand Lodge shall have been lawfully authorized by
three or more regularly constituted Lodges. '
8. That the ancient landmarks, customs and usages of the Craft shall
be strictly observed.
9. That no such Grand Lodge shall engage in religious or political
controversy and shall not tolerate a discussion of either in the Grand
Lodge or Lodges of its obedience.
We find, after due investigation, that the following Grand Lodges
are entitled to recognition: The Grand Lodge Unida Mexicana, the
Grand Lodge Francisco de Paula Santander, the Grand Lodge of the
State of Ceara, the Grand Symbolic Lodge of Rio Grande do Sul and the
Grand Lodge of Finland.
I.
GRAND LoDGE liNIDA MEXICANA

The Grand Lodge Unida Mexicana located in the State of Vera
Cruz, Republic of Mexico, and having its seat at Vera Cruz, is sovereign and independent and belongs to the Confederation composed of

II.
GRAND LoDGE FRANCISCO DE PAULA SANTANDER

The Grand Lodge Francisco de Paula Santander is seated at Cucuta,
Colombia. It is situated in the eastern part of Colombia, which is a cattle
country containing the head-waters of the Jungle rivers of South
America. We recognize the other three Grand Lodges domiciled in the
Republic of Colombia and this fourth Grand Lodge has recently been
organized and is asking for our recognition. The reason for the four
Grand Lodges in the Republic of Colombia is that the Andes Mountains
make great barriers, difficult to cross, between the valley sections in
which the Grand Lodges are situated. It is an unusual situation and
warrants the establishment of these several Grand Lodges. The National Grand Lodge of Colombia, which is recognized by us, changed
its Constitution to make it permissible for this Grand Lodge to be established as a Soreveign Grand Lodge with the consent of at least three
regularly constituted G~and Lodges. The newly created Grand Lodge
is now recognized by the Grand Lodge of the Republic at Bogata, the
National Grand Lodge at Cartagena and the National Grand Lodge
of Berranquilla, all of Colombia, and all recognized by us. The new
Grand Lodge occupies a territory comprising the States of Santander
and North Santander, which was ceded to it by the National Grand
Lodge of Barranquilla. One of the subordinates of the new Grand Lodge
works in the English language.
Roberto Ardila Ordonez is the Grand Master and Allan R. Corinaldi is Grand Secretary.
Your Committee recommends that the Grand Lodge of California
recognize the Grand Lodge of Francisco de Paula Santander.

III.
GRAND LoDGE OF THE STATE OF CEARA

The Grand Lodge of the State of Ceara, Brazil, was founded in
March 1928 by three lodges and it holds jurisdiction over the State of
Ceara, having its seat at Fortaleza, the capital of the State of Ceara.
It is situated south of the Amazon River and north of the State of Bahia
and is in the Tropics. It is presently composed of eighteen lodges, six
of them in Fortaleza and twelve in the several towns in the interior and
stands upon the same basis as the seven State Grand Lodges in Brazil

which are now recognized by the Grand Lodge of California. This
Grand Lodge is recognized by the Grand Lodges of New York, Louisi~

Julia Viana de Silva Tavares is the Grand Master and Luis Nepomu~
cano de Mattos is the Grand Secretary.
Your committee recommends that the Grand Lodge of California
recognize the Grand Lodge of the State of Ceara.

Your committee has applications for recognition from other Grand

Your committee has considered the application of the Syrian-Lebanese Grand Lodge .for recognition, but has not completed its investigation and recommends that the same await a more settled religious
and political condition in Syria, The Lebanon and Palestine.
We have before us a request for recognition of Grosse Freimaurerloge, Zuden Alten Pflichten, whose Orient is Berlin and which claims
to be descended from the Hamburg Grand Lodge, from which we have
not withdrawn our recognition, but with whom we have not had fraternal intercourse for several years, due to the war.
The petitioning Lodge has been established by eight of the Lodges
of the Grand Lodge of Hamburg, which were reorganized in 1946.
The representations made to your committee lead us to feel that we
would be justified in recognizing this Grand Lodge when the political
and social conditions are more settled in Germany. Your committee
therefore recommends that action on the application be postponed until
.
the next annual communication of Grand Lodge.
The situation in Italy, social. political and Masonic, is so confused
that the applications from the Grand Lodges claiming to represent Masonry in that country should be postponed until the codintions become
more stable and we are better able to choose from the contenders for
Masonic recognition.

IV.
GRAND SYMBOLIC LoDGE OF RIO GRANDE DO SUL

This Grand Lodge is the only Masonic power recognized in the
State of Rio Grande do Sul, which is a vast area in the southwest part of
Brazil. It is in the Temperate Zone, with climate much like the border- .
ing States of Argentina and Uruguay.
This Grand Lodge was organized in 1927 and has adopted the
principles and usages of the Craft as set for the in the Constitution
adopted by the United Grand Lodge of England in 1723. It does not invade the jurisdiction of any other Masonic power. It has the same status
as the other State Grand Lodges of Brazil. of which number we already
recognize seven.
Dr. Cezar Bomhgahren is the Grand Master and Jonas H. Py is ·
Secretary of Foreign Relations. The Grand Lodge has its seat at Porto
Alegre.
Your committee therefore recommends that the Grand Lodge of California recognize the Grand Symbolic Lodge of Rio Grande do Sul.

v.
GRAND LoDGE OF FINLAND

After many hardships during the past war years, the Grand Lodge of
Finland has been able to revive Masonic work in Finland, which it is
carrying on energetically in that borderland between East and West.
The first recognition of the Grand Lodge of Finland was granted by the
Grand Lodge of New York in May, 1924. The Constitution, practices
and principles of the Grand Lodge of Finland are based upon the Constitution of the Grand Lodge of New York and is practically the same.
The regulations, definitions and rules of order of the Grand Lodge of
New York are followed almost to the letter and the landmarks, old
charges and ritual are in strict conformity with those u~ed in the Grand
Lodge of New York. It is composed of three local Blue Lodges working
in Helsinki, one in Tampere, one in Turku and one in Pori.
The gallant Masons of Finland have made a brave fight for their
country and their Masonry and are recognized by the United Grand
Lodge of England, the Grand Lodges of Scotland, Ireland, The Netherlands, North Carolina, New York, Missouri, Kentucky and others.

GEORGE WASHINGTON MASONIC NATIONAL MEMORIAL

Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes, to which was
referred the report of the Special Committee on George Washington
Masonic Memorial. beg leave to report:
The Committee commends the effort of the Grand Master to bring
to completion that memorial and is in hearty accord with recommendation of the Committee to seek an amendment of the articles of incorporation of the Memorial Association to include the allied grand bodies of
Masonry as members of that Association.
A reading of the report indicates that much of the reform in the
structure and operation of the Memorial Association recommended by
this Grand Lodge at the 1947 Communication has been accomplished.
We therefor recommend that the l 5c per capita assessment be continued and that the requirement that each newly raised Master Mason
contribute the sum of One Dollar to the Endowment Fund of the

George Washington Masonic National Memorial be continued until
that endowment is completed. We further recommend that the officers
of this Grand Lodge invested with authority to act, do give careful
consideration as to whether it would now be advisable to release all or
part of the impounded funds which have been accumulated and set aside
for the construction of a Memorial.
Adopted.
OPEN INSTALLATIONS

Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has had under
consideration a communication from Brother John Isola, Past Master
of Speranza Italiana Lodge No. 219 submitting a "Motion" that Grand
Lodge forbid public installations. ·
Brother Isola, in support of his Motion, recites as follows: "I have
visited some Lodges which have had Public Installations. More or less
some errors have been made. For instance, in one particular Lodge I
saw two members give the Third Degree sign, and one of these was a
Past Master."
Your Committee recognizes that the giving of degree signs by a
careless or impulsive brother under the circumstances recited is most
regrettable, but bdieves sue~ occurences are extremely rare.
·
The holding of public installations is favored by a large number of
Lodges, giving much pleasure and satisfaction not only to officers and
members but also to their families and friends. These Lodges, your
Committee, is confident, would be loath to dispense with such ceremonials and we find no sufficient justification for requiring them to do so.
We therefore recommend that Brother lsola's Motion be rejected.
Adopted.

MASONIC INFORMATION BOOKLETS

Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes to which was
referred the report of the Committee on Masonic Information has given
the same its consideration and begs leave to report that it has read the
booklets prepared by that Committee for presentation to the candidates

256

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

at the conclusion of the conferring of the Fellow Craft and Master
Mason degree and find them to be of the same high character and educational value found in the two previous booklets prepared by the Committee.
Your Committee of Policy and General Purposes is of the opinion
that the work of the Committee on Masonic Education is of the highest
value to the Craft, and that we should make every effort to avail ourselves of its benefits.
Your Committee is informed that some Lodges have not taken
advantage of the opportunity thus afforded them to furnish their candidates with this fundamental knowledge of Masonry. We think that this
is a decided detriment to the Craft.
Probably at no time in the life of a man elected to receive the degrees
of Masonry will he be so receptive of efforts to inform him of the
institution as at the time of his receiving the degrees. Possibly some
candidates will never have any interest in Masonry beyond receiving
its degrees and participating in its social activities. On the other hand,
the great majority will seek further knowledge of the institution and
your Committee believes that these booklets will open the eyes of the
candidate to the wide field before him for further search and investigation.
Your Committee therefore recommends to Grand Lodge the publication of the "Book of the Fellowcraft" and the "Book of the Master
Mason" the texts of which have been submitted by the Committee on
Masonic Information, and we further recommend that the Lodges of
this Jurisdiction be required to present to each of its candidates at the
proper period in their progress as candidates, a copy of each of the four
booklets prepared by that Committee.
Adopted.
TWENTY-FIVE YEAR BUTTONS

Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes, to which was
referred the resolution offered by Pasadena Lodge No. 272, requesting
Grand Lodge to consider the feasibility of issuing 25-year buttons to
those Masons in this Jurisdiction who have been members of the fraternity for twenty-five years, has given the same consideration.
We think the word "feasibility" is not perhaps the most apt word
or the one conveying the exact intended meaning. We assume that
it would be desirable.
We now issue a 50-year button. There is much dignity and considerable honor attached to this decoration by those who have received
it. It comes to them at a period in life when hope of further honors as

(

257

the result of further personal effort is usually absent. It comes to those
who may have been honored by the gift of office in the fraternity and
it comes likewise to those who have never held office but by their long
attachment to the principles and the institution of Masonry have by
such fealty demonstrated their forthiness to receive this decoration.
The issuance of 25-year buttons would, we think, have none of these
reasons for justification and we further think such issue would cheapen
an emblem now issued to our veterans and to which the fraternity should
and does look with honor and reverence.
Adopted.

GRAND LODGE INCORPORATION
GRAND LODGE LEGAL REPRESENTATION

Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes to which was
referred, jointly with the Jurisprudence Committee, the Resolution
offered by M.W. Arthur W. Brouillet of the Jurisdiction Committee,
which resolution is divided into three parts, the first two of which deal
with the incorporation of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge as a legal
eutity under the Corporation Code of California as a non profit corporation and the third part with a participation in certain litigation now
pending in our civil courts, has had the same under consideration and
beg leave to report as follows:
Regarding the incorporation of this Grand Lodge, this Committee
is of the firm opinion that "The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of
Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California" organized in
strict accord with Masonic usage and legally existing in accordance with
the civil law of our State of California, possessed of a seal, and composed of nearly six hundred constituent Lodges and acting through their
representatives in Grand Lodge assembled, and represented by its
Grand Master and other officers, for, now, almost one hundred years,
is a duly constituted voluntary association of ancient and recognized
form existing in conformity to civil law and will be protected by the
codes of our civil law and by the rules of equity in the exclusive use
of that name as against appropriat~on by any organization, body politic
group or association clandestine or otherwise, in the use of the name
"The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of
the State of California". or of any name of similar words import or

258

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

implication, should an attempt be made to invade our right to the
exclusive use of the name we are amply protected in its use even to the
exdusion of an incorporated company that assumed to use the same.
The basis upon which this considered opinion is expressed lies in technical legal and equitable principles, which to any lawyer, are well known
and which to here incorporate would run this report to an unconscionable length and which if so expressed would be only confusing and
unintelligible to the layman.
We recommend that Grand Lodge do not incorporate itself either
in the manner proposed by the resolution or otherwise.
The third paragraph of that resolution proposes that Grand Lodge
shall engage lawyers and authorize them to appear in an action already
pending between two clandestine bodies claiming to be Masons, and
there file briefs as amici curiae ( friends of the court) and to make the
point that we are possessed of a prior right. There always remains the
possibility of an adverse decision and that perchance at some later date
we might be confronted with the statement that our right~ had been
adjudicated and that too, in a matter in which we are not rightly con~
cerned.
lrrespecive of whether the "Sons of Light" or " Hiram of Tyre" may
be successful in the pending litigation we are in nowise bound by that
litigation, and your Committee are of the opinion that is the wiser way
to leave it.
We therefore recommend that this part of the resolution be not
adopted.
Separate action was taken on each portion of the report and each
recommendation of the Committee was adopted.

GROUP DEGREES

Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes, to which has been
referred the resolution of Brother Henry H. Brown, Past Master of
Warren G. Harding Lodge No. 579, in which he proposes that the
Ritual Committee be instructed to modify the ritual to permit the initiation, passing and raising of candidates in groups of not to exceed .6ve
in the first and second section of the three degrees, begs leave to report
as follows:
We appreciate what the brother has in mind, but are of the opinion
that the conferring of degrees upon a class of candidates would not
accomplish the result he desires, that of increasing attendance and interest in degree meetings. We feel that every candidate who has been
found worthy to be elected into the fr~ternity is entitled to receive all
the light that can be conferred upon him personally and not as just a
member of a class. We feel that if this proposal were adopted, many
candidates would fail to receive the full value of the lessons we are
desirous of imparting.
We therefore offer the following recommendation and move its
adoption:
That the resolution of Brother Henry H. Brown, proposing that
our ritual be changed or modified to permit the conferring of the degrees
upon more than one candidate at the same time be not approved.
Adopted.

RELIEF OF LODGES

Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has carefully considered that portion of the Grand Master's Message recommending
that Grand Lodge extend a generous hand to North East Lodge No.

260

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

266 and Georgetown Lodge No. 25, to assist them in the rebuilding of
their Temples, which were destroyed by fire.
Your Committee feels that it should not become an established
policy of this Grand Lodge to loan or contribute its funds to constituent
Lodge. however worthy the cause may be.
If relief and charity are attributes of Masonry and it is obligatory
upon Masons to relieve d~stress among their brethren, so f~r as they
are able to do so, it naturally follows that it should also be mcumbent
upon Lodges to help other Lodges that have come upon evil days.
Section 126 of the Ordinances of Grand Lodge permits a Lodge to
solicit assistance from other Lodges, if granted permission to do so.
by the Grand Master.
Sections 157, 158 and 159, Ross Digest, enumerate the purposes for
which Lodge funds may be used and because it does not in~lu~e contributions to other Lodges, it has been correctly held that this is not a
proper use of Lodge funds.
We cannot believe that the brethren of this Jurisdiction are willing
to stand by and see some of the smaller and older Lodges cease to exist
because they have no place to meet. Masons have always answered the
call of the distressed and have never refused to extend a helping hand
to the needy within their ranks. Masonic Lodges should have the same
privilege.
We therefore offer the following recommendation and move its
adoption:
.
·
.
That a Lodge be permitted to contribute from its funds to the rehef
of other Lodges of this Jurisdiction, such amounts as it may deem
proper. if the request for assistance has been approved by the Grand
Master.

RESIDENCE REQUIREMENT REDUCTION

There has been referred to your Committee on Policy and General
Purposes a resolution by Brother Herbert R. Hargrave, Past Master
of Sun Garden Lodge No. 530, proposing that our Law regarding the
conferring of courtesy degrees on Entered Apprentice Masons and
Fellowcraft Masons of other Jurisdictions. which requires as a prerequisite twelve months residence in California, be changed to require
only six months residence.
Consideration has bttn given to the fact that these brethren from
other Jurisdictions may possess all the necessary qualifications to receive
the degrees of Masonry in California. But we cannot consider the
proposal favorably because we believe that six months would be too
short a time for us to ascertain this as a fact and to become acquainted
with these brethren. Moreover. there is apparently no need for rush,
after only Six months residence in California, in putting these brethren
through the degrees, nor for these brethren to make up their minds that
they wish to have their degrtts conferred upon them in California.
Experience has shown that one year at least is required to make sure
that an applicant meets our Masonic standards.
We therefore recommend that the resolution be not adopted.
Adopted.
GRAND LODGE MAGAZINE

..,

There has been referred to your Committee on Policy and General
Purposes the report of the Grand Lodge Magazine Committee proposing that Grand Lodge publish a regular bulletin for the information and
education of the members of its constituent Lodges. The Magazine
Committee recommended against the publication of a magazine by
Grand Lodge for the reasons that the successful publication of a
magazine would require excessive capital and personnel and would
depend on advertising. which might result in abuses. Your Committee
is of the opinion that the idea of a means of communication from
Grand Lodge to the Brethren is sound and should be fostered, but
that a regular bulletin such as proposed would be impracticable. Experience has shown that the time. energy and expense required to do
the job well is not warranted by any reader interest. Moreover, the
successful publication of such a bulletin at regular periods, as in the
case of a magazine, would require a staff of skilled editorial. composing,
news-gathering, and mailing personnel. This would present additional
and unnecessary problems. burdens and expense on Grand Lodge. not
justified by the results to be attained.
Furthermore, means of communication are now available which are
ample for the purpose. Regular communicationJ and Committee Reports
from Grand Lodge go forth to the Lodges. Visitations are made by

262

officers of Grand Lodge. The Committee on Correspondence gives to
the California Craft an annual resume of things Masonic which is most
complete and covers a wide field. ·
Your Committee therefore recommends that the proposal be not
adopted.
Adopted.

DECISIONS

Past Grand Master Hervey held (Digest Section 518) that an E. A.
or F. C. of a California Lodge cannot be granted a demit, and in the
event he desires to receive the remaining degrees and is unable to do so
in his Lodge, his Lodge may waive jurisdiction over him and permit him
to petition another Lodge for the remaining degrees.

I

Your Committee on Jurisprudence has carefully considered the
Decisions reported in the message of the Grand Master.
We recommend that Decisions numbered 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 9, 1O. 11,
12, as reported in the printed message of the Grand Master be approved.
Adopted.

J

The Grand Master held that a candidate that did not come forward
to take his Second and Third Degrees in Masonry stating the he was
"going away," was not entitled to the return of either his fees for the
second and third degrees or his contribution to the Masonic Home.
With this your Committee agrees.
The Grand Master further added that if the candidate moved from
the State, established a residence elsewhere, and asked for a waiver
of Jurisdiction to another Lodge, then Hornitos Lodge might properly
refund both the fees and contribution, if it granted the waiver.

be-

Section 173 of Ordinances sets forth the Rights of E. As. and F. Cs.
They are to sit in Lodge in which they received the degree or degrees
when open in a degree taken by them, and the right to advancement
therein after passing satisfactorily a strict examination in open Lodge.

It is the opinion of your Committee that the only way an E. A. or
F. C. of a California Lodge under our law can receive a degree or
degrees in a Lodge outside the Jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of
California is by courtesy. In every instance where "waiver of jurisdiction" is used tn our Ordinances regarding E. As. or F. Cs. it is confined to the Lodges in the State of California.
·
Your Committee therefore recommends that the ruling of the Grand
Master as to present return of fees and contributions be approved but
that his remarks regarding Waiver of Jurisdiction be. disapproved.
Adopted.
DECISION 6
The Grand Master states that in our Unity Lodge No. 368 a candidate received the E. A. degree. He then moved to and established a
domicile in Illinois and requested Courtesy Degrees to be conferred by a
Lodge in that State.

DECISION 5

When a profane petitions a Lodge in California he petitions for the
three degrees in Masonry. When he receives the E. A. degree in this
State he is subject to the Jurisdiction of his Lodge and can only receive
the F. C. and M. M. degrees by consent of his Lodge. When he
comes a M. M. in his Lodge he can take a demit or remain a member
of his Lodge as he chooses.

It is clear ·t hat in every case where the term is used the Lodge
retains jurisdiction over the E. A. or F. C. until he becomes a M. M.
This it would not be able to do if the term applied to Lodges not under
the control of" the Grand Lodge of California. It would have all the
effect of a demit if the term applied to Lodges outside the jurisdiction.

I
l

The Grand Master then states that pursuant to the Edict of Grand
Master Moore, dated January 11, 1947, California refused to make
the request. If the Grand Master means that he felt that the Edict issued
by Grand Master Moore governed the exercise of the discretion vested
in all Grand Masters in the matter of Courtesy Degrees, we think he
is in error. Grand Lodge held that the Edict issued by Grand Master
Moore was within his power to issue, but this ruling does not govern
the discretionary power of his successor. The discretion in such matter
is personal to each Grand Master. Anyway, the request was not made.
The issuance of a waiver of jurisdiction to enable a Chicago Lodge
to confer degrees on the candidate was error but, no use of such waiver
having been attempted, no harm was done. On Brother X's return to
California, none of the erroneous steps having caused any harm, the

INCORPORATION

The Grand Master recommends that our Ordinances be amended to
clearly show that a Lodge may use a Corporation for the ownership and
operation of its Temple. In this your Committee agrees.
The steps that our law has gone through in this respect may be of
interest to Grand Lodge.
On October 13, 1911, Grand Lodge adopted a new Constitution
which in addition to the theretofore existing Constitution incorporated
existing regulations and approved decisions. A new section numbered
87 on "Funds and Property" was included with the following explanatory note.
"The large number of decisions shows the necessity of a direct provision in the Constitution itself about Lodge Funds". Then follows citations of General Regulations and Decisions on the subject. One of the
Decisions cited is:
1878 p 420. Decisions by Grand Master G. M. Browne:
I am opposed to the incorporation of Lodges, believing the act to be
subversive of the principles of Masonic government and in opposition
to the prosperity of the Order. By it the State becomes paramount in
authority, annihilates and appellate jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge and
Grand Master, and subordinates the Masonic to the civil authorities. By
it a positive antagonism is arrayed against the self-management of the
internal affairs, and, in its ultimate, general, and permanent effects, the
Lodge would be less real, less stable, less solid. An independent corporation may be formed for the purpose of holding the title to real estate
or investing money, which would be controlled by the Courts, but no
Court ought to control the affairs of a Masonic Lodge.
Section 87 Funds and property-then adopted, in part, was as follows:
"A Lodge must retain the control of its own funds and property. It
cannot incorporate or intrust any of its funds or property to a corporation
formed within itself-except that its members may incorporate for the ·
purpose of erecting and maintaining a hall for its use, and incidentally
for rental purposes, and it may hold stock in such corporation".
The law thus stood until 1928 when ( Proc 1929 p 246) an amendment was recommended now covered by the last sentence of the present
section 155 of Ordinances. However, in amending section 87 of the
Constitution ( Proc 1928 p 284) to include the proposed amendment
the clause beginning "except that" was in the opinion of your present

Section 79. The Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California shall
be nine in number. The Deputy Grand Master, Senior Grand Warden
and Junior Grand Warden shall be Trustees ex-officio, the other six
Trustees shall be appointed by successive Grand Masters. The term
of appointive Trustees shall be three years from the close of the annual
communication of the Grand Lodge. Three appointive Trustees shall
be residents in the vicinity of the Home at Decoto and three shall be

residents in the vicinity of the Home at Covina. If a Trustee shall serve

AMENDMENT TO ARTICLE //, SECTION 3
Your Committee on Jurisprudence recommends that the Constitution of Grand Lodge be amended by adding to Article II, Section 3, the
words "an Assistant Grand Treasurer" following the words "a Grand
Orator" and preceding the words "an Assistant Grand Secretary".
Adopted by a 5/6 vote.
AMENDING ORDINANCES BY ADDING SECTION 41A
We further recommend that the Ordinances of Grand Lodge be
amended by adding thereto a new section to be designated Section 41 a
and entitled Assistant Grand Treasurer, the section to read as follows:
The Grand Treasurer may with the approval of the Grand Master,
appoint an Assistant Grand Treasurer, for whose official acts he shall
be responsible, and who shall be considered an appointed officer of the
Grand Lodge and who shall perform such duties as may be prescribed
by the Grand Treasurer.
Adopted by a 5/6 vote.
AMENDMENT TO ORDINANCES SECTION 72
Your Committee on Jurisprudence recommends that the Ordinances
of Grand Lodge be amended by eliminating Section 72 thereof.
Your Committee on Jurisprudence recommends that the Ordinances
of Grand Lodge be amended by striking from Section 70 line 4 the
words "on Accounts".
Adopted by a 5/6 vote.
AMENDMENT TO ORDINANCES-NEW SECTION 72
Your Committee on Jurisprudence recommends that the Ordinances
be amended by adding a new Sec~on to be known as Section 72 to read
as follows:
The Grand Master in consultation with the Grand Treasurer shall
designate a professional auditor whose duty it shall be to examine each
month such bills, claims and demands against the Grand Lodge as are

AMENDMENT TO ORDINANCES-SECTION 44-l 7TH

Report of Committee on Finance
The report of the Committee on Finance was presented by various
members of the committee as follows:
Relative to the Grand Secretary's Office and Grand Lodge Week
Activities Committee, by Robert G. Woll:
Relative to the Masonic Homes, the Memorial Temple, and the
Columbia Temple Restoration, by Ellsworth Barnett:
Relative to the Masonic Club Houses, Pay of Members, and the
George Washington Masonic National Memorial, by F. Wesley Davies:
Relative to the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund, ,by P. G. M.
Claude H. Morrison.
The remainder of the report was presented by the chairman P. G. M.
A'rthur S. Crites.
Each portion of the report was adopted separately, after which on
motion of the chairman, the report was adopted in its entirety, except
as per special action recorded at the end of the report.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Finance submits the following report:
AUDIT OP

ACCOUNTS

. Following precedent, your Committee has again employed Brother
Walter Parker to audit the accounting records of the Grand Treasurer,
Grand Secretary, Masonic Homes and the Endowment Fund.
The audit indicates that all receipts and disbursements have been
properly recorded and that all moneys and securities are on hand. A
copy of the report has been filed with the Grand Secretary. It will be
printed in the Annual Proceedings. The cost of the audit was, to the
Grand Lodge $250 and to the Masonic Homes $800.
PERMANENT MONTHLY AUDIT OP ACCOUNTS

The action of the Grand Lodge in voting to have the audit of the
Grand Secretary's and Grand Treasurer's accounts put on a monthly
basis has been referred to the Committee on Finance.
The Committee is heartily in favor of the procedure as voted upon.
The action came too late for the Committee to obtain any cost figures on
a monthly audit procedure, so no appropriation is suggested, but it is
the recommendation of your Committee that such expenditures, as will
be required to provide the monthly audit of the accounts of the Grand
Secretary and Grand Treasurer, be hereby authorized and that the
appropriation will be made at the next communication of Grand Lodge.

Your Committee on Finance recommends an appropriation of $7,000
to cover the traveling expenses of the Grand Master.

This Grand Lodge officer is again entitled to the commendation of
Grand Lodge for the able manner in which he is handling the manifold
financial transactions of Grand Lodge, the Masonic Homes, and the
Endowment Fund. The auditor's report indicates that all records are in
good order and all moneys and securities properly on hand.
The report of the Grand Treasurer indicates the extent of the
financial transactions to which he must give attention. As will be noted
by the report, the business of Grand Lodge has become big business.
Last session of Grand Lodge appropriated $1,200 for the use of the
Grand Treasurer in caring for the expenses of his office. Of this amount
$1,080 was required. For the coming year we recommend an appropriation of $1,200 with the understanding that should the Grand Treasurer
find this sum not sufficient to properly care for the expenses of this
office for the year, whatever additional amount he may find is needed
is to be considered appropriated.
REPORT OP GRAND SECRETARY

Your Committee on Finance each year looks with interest to the
report of the Grand Secretary and is pleased to note that a steady growth
is being made by Masonry in California.
The number of lodges in operation, as well as the total number of
members, indicates a healthy condition in our fraternity.
The Auditor's report indicates that all monies have been properly·
accounted for and apparently the finances and records of this office are
in good condition.
TRAVELING EXPENSES OP GRAND MASTER

This Committee again wishes to follow previously established precedent of encouraging the Grand Master to travel as extensively as he
finds it expedient to so do and expresses the thought that the visitations
of the Grand Master to all parts of the Jurisdiction are of distinctive
advantage to the Craft. The growth of the Jurisdiction makes additional
drafts upon the time of the Grand Master, both in administering the
affairs of Grand Lodge, as well as for visitations. Due to this growth
and these demands, it is difficult to determine what the requirements for
his expenses may be.
Your Committee has discussed with both the outgoing and the incoming Grand Masters the needs for the coming year. Basing its judgment upon these discussions, it is budgeting $7,000 for the purpose of
covering the Grand Master's expenses, with the understanding, however, that it is to be left to his good judgment to decide how much, if
any, additional he may consider necessary to expend in properly performing the duties of his office and that should the amount which is being

RETURN OP FUNDS BY THE MOST WORSHIPFUL CHESTER H. WARLOW

...l

It is the wish of your Committee on Finance to express to the Most
Worshipful Grand Master the appreciation of Grand Lodge for the
return to its treasury, out of the appropriation made to cover the necessary expenses of his office, the sum of $3,000. The Annual Message of
the Grand Master indicates some of the traveling which he has done
and the manifold duties performed. To have devoted the year to
Masonry as he has and to have been able to return $3,000 of the amount
allowed for expenses indicates the care exercised in the spending of
Grand Lodge funds. The Grand Master is also to be commended for
having maintained a careful record of expenditures. The Annual
Message of the Grand Master mentions the trip which he took to Cuba,
Yucatan, Guatemala and Mexico. This trip had in it good will value
for the Jurisdiction of California and yet no part of the expenses of this
trip was paid for from Grand Lodge funds.
GRAND MASTER'S STENOGRAPHIC SERVICE

For a number of years an allowance for stenographic services for
the Grand Master has been made. In order that the Grand Master may
properly perform the duties of his office, it is essential that he should
have the proper stenographic help. It is also entirely proper that Grand
Lodge should pay for such services.
For the year just closed the Grand Master was allowed $2,000 for
this purpose. It was found necessary to expend the entire amount.
In a discussion with the incoming Grand Master as to this needs for
an allowance for stenographic service during the coming year, it appears
probable that his requirements will be less than was required for the
year just closing and that the sum of $1,500 will suffice.
Your Committee therefore recommends an appropriation of $1,500
to care for stenographic help for the Grand Master during the coming
year.
PORTRAIT OP GRAND MASTER

It has been a long established policy of Grand Lodge to request each
retiring Grand Master to have his portrait painted so that it may be
included in the gallery of Past Grand Masters' portraits. We are sure
this Grand Lodge will want this pleasing custom continued.
Last year there was appropriated $500 for the purpose of having
painted the portrait of our then retiring Grand Master. This committee
has come to the conclusion that a satisfactory portrait cannot be had for

TRAVELING EXPENSES OP GRAND LECTURER AND ASSISTANTS

The regulations of Grand Lodge provide that the expenses of the
Grand Lecturer and his assistants, incurred in traveling and in their
efforts to maintain the excellence of the esoteric work of the Order, shall
be reimbursed to them. Last Grand Lodge appropriated $2.500 to cover
these expenses. Of this amount $2458.75 was expended.
The Grand Lecturer estimates that for this purpose for the coming
year $3,500 will be needed. Your Committee on Finance recommends
the appropiation of this sum.

PORTRAITS OF PRECEDING GRAND MASTERS

Each year this Committee has continued the appropriation for the
portraits of those past Grand Masters which have not been heretofore
included in the gallery.
During the year there have been added to the gallery portraits of
Past Grand Masters Claude H. Morrison, Frank M. Smith and John
R. Moore. Portraits of the following Past Grand Masters are still missing: Earl Warren, Gilbert C. DeForest and Arthur W. Brouillet.
In the opinion of this Committee there are three portraits in the
gallery of living Past Grand Masters that are not of sufficient likeness
and new portraits should be painted.
Your Committee on Finance therefore requests that these six Most
Worshipful Brothers have their portraits painted, bill for each to be in
an amount not to exceed $650.00 and when presented to the Grand Secretary to be paid by him and the portraits to be included in the gallery of
Past Grand Masters.

Grand Lodge regulations provide that the expenses of the Inspectors
incurred in visiting the lodges under their Jurisdiction and under such
regulations as may be set up by the Grand Lecturer, shall be returned to
them out of the funds of Grand Lodge.
Attention is again called to the outstanding work which is being
performed by these Masonic servants and the great amount of time
and expense they are out, and particularly to the small amount of expense which is asked for. This past year the same record has been made
by this excellent corps of officers. If the full amount which, under Grand
Lodge regulations is coming to these Brothers for their outstanding
Masonic service, was asked for, it would have cost Grand Lodge approximately $8,000, instead of $3355.34, the amount which has actually been
paid out. A year ago the appropriation made by Grand Lodge to take
care of these expenses was $3,000.
In discussing with the Grand Lecturer the amount which he considers should be set up to cover the traveling expenses of the Inspectors,
he has suggested ·a n allowance for this purpose for the coming year
of $3,500.
Your Committee on Finance concurs in this recommendation of the
Grand Lecturer and, therefore, recommends the appropriation of $3,500
for this purpose, with the understanding that should requests for return
of expenses be made by the lnspectos, in accordance with the regulations established by the Grand Lecturer, in excess of this amount. the
full amount of such requests are to be paid, regardless of the amount
which is being appropriated for that purpose.
